citations.quote: The **standard partial flag of type $\alpha$** is $$W_\bullet^{(\alpha)}:\quad W_i:=V_{d_i}=\langle e_1,\dots,e_{d_i}\rangle, \qquad \dim_{\mathbb F_q}W_i=d_i,$$ and its members are standard coordinate subspaces

The **standard flag** of $V=\mathbb F_q^n$ is the chain $$V_0:=\{0\}\subsetneq V_1:=\langle e_1\rangle\subsetneq V_2:=\langle e_1,e_2\rangle\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq V_n:=\langle e_1,\dots,e_n\rangle=V,$$ whose members are the **standard coordinate subspaces**

**Permutation matrices and the monomial subgroup.** Let $n\ge1$, let $q$ be a
prime power, let $G=\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$ with diagonal torus $T$ and
standard flag $V_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq V_n$ as in
[[def-standard-subgroups-of-gl-n-over-a-finite-field]], and let
$S_n:=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ be the symmetric group of the set
$\{1,\dots,n\}$ ([[def-symmetric-group]], [[lem-symmetric-group-is-a-group]]),
so that permutations are composed as functions and an element $\sigma\in S_n$ is
written in one-line notation as the list $\sigma(1),\sigma(2),\dots,\sigma(n)$.

For $\sigma\in S_n$ the **permutation matrix** $P_\sigma\in G$ is the matrix with
$$(P_\sigma)_{ij}=\begin{cases}1,&i=\sigma(j),\\0,&i\ne\sigma(j),\end{cases}$$
that is, the $j$-th column of $P_\sigma$ is the standard basis vector
$e_{\sigma(j)}$, so that the $j$-th column has its unique entry $1$ in row
$\sigma(j)$. In particular $P_{\mathrm{id}}=I_n$, and multiplying matrices gives
$$P_\sigma P_\tau=P_{\sigma\circ\tau}\qquad(\sigma,\tau\in S_n),$$
because the $(i,k)$ entry of $P_\sigma P_\tau$ is $\sum_j(P_\sigma)_{ij}(P_\tau)_{jk}$,
which is $1$ exactly when $j=\tau(k)$ and $i=\sigma(j)=\sigma(\tau(k))$, and $0$
otherwise. A matrix $m\in G$ is **monomial** when every row and every column of
$m$ has exactly one nonzero entry. The **monomial subgroup** of $G$ is
$$N:=\{\,m\in G:m\text{ is monomial}\,\}.$$
Every $m\in N$ has a unique expression
$$m=t\,P_\sigma,\qquad t=\operatorname{diag}(t_1,\dots,t_n)\in T,\quad\sigma\in S_n,$$
namely with $\sigma(j)$ the row of the nonzero entry of column $j$ and
$t_{\sigma(j)}$ that entry; conversely $tP_\sigma$ is monomial with nonzero
entries $t_i$ in the rows and columns determined by $\sigma$. Consequently
$$N=T\cdot\{P_\sigma:\sigma\in S_n\}=\{P_\sigma t':\sigma\in S_n,\ t'\in T\},$$
since diagonal matrices may be moved across a permutation matrix.
$N$ is a subgroup of $G$: it contains $I_n=P_{\mathrm{id}}$, the product
$m m'$ of monomial matrices is monomial because the unique nonzero entry of each
column of $m'$ is transported to a unique nonzero entry of the corresponding
column of $mm'$, and the inverse of a monomial matrix is monomial since
permuting and rescaling rows and columns can be undone. Moreover $T\le N$ and
$T\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}N$.

**The Weyl group.** Define the **sign permutation** of a monomial matrix by
$$w:N\longrightarrow S_n,\qquad w(tP_\sigma):=\sigma,$$
which is well defined by the uniqueness of the decomposition. It is a group
homomorphism: if $m=tP_\sigma$ and $m'=t'P_\tau$, then
$t''':=P_\sigma t'P_\sigma^{-1}$ is diagonal, so
$mm'=t\,t'''\,P_\sigma P_\tau=t\,t'''\,P_{\sigma\tau}$ by
[[thm-matrix-multiplication-laws]], whence $w(mm')=\sigma\circ\tau=w(m)w(m')$.
Its kernel is exactly $T$, since $w(tP_\sigma)=\mathrm{id}$ says
$\sigma=\mathrm{id}$ and then $tP_{\mathrm{id}}=t$. Being a surjective
homomorphism, $w$ has kernel $T\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}N$ by
[[def-normal-subgroup]], and the induced map on cosets
$$W:=N/T\longrightarrow S_n,\qquad mT\longmapsto w(m),$$
is well defined (left multiplication by an element of $T=\ker w$ does not change
$w$) and is an isomorphism of groups, with inverse $\sigma\mapsto P_\sigma T$;
here $N/T$ is the quotient group of [[def-quotient-group]]. We call
$$W=N/T\cong S_n$$
the **(split) Weyl group** of $G$. Note that $W$ is defined as a quotient of the
monomial subgroup $N$ and **not** as the quotient $N_G(T)/T$ of the normaliser
of $T$ inside $G$: at $q=2$ the torus $T$ is trivial and $N_G(T)/T$ is all of
$G$, while $N/T\cong S_n$ still holds. For $\sigma\in S_n$ we write $w_\sigma$ for
the class of $P_\sigma$ in $W$, so that $w_\sigma w_\tau=w_{\sigma\tau}$ and the
isomorphism above sends $w_\sigma$ to $\sigma$; we write $1:=w_{\mathrm{id}}$
for the identity of $W$.

**Simple reflections.** For $1\le i<n$ let $s_i:=(i\ i+1)\in S_n$ be the
adjacent transposition of $i$ and $i+1$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), and put
$$\mathbf s_i:=w_{s_i}=P_{s_i}T\in W .$$
The elements $\mathbf s_1,\dots,\mathbf s_{n-1}$ are the **simple reflections** of
$W$; they generate $W$, because the adjacent transpositions generate $S_n$
([[thm-adjacent-transpositions-generate-the-symmetric-group]]) and $w$ is
surjective.

**Inversion length.** For $\sigma\in S_n$ the **inversion set** and **length**
are
$$\operatorname{Inv}(\sigma):=\{\,(i,j):1\le i<j\le n,\ \sigma(i)>\sigma(j)\,\}, \qquad \ell(\sigma):=\#\operatorname{Inv}(\sigma),$$
and for $w_\sigma\in W$ we set $\ell(w_\sigma):=\ell(\sigma)$, which is
well defined because every element of $W$ has the form $w_\sigma$ for exactly
one $\sigma$. Thus $\ell(1)=0$ and $\ell(w_{s_i})=1$ for every $i$, a single
inversion being created by the transposition of adjacent entries. Length is
invariant under inversion of the permutation: the map
$(i,j)\mapsto(\sigma(j),\sigma(i))$ is a bijection from $\operatorname{Inv}(\sigma)$
to $\operatorname{Inv}(\sigma^{-1})$ — if $i<j$ and $\sigma(i)>\sigma(j)$, then
setting $a:=\sigma(j)<b:=\sigma(i)$ gives $a<b$ while
$\sigma^{-1}(a)=j>i=\sigma^{-1}(b)$ — hence
$$\ell(w^{-1})=\ell(w)\qquad(w\in W).$$
We stress that $\ell$ is here defined combinatorially as an inversion count and
that no Coxeter-theoretic description of it as a minimal word length is used on
this page.

**Parabolic Weyl subgroups.** Let $\alpha=(a_1,\dots,a_r)$ be a composition of
$n$ with blocks $I_1,\dots,I_r$ and standard parabolic $P_\alpha$ and Levi
$L_\alpha$ ([[def-compositions-partial-flags-and-standard-parabolics]]). The
**standard parabolic subgroup of $W$** attached to $\alpha$ is
$$W_\alpha:=\{\,\sigma\in S_n:\sigma(I_i)=I_i\text{ for every }1\le i\le r\,\},$$
the group of permutations preserving each block of $\alpha$ as a set; it is
isomorphic to $S_{a_1}\times\cdots\times S_{a_r}$ by restriction to the blocks,
and its elements are exactly the $\sigma$ whose length is the sum of the lengths
of the restrictions $\sigma|_{I_i}$. In terms of the monomial subgroup, a
monomial matrix lies in $P_\alpha$ exactly when its permutation matrix has
$\sigma(I_i)=I_i$ for all $i$, that is, exactly when $\sigma\in W_\alpha$;
consequently
$$N\cap P_\alpha=N\cap L_\alpha=T\cdot\{\,P_\sigma:\sigma\in W_\alpha\,\}, \qquad W_\alpha=w(N\cap P_\alpha),$$
and $\{P_\sigma:\sigma\in W_\alpha\}$ is a complement to $T$ in $N\cap P_\alpha$: its intersection with $T$ is $\{I_n\}$ and every element has the unique form $tP_\sigma$. The two extreme
cases are
$$W_{(n)}=S_n,\qquad W_{(1^n)}=\{1\},$$
corresponding to $P_{(n)}=G=L_{(n)}$ and to $P_{(1^n)}=B$ with $L_{(1^n)}=T$
and $W_{(1^n)}=w(T)=\{1\}$: the single block of $(n)$ is preserved by every
permutation, while each singleton block of $(1^n)$ must be fixed, so only the
identity survives.

3. **Decomposition.** $G$ is the disjoint union $$G=\bigsqcup_{\sigma\in S_n}BP_\sigma B,$$ so the map $\sigma\mapsto BP_\sigma B$ is a bijection from $S_n$ onto the set of double cosets $BxB$ of $G$, and $B\backslash G/B$ is in bijection with $S_n$ and with the Weyl group $W$.

2. **Intersection dimensions.** For $x\in G$ and all $1\le i,j\le n$, $$\dim_{\mathbb F_q}(V_i\cap xV_j)=j-r_{i+1,j}(x),$$ where $r_{i+1,j}(x)$ is the rank of the submatrix of $x$ on the rows $i+1,\dots,n$ and the columns $1,\dots,j$, with the convention $r_{n+1,j}(x):=0$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $q$ be a prime power, put $G=\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$
with standard Borel subgroup $B$, and for $g\in M_n(\mathbb F_q)$ and
$1\le i,j\le n$ let $r_{i,j}(g)$ denote the rank of the submatrix of $g$ on the
rows $i,i+1,\dots,n$ and the columns $1,2,\dots,j$
([[def-row-space-column-space-nullspace-and-matrix-ranks]]). Then:

1. $r_{i,j}(bg)=r_{i,j}(g)=r_{i,j}(gb)$ for all $b\in B$, so $r_{i,j}$ is
   constant on each double coset $BgB$;
2. if $g\in BwB$ for a permutation matrix $w=P_\sigma$
   ([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]), then
   $$r_{i,j}(g)=\#\{\,k\le j:\sigma(k)\ge i\,\};$$
3. for $g\in G$, triangular elimination supplies a permutation matrix
   with $g\in BP_\sigma B$
   ([[lem-gaussian-elimination-produces-a-pivot-permutation]]), and the rank matrix $(r_{i,j}(g))_{1\le i,j\le n}$ determines
   $\sigma$, and hence determines the double coset $BgB$, uniquely.

A **permutation** of $X$ is a bijection $f : X \to X$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). The **symmetric group of $X$** is the set of all permutations of $X$, $$\operatorname{Sym}(X) \;:=\; \{\, f : X \to X \;:\; f \text{ is a bijection} \,\},$$ equipped with **composition** as its operation,
For every set $X$, the triple $(\operatorname{Sym}(X), \circ, \mathrm{id}_X)$ of [[def-symmetric-group]] is a group ([[def-group]]); the inverse of a permutation $f$ is its inverse function $f^{-1}$.

By (W2) the vector addition of $V$ restricts to a binary operation $W \times W \to W$, and by (W3) the scalar multiplication restricts to a map $F \times W \to W$. With these and the element $0_V$, the set $W$ is a vector space over $F$:
A function $T:V\to W$ is **linear** when $$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$ for all $a,b\in F$ and $u,v\in V$.
For $A\in M_n(F)$, the following are equivalent: 1. $A$ is invertible; 2. $x\mapsto Ax$ is a linear isomorphism;

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$ finite-dimensional. Then $$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$ Equivalently, $$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$
Two finite-dimensional vector spaces over the same field $F$ are linearly isomorphic if and only if they have the same dimension.
$f$ is **injective** (one-to-one) if $f(x) = f(y)$ implies $x = y$, for all $x, y \in A$.

A subset $W \subseteq V$ is a **linear subspace** of $V$ when - **(W1)** $0_V \in W$; - **(W2)** $W$ is closed under the vector addition: $u, v \in W$ implies $u + v \in W$; - **(W3)** $W$ is closed under scalar multiplication:

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) that is finite-dimensional with $\dim_F V = n$ ([[def-dimension]]), and let $U$ be a linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Then 1. $U$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ and $\dim_F U \le n$;

derivations.claim: Every $x\in G$ has exactly one Bruhat index $\sigma(x)\in S_n$ with $x\in BP_{\sigma(x)}B$, and $\sigma(P_\tau)=\tau$ for every $\tau\in S_n$.
For $C_{ij}(x):=\dim_{\mathbb F_q}(V_{d_i}\cap xV_{e_j})$ one has $C_{ij}(x)=\#\{k\le e_j:\sigma(x)(k)\le d_i\}=\sum_{i'\le i}\sum_{j'\le j}M(\sigma(x))_{i'j'}$.
The block-count matrix satisfies $\sum_j M(\tau)_{ij}=a_i$ and $\sum_i M(\tau)_{ij}=b_j$, with nonnegative integer entries.
$M(u\tau v)=M(\tau)$ for all $u\in W_\alpha$, $v\in W_\beta$, $\tau\in S_n$.

For every matrix $m$ with nonnegative integer entries, row sums $a_i$ and column sums $b_j$, the monotone matching $\sigma_m$ is a well-defined $(\alpha,\beta)$-block-increasing permutation with $M(\sigma_m)=m$.
For σ and the monotone matching σ_m of its block-count matrix, choose v∈W_β mapping each S_ij increasingly onto T_ij. Then u=σv^{-1}σ_m^{-1} preserves every α-block, so σ=uσ_mv with u∈W_α.
For all $\rho,\rho'\in S_n$, $\ell(\rho\rho')=\ell(\rho)+\ell(\rho')-2N(\rho,\rho')$, hence $\ell(\rho\rho')\le\ell(\rho)+\ell(\rho')$.
The assignment $\Psi(W_\alpha w_\sigma W_\beta):=P_\alpha P_\sigma P_\beta$ is well defined on $(W_\alpha,W_\beta)$-double cosets.
Second differences of step 1.2 give $M(\sigma(x))_{ij}=C_{ij}-C_{i-1,j}-C_{i,j-1}+C_{i-1,j-1}$, so $C(x)$ determines $M(\sigma(x))$.
For $p\in P_\alpha$, $q\in P_\beta$ one has $C_{ij}(pxq)=C_{ij}(x)$, because $p,q$ preserve the respective partial flags and an invertible linear map preserves intersections and dimensions.
For every $x\in G$, $P_\alpha xP_\beta=P_\alpha P_{\sigma(x)}P_\beta$.
$\tau\mapsto M(\tau)$ induces a bijection from $W_\alpha\backslash W/W_\beta$ onto the matrices with nonnegative integer entries, row sums $a_i$ and column sums $b_j$.
If $\rho$ is increasing on each $\beta$-block and $\rho'\in W_\beta$, then $N(\rho,\rho')=0$ and hence $\ell(\rho\rho')=\ell(\rho)+\ell(\rho')$.
$\ell(\rho s_i)=\ell(\rho)+1-2[\rho(i)>\rho(i+1)]$ and $\ell(s_i\rho)=\ell(\rho)+1-2[\rho^{-1}(i)>\rho^{-1}(i+1)]$.
Two $(\alpha,\beta)$-block-increasing permutations with the same block-count matrix are equal.
$M\circ\sigma$ is constant on $(P_\alpha,P_\beta)$-double cosets: $M(\sigma(pxq))=M(\sigma(x))$ for all $p\in P_\alpha$, $q\in P_\beta$, $x\in G$.
Every element of minimal length in a $(W_\alpha,W_\beta)$-double coset is $(\alpha,\beta)$-block-increasing.
$\Psi$ is surjective onto the set of $(P_\alpha,P_\beta)$-double cosets.
$\Psi$ is injective: $P_\alpha P_\sigma P_\beta=P_\alpha P_\tau P_\beta$ forces $M(\sigma)=M(\tau)$, hence $W_\alpha\sigma W_\beta=W_\alpha\tau W_\beta$.

Each $(W_\alpha,W_\beta)$-double coset has exactly one $(\alpha,\beta)$-block-increasing element $\sigma_m$, equal to the monotone matching of its block-count matrix $m$, and this is its unique element of minimal length.

Claim 3 of the statement holds: every double coset contains exactly one block-increasing permutation, it is the monotone matching $\sigma_M$ of its block-count matrix, and it is the strict length minimum.

The boundary cases are covered: $n=1$ gives one double coset with representative $\mathrm{id}$; $r=1$ ($\alpha=(n)$, $W_\alpha=S_n$) and $s=1$ ($\beta=(n)$) each give one double coset with representative $\mathrm{id}$.

Claims 1 and 2 of the statement hold and the proof is complete: $\Psi$ is a bijection (steps 1.8, 3.3, 3.4); $M(\sigma(x))=M(\sigma(y))\Leftrightarrow W_\alpha\sigma(x)W_\beta=W_\alpha\sigma(y)W_\beta\Leftrightarrow P_\alpha xP_\beta=P_\alpha yP_\beta$ (steps 2.4, 2.3, 3.1).

boundaries.evidence: Compositions of $n\ge1$ have no empty parts, and the only empty index sets are the initial ones: step 1.5 uses the empty sums $\sum_{j'<1}$ and empty predecessor lists with the conventions $d_0=e_0=0$, and step 2.1 uses $C_{0,j}=C_{i,0}=0$ coming from $V_0=\{0\}$ (step 5.2 records the case $n=1$, where $\alpha=\beta=(1)$ and there is one double coset).

Zero entries of a block-count matrix are allowed: step 1.5 assigns the empty set $A_{ij}$ when $m_{ij}=0$, and step 3.2 compares lengths (integers) without dividing by any block count or length; step 5.2 exhibits the extreme matrices of the cases $r=1$ and $s=1$ with all mass in one row or column.

Step 5.2: for $n=1$ one has $\alpha=\beta=(1)$, $W_\alpha=W_\beta=\{1\}$, a single $(W_\alpha,W_\beta)$-double coset with $M(\mathrm{id})=(1)$, and step 4.1 makes $\mathrm{id}$ its unique minimal block-increasing element.

Degenerate parabolic data are covered by step 5.2: $r=1$ ($P_\alpha=G$, $W_\alpha=S_n$) and $s=1$ ($P_\beta=G$) each leave one double coset with representative $\mathrm{id}$; when instead $\alpha=\beta=(1^n)$ every double coset is a singleton $\{\tau\}$ and $\tau$ is block-increasing (increasing on a one-element block is vacuous), so step 4.1 applies to each of the $n!$ classes.

The extreme parabolics are handled inside the general statement: $P_\alpha=G$ and $P_\beta=G$ are step 5.2, while $P_\alpha=P_\beta=B$ corresponds to $\alpha=\beta=(1^n)$, where $W_\alpha=W_\beta=\{1\}$ by [L2], so $\Psi$ is the Bruhat parametrisation of step 1.1 and the block-count matrix of $\tau$ is its $n\times n$ permutation matrix, whose monotone matching is $\tau$ by step 2.7.

boundaries.reason: No choice is made anywhere: $\sigma_m$ is defined by an explicit allocation rule in step 1.5, $v$ and $u$ in step 1.6 are defined by explicit formulas on finite blocks, and every set occurring in the argument is finite; the data $\alpha,\beta,x,\tau$ are given, not selected.

citations.quote: **The standard parabolic subgroup of type $\alpha$.** A matrix $p=(p_{kl})\in M_n(\mathbb F_q)$ is **upper block triangular of type $\alpha$** when $$p_{kl}=0\quad\text{whenever }\operatorname{blk}(k)>\operatorname{blk}(l),$$ that is, whenever $k$ lies in a strictly later block than $l$; entries with $\operatorname{blk}(k)\le\operatorname{blk}(l)$ are unconstrained. Thus $p$ is upper block triangular of type $\alpha$ exactly when it has the block shape $$\begin{pmatrix} A_{11}&A_{12}&\cdots&A_{1r}\\ 0&A_{22}&\cdots&A_{2r}\\ \vdots&\ddots&\ddots&\vdots\\ 0&\cdots&0&A_{rr} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad A_{ij}\in M_{a_i\times a_j}(\mathbb F_q),$$ with square diagonal blocks $A_{ii}$ and arbitrary blocks above the diagonal. The **standard parabolic subgroup of type $\alpha$** is $$P_\alpha:=\{\,p\in G:p\text{ is upper block triangular of type }\alpha\,\},$$ and it is a subgroup of $G$: it contains $I_n$, and sums and products of upper block triangular matrices, as well as inverses of invertible ones, are again upper block triangular, because the block shape is stable under the block matrix operations of [[thm-matrix-multiplication-laws]]. It is the stabiliser in $G$ of the standard partial flag of type $\alpha$, as verified below, and the two extreme cases are $$P_{(n)}=G,\qquad P_{(1^n)}=B,$$ the second because "upper block triangular of type $(1^n)$" says $p_{kl}=0$ for $k>l$, which is exactly the definition of an upper triangular matrix ([[def-triangular-and-diagonal-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]]), whose invertible members form $B$ by [[def-standard-subgroups-of-gl-n-over-a-finite-field]]. The subgroup $P_\alpha$ is the **standard parabolic** subgroup containing $B$, and $B\le P_\alpha\le G$ for every composition $\alpha$. **Partial flags as the coset space $G/P_\alpha$.** The group $G$ acts on the set $\mathcal F_\alpha$ of partial flags of type $\alpha$ by $g\cdot F_\bullet:=(\,g(F_0),\dots,g(F_r)\,)$; this is a well-defined left action because $g$ is an invertible linear map, so it preserves strict inclusions and dimensions, with $I_n$ acting trivially. The action is transitive: given $F_\bullet\in\mathcal F_\alpha$, choose vectors as follows. Extending a basis of $F_{i-1}$ to a basis of $F_i$ is possible by the extension clause of [[thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace]], and doing this successively for $i=1,\dots,r$ produces an ordered basis $v_1,\dots,v_n$ of $V$ with $$F_i=\langle v_1,\dots,v_{d_i}\rangle\qquad(0\le i\le r);$$ the linear map $g$ with $g(e_j)=v_j$ then has an invertible matrix in the standard basis ([[thm-complete-flags-form-gl-n-over-b]], where the same argument produces an element of $G$) and satisfies $g(W_i)=F_i$ for all $i$, that is, $g\cdot W_\bullet^{(\alpha)}=F_\bullet$. The stabiliser of the standard partial flag is $P_\alpha$: a matrix $p\in G$ satisfies $p(W_i)=W_i$ for all $i$ exactly when $p(W_i)\subseteq W_i$ for all $i$, because $p$ is injective and $\dim_{\mathbb F_q}p(W_i)=\dim_{\mathbb F_q}W_i=d_i$; and $p(W_i)\subseteq W_i$ means that the column block $l$ of $p$ has no nonzero entries below block $i$ whenever $\operatorname{blk}(l)\le i$, which is exactly $p_{kl}=0$ for $\operatorname{blk}(k)>\operatorname{blk}(l)$. Consequently the orbit map $$G/P_\alpha\longrightarrow\mathcal F_\alpha,\qquad gP_\alpha\longmapsto g\cdot W_\bullet^{(\alpha)},$$ is a $G$-equivariant bijection by [[thm-transitive-actions-are-coset-actions]] and [[def-group-action]], so partial flags of type $\alpha$ are the left cosets of $P_\alpha$. **Block Levis and unipotent radicals.** With $\alpha$ fixed, the **standard Levi subgroup** of type $\alpha$ is the group of block diagonal matrices $$L_\alpha:=\{\,l\in P_\alpha:l_{kl}=0\text{ whenever }\operatorname{blk}(k)\ne\operatorname{blk}(l)\,\},$$ isomorphic to $\operatorname{GL}_{a_1}(\mathbb F_q)\times\cdots\times\operatorname{GL}_{a_r}(\mathbb F_q)$ by the block diagonal blocks, and the **standard unipotent radical** is $$U_\alpha:=\{\,u\in P_\alpha:u_{kk}=1\text{ for all }k,\text{ and }u_{kl}=0\text{ whenever }k\ne l\text{ and }\operatorname{blk}(k)\ge\operatorname{blk}(l)\,\},$$ the upper block triangular matrices with identity diagonal blocks and the off-diagonal blocks above the block diagonal.

Then $L_\alpha$ and $U_\alpha$ are subgroups of $P_\alpha$, $L_\alpha\cap U_\alpha=\{I_n\}$, $U_\alpha\trianglelefteq P_\alpha$, and the multiplication map $$L_\alpha\times U_\alpha\longrightarrow P_\alpha,\qquad (l,u)\longmapsto lu,$$ is a bijection; equivalently $$P_\alpha=L_\alpha\ltimes U_\alpha .$$

**Permutation matrices and the monomial subgroup.** Let $n\ge1$, let $q$ be a
prime power, let $G=\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$ with diagonal torus $T$ and
standard flag $V_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq V_n$ as in
[[def-standard-subgroups-of-gl-n-over-a-finite-field]], and let
$S_n:=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ be the symmetric group of the set
$\{1,\dots,n\}$ ([[def-symmetric-group]], [[lem-symmetric-group-is-a-group]]),
so that permutations are composed as functions and an element $\sigma\in S_n$ is
written in one-line notation as the list $\sigma(1),\sigma(2),\dots,\sigma(n)$.

For $\sigma\in S_n$ the **permutation matrix** $P_\sigma\in G$ is the matrix with
$$(P_\sigma)_{ij}=\begin{cases}1,&i=\sigma(j),\\0,&i\ne\sigma(j),\end{cases}$$
that is, the $j$-th column of $P_\sigma$ is the standard basis vector
$e_{\sigma(j)}$, so that the $j$-th column has its unique entry $1$ in row
$\sigma(j)$. In particular $P_{\mathrm{id}}=I_n$, and multiplying matrices gives
$$P_\sigma P_\tau=P_{\sigma\circ\tau}\qquad(\sigma,\tau\in S_n),$$
because the $(i,k)$ entry of $P_\sigma P_\tau$ is $\sum_j(P_\sigma)_{ij}(P_\tau)_{jk}$,
which is $1$ exactly when $j=\tau(k)$ and $i=\sigma(j)=\sigma(\tau(k))$, and $0$
otherwise. A matrix $m\in G$ is **monomial** when every row and every column of
$m$ has exactly one nonzero entry. The **monomial subgroup** of $G$ is
$$N:=\{\,m\in G:m\text{ is monomial}\,\}.$$
Every $m\in N$ has a unique expression
$$m=t\,P_\sigma,\qquad t=\operatorname{diag}(t_1,\dots,t_n)\in T,\quad\sigma\in S_n,$$
namely with $\sigma(j)$ the row of the nonzero entry of column $j$ and
$t_{\sigma(j)}$ that entry; conversely $tP_\sigma$ is monomial with nonzero
entries $t_i$ in the rows and columns determined by $\sigma$. Consequently
$$N=T\cdot\{P_\sigma:\sigma\in S_n\}=\{P_\sigma t':\sigma\in S_n,\ t'\in T\},$$
since diagonal matrices may be moved across a permutation matrix.
$N$ is a subgroup of $G$: it contains $I_n=P_{\mathrm{id}}$, the product
$m m'$ of monomial matrices is monomial because the unique nonzero entry of each
column of $m'$ is transported to a unique nonzero entry of the corresponding
column of $mm'$, and the inverse of a monomial matrix is monomial since
permuting and rescaling rows and columns can be undone. Moreover $T\le N$ and
$T\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}N$.

**The Weyl group.** Define the **sign permutation** of a monomial matrix by
$$w:N\longrightarrow S_n,\qquad w(tP_\sigma):=\sigma,$$
which is well defined by the uniqueness of the decomposition. It is a group
homomorphism: if $m=tP_\sigma$ and $m'=t'P_\tau$, then
$t''':=P_\sigma t'P_\sigma^{-1}$ is diagonal, so
$mm'=t\,t'''\,P_\sigma P_\tau=t\,t'''\,P_{\sigma\tau}$ by
[[thm-matrix-multiplication-laws]], whence $w(mm')=\sigma\circ\tau=w(m)w(m')$.
Its kernel is exactly $T$, since $w(tP_\sigma)=\mathrm{id}$ says
$\sigma=\mathrm{id}$ and then $tP_{\mathrm{id}}=t$. Being a surjective
homomorphism, $w$ has kernel $T\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}N$ by
[[def-normal-subgroup]], and the induced map on cosets
$$W:=N/T\longrightarrow S_n,\qquad mT\longmapsto w(m),$$
is well defined (left multiplication by an element of $T=\ker w$ does not change
$w$) and is an isomorphism of groups, with inverse $\sigma\mapsto P_\sigma T$;
here $N/T$ is the quotient group of [[def-quotient-group]]. We call
$$W=N/T\cong S_n$$
the **(split) Weyl group** of $G$. Note that $W$ is defined as a quotient of the
monomial subgroup $N$ and **not** as the quotient $N_G(T)/T$ of the normaliser
of $T$ inside $G$: at $q=2$ the torus $T$ is trivial and $N_G(T)/T$ is all of
$G$, while $N/T\cong S_n$ still holds. For $\sigma\in S_n$ we write $w_\sigma$ for
the class of $P_\sigma$ in $W$, so that $w_\sigma w_\tau=w_{\sigma\tau}$ and the
isomorphism above sends $w_\sigma$ to $\sigma$; we write $1:=w_{\mathrm{id}}$
for the identity of $W$.

**Simple reflections.** For $1\le i<n$ let $s_i:=(i\ i+1)\in S_n$ be the
adjacent transposition of $i$ and $i+1$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), and put
$$\mathbf s_i:=w_{s_i}=P_{s_i}T\in W .$$
The elements $\mathbf s_1,\dots,\mathbf s_{n-1}$ are the **simple reflections** of
$W$; they generate $W$, because the adjacent transpositions generate $S_n$
([[thm-adjacent-transpositions-generate-the-symmetric-group]]) and $w$ is
surjective.

**Inversion length.** For $\sigma\in S_n$ the **inversion set** and **length**
are
$$\operatorname{Inv}(\sigma):=\{\,(i,j):1\le i<j\le n,\ \sigma(i)>\sigma(j)\,\}, \qquad \ell(\sigma):=\#\operatorname{Inv}(\sigma),$$
and for $w_\sigma\in W$ we set $\ell(w_\sigma):=\ell(\sigma)$, which is
well defined because every element of $W$ has the form $w_\sigma$ for exactly
one $\sigma$. Thus $\ell(1)=0$ and $\ell(w_{s_i})=1$ for every $i$, a single
inversion being created by the transposition of adjacent entries. Length is
invariant under inversion of the permutation: the map
$(i,j)\mapsto(\sigma(j),\sigma(i))$ is a bijection from $\operatorname{Inv}(\sigma)$
to $\operatorname{Inv}(\sigma^{-1})$ — if $i<j$ and $\sigma(i)>\sigma(j)$, then
setting $a:=\sigma(j)<b:=\sigma(i)$ gives $a<b$ while
$\sigma^{-1}(a)=j>i=\sigma^{-1}(b)$ — hence
$$\ell(w^{-1})=\ell(w)\qquad(w\in W).$$
We stress that $\ell$ is here defined combinatorially as an inversion count and
that no Coxeter-theoretic description of it as a minimal word length is used on
this page.

**Parabolic Weyl subgroups.** Let $\alpha=(a_1,\dots,a_r)$ be a composition of
$n$ with blocks $I_1,\dots,I_r$ and standard parabolic $P_\alpha$ and Levi
$L_\alpha$ ([[def-compositions-partial-flags-and-standard-parabolics]]). The
**standard parabolic subgroup of $W$** attached to $\alpha$ is
$$W_\alpha:=\{\,\sigma\in S_n:\sigma(I_i)=I_i\text{ for every }1\le i\le r\,\},$$
the group of permutations preserving each block of $\alpha$ as a set; it is
isomorphic to $S_{a_1}\times\cdots\times S_{a_r}$ by restriction to the blocks,
and its elements are exactly the $\sigma$ whose length is the sum of the lengths
of the restrictions $\sigma|_{I_i}$. In terms of the monomial subgroup, a
monomial matrix lies in $P_\alpha$ exactly when its permutation matrix has
$\sigma(I_i)=I_i$ for all $i$, that is, exactly when $\sigma\in W_\alpha$;
consequently
$$N\cap P_\alpha=N\cap L_\alpha=T\cdot\{\,P_\sigma:\sigma\in W_\alpha\,\}, \qquad W_\alpha=w(N\cap P_\alpha),$$
and $\{P_\sigma:\sigma\in W_\alpha\}$ is a complement to $T$ in $N\cap P_\alpha$: its intersection with $T$ is $\{I_n\}$ and every element has the unique form $tP_\sigma$. The two extreme
cases are
$$W_{(n)}=S_n,\qquad W_{(1^n)}=\{1\},$$
corresponding to $P_{(n)}=G=L_{(n)}$ and to $P_{(1^n)}=B$ with $L_{(1^n)}=T$
and $W_{(1^n)}=w(T)=\{1\}$: the single block of $(n)$ is preserved by every
permutation, while each singleton block of $(1^n)$ must be fixed, so only the
identity survives.
Their **matrix product** is the matrix $AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are $$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

Matrix multiplication over a field is associative and unital, distributes over entrywise addition on both sides, and is compatible with scalar multiplication. Precisely, whenever the displayed products have compatible shapes, $$A(BC)=(AB)C,\qquad I_mA=A=AI_n,$$
Their **matrix product** is the matrix $AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are $$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

Matrix multiplication over a field is associative and unital, distributes over entrywise addition on both sides, and is compatible with scalar multiplication. Precisely, whenever the displayed products have compatible shapes, $$A(BC)=(AB)C,\qquad I_mA=A=AI_n,$$ $$(A+A')B=AB+A'B,\qquad A(B+B')=AB+AB',$$ $$0B=0=A0,\qquad (\lambda A)B=\lambda(AB)=A(\lambda B).$$

Let $G$ be a group ([[def-group]]) and let $\mathcal{H}$ be a nonempty set of subgroups of $G$ ([[def-subgroup]]). Then the intersection $$K \;=\; \bigcap_{H \in \mathcal{H}} H \;=\; \{\, x \in G \;:\; x \in H \text{ for every } H \in \mathcal{H} \,\}$$ is a subgroup of $G$. In particular the intersection of two subgroups is a subgroup.
The subgroup $N$ is **normal in $G$** when $$gNg^{-1}=N\qquad\text{for every }g\in G.$$
For $g\in G$, the **left coset** and **right coset** of $H$ represented by $g$ are $$gH:=\{gh:h\in H\},\qquad Hg:=\{hg:h\in H\}.$$

A subset $H \subseteq G$ is a **subgroup** of $G$, written $H \le G$, when - **(S1)** $e \in H$; - **(S2)** $H$ is closed under the operation: $x, y \in H$ implies $xy \in H$ ([[def-binary-operation]]); - **(S3)** $H$ is closed under inverses: $x \in H$ implies $x^{-1} \in H$.

1. **Double cosets.** The assignment $\Psi\bigl(W_\alpha w_\tau W_\beta\bigr):=P_\alpha P_\tau P_\beta$ is a well-defined bijection from the set of $(W_\alpha,W_\beta)$-double cosets of $W$ onto the set of $(P_\alpha,P_\beta)$-double cosets of $G$. 2. **Block counts are a complete invariant.** For all $x,y\in G$ one has $M(\sigma(x))=M(\sigma(y))$ if and only if $P_\alpha xP_\beta=P_\alpha yP_\beta$, if and only if $W_\alpha\sigma(x)W_\beta=W_\alpha\sigma(y)W_\beta$; and $\tau\mapsto M(\tau)$ induces a bijection from $W_\alpha\backslash W/W_\beta$ onto the set of all matrices with nonnegative integer entries whose row sums are $a_1,\dots,a_r$ and whose column sums are $b_1,\dots,b_s$. 3. **Unique minimal representative.** Every $(W_\alpha,W_\beta)$-double coset contains exactly one $(\alpha,\beta)$-block-increasing permutation, and this permutation is the unique element of the coset of minimal inversion length; every other element of the coset has strictly larger length.
A **left action** of $G$ on $X$ is a function $G\times X\to X$, written $(g,x)\mapsto g\cdot x$, such that $$e\cdot x=x,\qquad (gh)\cdot x=g\cdot(h\cdot x)$$

and the two extreme cases are $$P_{(n)}=G,\qquad P_{(1^n)}=B,$$ the second because "upper block triangular of type $(1^n)$" says $p_{kl}=0$ for $k>l$, which is exactly the definition of an upper triangular matrix ([[def-triangular-and-diagonal-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]]), whose invertible members form $B$ by [[def-standard-subgroups-of-gl-n-over-a-finite-field]]. The subgroup $P_\alpha$ is the **standard parabolic** subgroup containing $B$, and $B\le P_\alpha\le G$ for every composition $\alpha$. **Partial flags as the coset space $G/P_\alpha$.** The group $G$ acts on the set $\mathcal F_\alpha$ of partial flags of type $\alpha$ by $g\cdot F_\bullet:=(\,g(F_0),\dots,g(F_r)\,)$; this is a well-defined left action because $g$ is an invertible linear map, so it preserves strict inclusions and dimensions, with $I_n$ acting trivially. The action is transitive: given $F_\bullet\in\mathcal F_\alpha$, choose vectors as follows. Extending a basis of $F_{i-1}$ to a basis of $F_i$ is possible by the extension clause of [[thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace]], and doing this successively for $i=1,\dots,r$ produces an ordered basis $v_1,\dots,v_n$ of $V$ with $$F_i=\langle v_1,\dots,v_{d_i}\rangle\qquad(0\le i\le r);$$ the linear map $g$ with $g(e_j)=v_j$ then has an invertible matrix in the standard basis ([[thm-complete-flags-form-gl-n-over-b]], where the same argument produces an element of $G$) and satisfies $g(W_i)=F_i$ for all $i$, that is, $g\cdot W_\bullet^{(\alpha)}=F_\bullet$. The stabiliser of the standard partial flag is $P_\alpha$: a matrix $p\in G$ satisfies $p(W_i)=W_i$ for all $i$ exactly when $p(W_i)\subseteq W_i$ for all $i$, because $p$ is injective and $\dim_{\mathbb F_q}p(W_i)=\dim_{\mathbb F_q}W_i=d_i$; and $p(W_i)\subseteq W_i$ means that the column block $l$ of $p$ has no nonzero entries below block $i$ whenever $\operatorname{blk}(l)\le i$, which is exactly $p_{kl}=0$ for $\operatorname{blk}(k)>\operatorname{blk}(l)$. Consequently the orbit map $$G/P_\alpha\longrightarrow\mathcal F_\alpha,\qquad gP_\alpha\longmapsto g\cdot W_\bullet^{(\alpha)},$$ is a $G$-equivariant bijection by [[thm-transitive-actions-are-coset-actions]] and [[def-group-action]], so partial flags of type $\alpha$ are the left cosets of $P_\alpha$. **Block Levis and unipotent radicals.** With $\alpha$ fixed, the **standard Levi subgroup** of type $\alpha$ is the group of block diagonal matrices $$L_\alpha:=\{\,l\in P_\alpha:l_{kl}=0\text{ whenever }\operatorname{blk}(k)\ne\operatorname{blk}(l)\,\},$$ isomorphic to $\operatorname{GL}_{a_1}(\mathbb F_q)\times\cdots\times\operatorname{GL}_{a_r}(\mathbb F_q)$ by the block diagonal blocks, and the **standard unipotent radical** is $$U_\alpha:=\{\,u\in P_\alpha:u_{kk}=1\text{ for all }k,\text{ and }u_{kl}=0\text{ whenever }k\ne l\text{ and }\operatorname{blk}(k)\ge\operatorname{blk}(l)\,\},$$ the upper block triangular matrices with identity diagonal blocks and the off-diagonal blocks above the block diagonal. Thus $U_{(n)}=\{I_n\}$ and $U_{(1^n)}=U$ is the standard maximal unipotent subgroup of $G$.

Moreover the block diagonal map is an isomorphism of groups $$L_\alpha\longrightarrow \operatorname{GL}_{a_1}(\mathbb F_q)\times\cdots\times\operatorname{GL}_{a_r}(\mathbb F_q),\qquad l\longmapsto(A_{11},\dots,A_{rr}),$$ whose inverse assembles the blocks, and the two extreme cases are $P_{(n)}=G=L_{(n)}$, $U_{(n)}=\{I_n\}$ and $P_{(1^n)}=B=L_{(1^n)}\ltimes U_{(1^n)}$ with $L_{(1^n)}=T$ the diagonal torus and $U_{(1^n)}=U$ the standard maximal unipotent subgroup.

**The basic structure.** $B$, $T$ and $U$ are subgroups of $G$, we have $T\le B$ and $U\le B$, and $T\cap U=\{I_n\}$. Here $I_n\in B\cap T\cap U$, and each of the three sets is closed under products and inverses: the product of two upper triangular (respectively diagonal, respectively unitriangular) matrices is upper triangular (respectively diagonal, respectively unitriangular), and the inverse of an invertible upper triangular matrix is upper triangular, with diagonal entries $a_{ii}^{-1}$ in the diagonal case. For instance, if $u=I_n+N$ with $N$ strictly upper triangular, then $N^n=0$ and $$u^{-1}=I_n-N+N^2-\cdots+(-1)^{n-1}N^{n-1},$$ which is again unitriangular; the displayed product is computed with the associative multiplication and distributivity of [[thm-matrix-multiplication-laws]], and $N^n=0$ because $N$ moves every vector at least one step up the flag $0\le\langle e_1\rangle\le\langle e_1,e_2\rangle\le\cdots\le\mathbb F_q^n$. The notation $U$ is consistent with "unipotent": every $u\in U$ satisfies $(u-I_n)^n=0$. **Every element of $B$ is a unique product $tu$.** Let $b=(b_{ij})\in B$. Since $b$ is upper triangular and invertible, its determinant is the product $b_{11}b_{22}\cdots b_{nn}$ ([[thm-determinant-of-a-triangular-matrix]]), so $b_{ii}\ne0$ for every $i$; hence $$t:=\operatorname{diag}(b_{11},\dots,b_{nn})\in T,\qquad u:=t^{-1}b,$$ where $t^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}(b_{11}^{-1},\dots,b_{nn}^{-1})$. A product of a diagonal and an upper triangular matrix is upper triangular with diagonal entries $b_{ii}^{-1}b_{ii}=1$, so $u\in U$ and $b=tu$ with $t\in T$, $u\in U$. Conversely, if $b=t'u'$ with $t'\in T$ and $u'\in U$, then comparing diagonal entries gives $t'=t$, and then $u'=t'^{-1}b=t^{-1}b=u$. So the multiplication map $$T\times U\longrightarrow B,\qquad (t,u)\longmapsto tu,$$ is a bijection: every $b\in B$ has a unique factorisation $b=tu$ with $t\in T$ and $u\in U$. **Semidirect product structure.** $U$ is normal in $B$: for $t\in T$ and $u\in U$ the conjugate $tut^{-1}$ is again unitriangular, and for $g\in B$, written $g=t_0u_0$ with $t_0\in T$, $u_0\in U$, one gets $gug^{-1}=t_0(u_0uu_0^{-1})t_0^{-1}\in U$ because $U$ is a subgroup and $T$ normalises $U$. Since $B=TU$, $T\cap U=\{I_n\}$ and $U\trianglelefteq B$, the group $B$ is the internal semidirect product $$B=T\ltimes U,$$ with $T$ acting on $U$ by conjugation. In particular every $b\in B$ has the form $tu$ with $t\in T$, $u\in U$ and this expression is unique, which is the structure used throughout this page. **Two special cases.** For $n=1$ all matrices are $1\times1$, so $G=B=T=\mathbb F_q^{\times}$ and $U=\{I_1\}$ is trivial.

derivations.claim: **The transported blocks and the groups $M,V,X$.** Put $\kappa(k):=\operatorname{blk}_\beta(\tau^{-1}(k))$ for $1\le k\le n$, so that $k\in\tau(J_j)$ exactly when $\kappa(k)=j$; by [L2] one has $(wAw^{-1})_{kl}=A_{\tau^{-1}(k),\tau^{-1}(l)}$ for every matrix $A$, so applying the criteria of [L1] to the composition $\beta$ gives $$X=\{\,g:g_{kl}=0\text{ whenever }\kappa(k)>\kappa(l)\,\},\qquad M=\{\,g:g_{kl}=0\text{ whenever }\kappa(k)\ne\kappa(l)\,\},\qquad V=\{\,g\in X:g_{kk}=1\text{ for all }k,\ g_{kl}=0\text{ whenever }k\ne l\text{ and }\kappa(k)\ge\kappa(l)\,\},$$ and then $M,V\subseteq X$, $M\cap V=\{I_n\}$ (both contain $wI_nw^{-1}=I_n$, and an element $wpw^{-1}=wqw^{-1}$ with $p\in L_\beta$, $q\in U_\beta$ satisfies $p=q\in L_\beta\cap U_\beta=\{I_n\}$), $X=MV$ (as $P_\beta=L_\beta U_\beta$), $X,M,V$ are subgroups of $G$ and $V\trianglelefteq X$, because products and inverses are carried by $w(pq)w^{-1}=(wpw^{-1})(wqw^{-1})$ and $(wqw^{-1})^{-1}=wq^{-1}w^{-1}$ by [L3], and for $x=wpw^{-1}\in X$ and $v=wuw^{-1}\in V$ one has $xvx^{-1}=w(pup^{-1})w^{-1}\in V$ since $pup^{-1}\in U_\beta$ by [L1]. [L1, L2, L3]

**The subgroups $C,A,D$.** The sets $C=L_\alpha\cap M$, $A=L_\alpha\cap V$ and $D=U_\alpha\cap M$ are subgroups of $G$ by [L4], and $C\subseteq L_\alpha$, $C\subseteq M$, $A\subseteq V$, $D\subseteq U_\alpha$ hold by definition; moreover $A\cap C\subseteq V\cap M=\{I_n\}$ by step 1.1. [step 1.1, L4]

**The projection onto $M$.** Since $X=MV$ with $M\cap V=\{I_n\}$ and $V\trianglelefteq X$ by step 1.1, every $g\in X$ has a unique factorisation $g=m\,u$ with $m\in M$ and $u\in V$: if $m_1u_1=m_2u_2$ with $m_i\in M$, $u_i\in V$, then $m_2^{-1}m_1=u_2u_1^{-1}\in M\cap V=\{I_n\}$, so $m_1=m_2$ and $u_1=u_2$. Define $\pi:X\to M$ by $\pi(g):=m$ for $g=mu$; then $\pi(g)^{-1}g\in V$ for all $g\in X$, and $\pi$ is a group homomorphism with kernel $V$, because for $g=mu$ and $g'=m'u'$ one has $gg'=m\,m'\,(m'^{-1}um'\,u')$ with $m'^{-1}um'\in V$ and $u'\in V$ by [L3] and step 1.1, so the factorisation of $gg'$ is $(mm')\cdot(m'^{-1}um'u')$ and $\pi(gg')=mm'=\pi(g)\pi(g')$, while $\pi(g)=I_n$ holds exactly when $g\in V$. [step 1.1, L3]

**The components of $P_\alpha\cap X$ lie in $X$.** Let $g\in P_\alpha\cap X$ and let $g=l_0u_0$ be its factorisation from [L1] with $l_0\in L_\alpha$ and $u_0\in U_\alpha$; put $l:=l_0$ and $u:=gl_0^{-1}=l_0u_0l_0^{-1}\in U_\alpha$, so that $g=u\,l$ with $u\in U_\alpha$ and $l\in L_\alpha$. Then $l$ is the $\alpha$-block diagonal part of $g$: if $k,j$ lie in the same $\alpha$-block $I_t$, then, since $l$ is block diagonal and $u$ has identity diagonal blocks, $g_{kj}=(ul)_{kj}=\sum_m u_{km}l_{mj}=\sum_{m\in I_t}u_{km}l_{mj}=l_{kj}$; entries of $l$ between different $\alpha$-blocks are zero. Hence $l\in X$: if $\kappa(k)>\kappa(j)$ then either $\operatorname{blk}_\alpha(k)\ne\operatorname{blk}_\alpha(j)$ and $l_{kj}=0$, or $\operatorname{blk}_\alpha(k)=\operatorname{blk}_\alpha(j)$ and $l_{kj}=g_{kj}=0$ because $g\in X$ by the criterion of step 1.1. Finally $u=gl^{-1}\in X$, because $X$ is a subgroup containing $g$ and $l$ by step 1.1. [step 1.1, L1, L3]

**$\Phi$ is well defined.** First, changing representatives of the two cosets does not change the image. If $a\in A=L_\alpha\cap V$, then $m^{-1}am\in V$ because $M$ normalises $V$ by step 1.1; hence $U_\alpha l a m wU_\beta=U_\alpha l m(m^{-1}am)wU_\beta=U_\alpha l m wU_\beta$, because $w^{-1}(m^{-1}am)w\in U_\beta$. If $d\in D=U_\alpha\cap M$, then $ldl^{-1}\in U_\alpha$ by [L1], so $U_\alpha l d m wU_\beta=U_\alpha l m wU_\beta$. Second, for $c\in C$ the two sides of the generating balancing relation have the same image, since $(lc)m=l(cm)$ by [L3]: $$U_\alpha\,(lc)\,m\,w\,U_\beta=U_\alpha\,l\,(cm)\,w\,U_\beta .$$ Finally, $\Phi$ takes values in the specified $(U_\alpha,U_\beta)$-double cosets inside $P_\alpha wP_\beta$: writing $m=wm_0w^{-1}$ with $m_0\in L_\beta$ gives $lmw=lwm_0\in P_\alpha wP_\beta$. [step 1.1, L1, L3]

**Normalisation by $C$.** Let $c\in C$. Then $cL_\alpha c^{-1}=L_\alpha$ and $cU_\alpha c^{-1}=U_\alpha$, because $C\subseteq L_\alpha\subseteq P_\alpha$ and $U_\alpha\trianglelefteq P_\alpha$ by [L1]; and $cMc^{-1}=M$, because $C\subseteq M$; and $cVc^{-1}=V$, because $C\subseteq X$ and $V\trianglelefteq X$ by step 1.1. Hence $cAc^{-1}=c\,(L_\alpha\cap V)\,c^{-1}=(cL_\alpha c^{-1})\cap(cVc^{-1})=L_\alpha\cap V=A$ and $cDc^{-1}=c\,(U_\alpha\cap M)\,c^{-1}=(cU_\alpha c^{-1})\cap(cMc^{-1})=U_\alpha\cap M=D$, so $C$ normalises $A$ and $D$. Consequently right multiplication by $C$ on $L_\alpha/A$ and left multiplication by $C$ on $D\backslash M$ are well defined. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L1, L4]

**The $\kappa$-block diagonal part, and $L_\alpha\cap X$.** For $g\in X$ let $d$ be the $\kappa$-block diagonal part of $g$, that is $d_{kl}:=g_{kl}$ when $\kappa(k)=\kappa(l)$ and $d_{kl}:=0$ otherwise; then $d=\pi(g)$. Indeed, write $g=wpw^{-1}$ with $p\in P_\beta$ and $p=\lambda u$ with $\lambda\in L_\beta$, $u\in U_\beta$ as in [L1]; the conjugation formula of [L2] gives $d=w\lambda w^{-1}$, and $w\lambda w^{-1}\in M=\{\,g:g_{kl}=0\text{ whenever }\kappa(k)\ne\kappa(l)\,\}$ by step 1.1, while $d^{-1}g=w(\lambda^{-1}p)w^{-1}\in V$ by [L1], so the factorisation $g=d\cdot(d^{-1}g)$ with $d\in M$ and $d^{-1}g\in V$ is the one of step 2.2 and $d=\pi(g)$. Consequently, for $g\in L_\alpha\cap X$ the element $\pi(g)$ lies in $L_\alpha$: its entries are entries of $g$ inside $\kappa$-blocks and zero elsewhere, and $g$ vanishes off the $\alpha$-block diagonal by [L1]; hence $\pi(g)\in C=L_\alpha\cap M$. Moreover $g=a\,\pi(g)$ with $a:=\pi(g)\,\bigl(\pi(g)^{-1}g\bigr)\,\pi(g)^{-1}$: here $\pi(g)^{-1}g\in V$ by step 2.2, and $a\in V$ because $\pi(g)\in M\subseteq X$ normalises the normal subgroup $V\trianglelefteq X$ of step 1.1, while $a\in L_\alpha$ as a product of elements of $L_\alpha$; so $a\in A=L_\alpha\cap V$. [step 1.1, step 2.2, L1, L2, L3]

**$\Phi$ is surjective.** Let $x\in P_\alpha wP_\beta$, say $x=p\,w\,q$ with $p\in P_\alpha$ and $q\in P_\beta$. By [L1] write $p=lu$ with $l\in L_\alpha$, $u\in U_\alpha$ and $q=m_0u_0$ with $m_0\in L_\beta$, $u_0\in U_\beta$, and put $m:=wm_0w^{-1}\in M$, so that $wm_0=mw$ and $x=l\,u\,m\,w\,u_0$. Then $$U_\alpha xU_\beta=U_\alpha\,l\,u\,m\,w\,u_0\,U_\beta=U_\alpha\,l\,m\,w\,U_\beta=\Phi\bigl([lA,Dm]\bigr),$$ because $lul^{-1}\in U_\alpha$ (as $U_\alpha\trianglelefteq P_\alpha$ and $l\in L_\alpha\subseteq P_\alpha$ by [L1]) makes $U_\alpha lu=U_\alpha l$, and $u_0U_\beta=U_\beta$ since $u_0\in U_\beta$. Hence every $(U_\alpha,U_\beta)$-double coset inside $P_\alpha wP_\beta$ lies in the image of $\Phi$. [step 1.1, step 2.4, L1, L3]

**Claim 3: the two biset structures agree.** For $a\in L_\alpha$ and $b\in L_\beta$ the formulas $a\cdot(U_\alpha xU_\beta):=U_\alpha axU_\beta$ and $(U_\alpha xU_\beta)\cdot b:=U_\alpha xbU_\beta$ are well defined (as $aU_\alpha a^{-1}=U_\alpha$ and $bU_\beta b^{-1}=U_\beta$ by [L1]) and satisfy the axioms of [L6], so they are a left action of $L_\alpha$ and a right action of $L_\beta$. On the balanced product the formulas $a\cdot[lA,Dm]:=[alA,Dm]$ and $[lA,Dm]\cdot b:=[lA,D\,m\,wbw^{-1}]$ are well defined, because they carry the generating relation to a relation of the same form, $((al)cA,Dm)\sim(alA,Dcm)$ and $(lcA,D\,m\,wbw^{-1})\sim(lA,D\,c\,m\,wbw^{-1})$ for $c\in C$; they are actions because $M$ is a subgroup and $b\mapsto wbw^{-1}$ is a homomorphism $L_\beta\to M$ (it is conjugation by the fixed element $w$ and $wL_\beta w^{-1}=M$, while $w(bb')w^{-1}=(wbw^{-1})(wb'w^{-1})$ and $wI_nw^{-1}=I_n$ by [L3]). Finally, for $b^w:=wbw^{-1}$ one has $b^ww=wb$, so $$\Phi\bigl(a\cdot[lA,Dm]\bigr)=U_\alpha\,a\,l\,m\,w\,U_\beta=a\cdot\Phi\bigl([lA,Dm]\bigr),\qquad \Phi\bigl([lA,Dm]\cdot b\bigr)=U_\alpha\,l\,m\,b^w\,w\,U_\beta=U_\alpha\,l\,m\,w\,b\,U_\beta=\Phi\bigl([lA,Dm]\bigr)\cdot b .$$ [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.4, L1, L3, L6]

**The $M$-component of $U_\alpha\cap X$.** For $u\in U_\alpha\cap X$ one has $\pi(u)\in D=U_\alpha\cap M$. Indeed $\pi(u)$ is the $\kappa$-block diagonal part $d$ of $u$ by step 3.2, so $d\in M$ and $d_{kk}=u_{kk}=1$ for all $k$, while $d_{kl}=0$ whenever $k\ne l$ and $\operatorname{blk}_\alpha(k)\ge\operatorname{blk}_\alpha(l)$: if $\kappa(k)\ne\kappa(l)$ then $d_{kl}=0$, and if $\kappa(k)=\kappa(l)$ then $d_{kl}=u_{kl}=0$ by the criterion for $U_\alpha$ in [L1]. Hence $d\in U_\alpha$ and $d\in D$. [step 3.2, L1]

**$\Phi$ is injective.** Let $l,l'\in L_\alpha$ and $m,m'\in M$ with $\Phi([l'A,Dm'])=\Phi([lA,Dm])$, that is $U_\alpha l'm'wU_\beta=U_\alpha lmwU_\beta$. Then there are $u_0\in U_\alpha$ and $u_2\in U_\beta$ with $l'm'wu_2=u_0lmw$; putting $v:=wu_2w^{-1}\in V$ gives $l'm'v=u_0lm$ and hence $$m'=l'^{-1}u_0lmv^{-1}=(l'^{-1}u_0l')\,(l'^{-1}l)\,m\,v^{-1}=u'\,\lambda\,m\,v_1,$$ where $u':=l'^{-1}u_0l'\in U_\alpha$, $\lambda:=l'^{-1}l\in L_\alpha$ and $v_1:=v^{-1}\in V$. Therefore $m'm^{-1}=u'\lambda\,(mv_1m^{-1})=u'\lambda v_2$ with $v_2:=mv_1m^{-1}\in V$, because $m\in M\subseteq X$ normalises $V\trianglelefteq X$ by step 1.1; so $u'\lambda=(m'm^{-1})v_2^{-1}\in M\cdot V\subseteq X$ by step 1.1 and $u'\lambda\in U_\alpha L_\alpha=P_\alpha$ by [L1], that is $u'\lambda\in P_\alpha\cap X$, and step 2.3 gives $u'\in X$ and $\lambda\in X$. Applying the homomorphism $\pi$ of step 2.2 to $m'm^{-1}=u'\lambda v_2$ gives $$m'm^{-1}=\pi(m'm^{-1})=\pi(u')\,\pi(\lambda)\,\pi(v_2)=\pi(u')\,\pi(\lambda),$$ since $m'm^{-1}\in M$ satisfies $\pi(m'm^{-1})=m'm^{-1}$ and $v_2\in V=\ker\pi$ by step 2.2; with $d:=\pi(u')\in D$ by step 4.1 and $c:=\pi(\lambda)\in C$ by step 3.2 this is $m'=d\,c\,m$. By step 3.2 applied to $\lambda\in L_\alpha\cap X$ we have $\lambda=a\,c$ with $a\in A$, so $l'=l\lambda^{-1}=l\,c^{-1}a^{-1}$. Hence $l'A=lc^{-1}A$ and $Dm'=Dcm$, and the pair $(l'A,Dm')=(lc^{-1}A,Dcm)$ is related to $(lA,Dm)$ by the generating relation, because $(lc^{-1})\,c=l$ and $c\,(Dm)=Dcm$; therefore $[l'A,Dm']=[lA,Dm]$, so $\Phi$ is injective. [step 1.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, step 3.2, step 4.1, L1, L3, L4]

**Claims 1 and 2.** Steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1 prove claim 1. Step 2.4 shows that $\Phi$ is well defined on the balanced product, step 3.3 that it is surjective onto the set of $(U_\alpha,U_\beta)$-double cosets inside $P_\alpha wP_\beta$, and step 5.1 that it is injective; hence $\Phi$ is a bijection, which is claim 2, the set $P_\alpha wP_\beta$ being by [L5] the double coset attached to the $(W_\alpha,W_\beta)$-double coset of $\tau$. The entry and projection arguments above used no block-increasing hypothesis. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 2.4, step 3.3, step 5.1, L5]

**The extreme cases.** For $\alpha=\beta=(n)$ one has $U_\alpha=U_\beta=\{I_n\}$ and $L_\alpha=L_\beta=G$ by [L7], so $M=X=G=L_\alpha$, $V=\{I_n\}$, $C=G$ and $A=D=\{I_n\}$; the balanced product is the quotient of $G\times G$ by $(gc,m)\sim(g,cm)$ and is in bijection with $G$ via the well-defined map $(l,m)\mapsto lm$ (with inverse $g\mapsto(g,I_n)$), while the double cosets inside $P_\alpha wP_\beta=G$ are the singletons, so claim 2 reads $G\cong G$ via $g\mapsto gw$, each target double coset being a singleton. For $\alpha=\beta=(1^n)$ one has $U_\alpha=U_\beta=U$ and $L_\alpha=L_\beta=T$ by [L7], so $M=wTw^{-1}=T$ (the conjugation formula of [L2] only permutes the diagonal positions), $V=wUw^{-1}$, $C=T\cap T=T$, and $A=T\cap V=\{I_n\}$, $D=U\cap T=\{I_n\}$ because $T\cap U=\{I_n\}$ by [L7] and $V$ is a conjugate of $U$; the balanced product is therefore $(T/\{I_n\})\times_T(\{I_n\}\backslash T)\cong T$ and claim 2 specialises to a bijection $T\to U\backslash(BwB)/U$. For $n=1$ one has $\alpha=\beta=(1)$, $G=B=T=\mathbb F_q^\times$ and $U=\{I_1\}$ by [L7], so $M=C=G$, $A=D=\{I_1\}$ and claim 2 is the tautological bijection from $G$ onto the singletons $\{g\}=U_\alpha\{g\}U_\beta$ inside $P_\alpha wP_\beta=G$. [step 2.1, step 6.1, L1, L2, L7]
**Conclusion.** Claims 1, 2 and 3 of the statement are steps 6.1, 6.1 and 3.4, with the extreme cases verified in step 7.1; the proof is complete. ∎ [step 6.1, step 3.4, step 7.1]
