citations.quote:
Take $m=2$, so that the doubled line quiver has vertices $0,1,2$ and arrows
$(0|1),(1|2)$ and $(1|0),(2|1)$, and let $A_2$ be the Khovanov–Seidel type A
algebra of [[def-khovanov-seidel-type-a-quiver-algebra]]. Then:

1. **Basis.** $A_2$ is free of rank $4\cdot2+1=9$ on the classes of the nine
   paths
   $$(0),\ (1),\ (2),\qquad (0|1),\ (1|2),\qquad (1|0),\ (2|1),\qquad (1|0|1),\ (2|1|2),$$
   of internal degrees $0,0,0$ (vertices), $0,0$ (ascending arrows), $1,1$
   (descending arrows) and $1,1$ (returns). The relations specialised to $m=2$
   are $(0|1|2)=0$, $(2|1|0)=0$ and $(0|1|0)=0$ for the two compositions
   through the unique interior vertex $1$ and for the loop at $0$, together with
   the single identification $(1|2|1)=(1|0|1)$ of the two returns at the
   interior vertex $1$; there is no relation involving a vertex $3$.
2. **Multiplication.** Products of non-composable basis paths are $0$, products
   of composable paths are their left-to-right concatenation, every concatenation
   of three or more arrows is $0$ in $A_2$, and the two nontrivial length-two
   products are
   $$(1|0)(0|1)=(1|0|1)=(1|2|1)=(1|2)(2|1),\qquad (2|1)(1|2)=(2|1|2),$$
   while $(0|1)(1|0)=(0|1|0)=0$ and $(1|2)(2|1)$ has just been computed.
3. **Vertex projectives.** The left modules $P_j=A_2e_j$ are free $\mathbb Z$-modules
   on the paths ending at $j$:
   $$P_0=\mathbb Z(0)\oplus\mathbb Z(1|0),\qquad P_1=\mathbb Z(1)\oplus\mathbb Z(0|1)\oplus\mathbb Z(2|1)\oplus\mathbb Z(1|0|1),\qquad P_2=\mathbb Z(2)\oplus\mathbb Z(1|2)\oplus\mathbb Z(2|1|2),$$
   of ranks $2,4,3$ and with graded ranks $P_0=(1,1)$, $P_1=(2,2)$, $P_2=(2,1)$
   in internal degrees $d=0,1$. Ignoring all arrows gives
   $A_2/(\text{arrows})=\mathbb Z^{3}$ spanned by the three vertex idempotents.
4. **Right projectives.** Symmetrically ${}_jP=e_jA_2$ is free on the paths
   beginning at $j$, so ${}_0P=\mathbb Z(0)\oplus\mathbb Z(0|1)$,
   ${}_1P=\mathbb Z(1)\oplus\mathbb Z(1|0)\oplus\mathbb Z(1|2)\oplus\mathbb Z(1|0|1)$
   and ${}_2P=\mathbb Z(2)\oplus\mathbb Z(2|1)\oplus\mathbb Z(2|1|2)$, again of
   ranks $2,4,3$.

Fix $m\ge1$, let $A_m$ be the Khovanov–Seidel type A algebra of
[[def-khovanov-seidel-type-a-quiver-algebra]] with vertex idempotents
$e_j=(j)$ and internal degree, and let $A_m\text{-mod}$ be the category of
[[def-graded-khovanov-seidel-module-category-and-projectives]].

**The vertex modules.** For $0\le i\le m$ let $S_i$ be the graded left
$A_m$-module whose underlying graded abelian group is
$$(S_i)_0=\mathbb Z,\qquad (S_i)_d=0\quad(d\ne0),$$
and on which a path $p$ of $\mathbb Z\Gamma_m$ acts by
$$e_i\cdot1=1,\qquad e_j\cdot1=0\ (j\ne i),\qquad p\cdot1=0\text{ for every positive-length path }p.$$
Equivalently, $e_i$ acts as the identity, every other vertex idempotent acts as
zero, and every path of positive length acts as zero. The claims that this
assignment is well defined on the quotient $A_m$, that it makes $S_i$ a
finitely generated graded left $A_m$-module and that it is not the zero module
are proved below, so the notation denotes.

**Prime quotients.** For a prime $p$, $pS_i$ is the $A_m$-submodule generated
by $p\cdot1$ and $S_i/pS_i$ is the quotient module; it is the corresponding
$\mathbb Z/p$ **vertex module**, that is the graded left $A_m$-module
$(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)$ in internal degree $0$, with the induced action in
which $e_i$ acts as the identity and every other vertex idempotent and every
positive-length path acts as zero. The sequence
$$0\to S_i\xrightarrow{p}S_i\to S_i/pS_i\to0$$
is degreewise exact for every prime $p$; exactness at both non-end terms is
proved below, so the notation denotes.

**Shifts.** The internal shifts of $S_i$ are inherited from $A_m\text{-mod}$:
$S_i\{r\}$ is the internal shift of the definition of
[[def-graded-khovanov-seidel-module-category-and-projectives]], so that
$(S_i\{r\})_{r}=\mathbb Z$ and all other graded pieces vanish and the same
action rule applies. The vertex module $S_i$ is the quotient of the vertex
projective $P_i=A_me_i$ by its positive-length-path submodule; the
identifications with the quotients $P_i/A_m\{u_{i-1},d_i,r_i\}$ (omitting $u_{-1}$, $d_m$ and $r_0$ at the endpoints, and writing $r_i=(i|i-1|i)$ for $1\le i\le m$) and with the
$\mathbb Z/p$ reductions are proved on the pages that use them.

Let $A$ be an object of an abelian category. A **projective resolution of $A$** is an augmented chain complex $$\cdots \to P_2\to P_1\to P_0\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}A\to0$$ such that every $P_n$ is projective and the augmented complex is exact at every displayed term.

Thus a projective resolution is an exact way of recovering $A$ from projective objects arranged in homological degrees.

Fix $m\ge1$ and $0\le i\le m$, let $A_m$ be the type A algebra of
[[def-khovanov-seidel-type-a-quiver-algebra]], let $A_m\text{-mod}$ be the
category of [[def-graded-khovanov-seidel-module-category-and-projectives]] with
vertex projectives $P_j=A_me_j$ and internal shifts $\{p\}$, and let $S_i$ and
$S_i/pS_i$ be the vertex modules of [[def-vertex-khovanov-seidel-modules]].

Write $j(p,q):=i+p-q$ and put
$$C_{p,q}:=\begin{cases}P_{j(p,q)}\{p\},& p\ge0,\ q\ge0,\ p\le m-i,\ q\le i+p,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}$$
so that the nonzero entries form the staircase
$$0\le p\le m-i,\qquad 0\le q\le i+p,$$
on which the projective index $j=i+p-q$ runs from $j=i+p$ down to $j=0$. Let
$$h_{p,q}:C_{p,q}\to C_{p-1,q},\quad x\mapsto x\cdot(j(p,q)\,\big|\,j(p,q)-1),$$
$$v_{p,q}:C_{p,q}\to C_{p,q-1},\quad x\mapsto(-1)^p\,x\cdot(j(p,q)\,\big|\,j(p,q)+1),$$
where a symbol $(j|j-1)$ with $j=0$, a symbol $(j|j+1)$ with $j=m$, and any
symbol whose source or target module is zero denote the zero map, and where right multiplication
by a path $\alpha$ means $x\mapsto x\alpha$ in the ring $A_m$. Then:

1. $(C,h,v)$ is a first-quadrant homological double complex of graded
   $A_m$-modules, and its direct-sum total complex
   $\operatorname{Tot}_\bullet$, with differential $d=h+v$ and
   $\operatorname{Tot}_n=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}C_{p,q}$, is a finite graded
   projective resolution of $S_i$: every term is a finite direct sum of internal
   shifts of the $P_j$, only finitely many terms are nonzero, $H_0$ is
   $C_{0,0}=P_i$ modulo the image of $d_1$ and $H_n(\operatorname{Tot})=0$
   for $n\ne0$, the augmentation being the quotient map
   $P_i\to P_i/A_m\{u_{i-1},d_i,r_i\}\cong S_i$, with the endpoint omissions of [[def-vertex-khovanov-seidel-modules]].
2. For every prime $p$, the mapping cone of multiplication by $p$ on
   $\operatorname{Tot}_\bullet$ is a finite graded projective resolution of
   $S_i/pS_i$.

Take $m=2$, so that the doubled line quiver has vertices $0,1,2$ and arrows
$(0|1),(1|2)$ and $(1|0),(2|1)$, and let $A_2$ be the Khovanov–Seidel type A
algebra of [[def-khovanov-seidel-type-a-quiver-algebra]]. Then:

1. **Basis.** $A_2$ is free of rank $4\cdot2+1=9$ on the classes of the nine
   paths
   $$(0),\ (1),\ (2),\qquad (0|1),\ (1|2),\qquad (1|0),\ (2|1),\qquad (1|0|1),\ (2|1|2),$$
   of internal degrees $0,0,0$ (vertices), $0,0$ (ascending arrows), $1,1$
   (descending arrows) and $1,1$ (returns). The relations specialised to $m=2$
   are $(0|1|2)=0$, $(2|1|0)=0$ and $(0|1|0)=0$ for the two compositions
   through the unique interior vertex $1$ and for the loop at $0$, together with
   the single identification $(1|2|1)=(1|0|1)$ of the two returns at the
   interior vertex $1$; there is no relation involving a vertex $3$.
2. **Multiplication.** Products of non-composable basis paths are $0$, products
   of composable paths are their left-to-right concatenation, every concatenation
   of three or more arrows is $0$ in $A_2$, and the two nontrivial length-two
   products are
   $$(1|0)(0|1)=(1|0|1)=(1|2|1)=(1|2)(2|1),\qquad (2|1)(1|2)=(2|1|2),$$
   while $(0|1)(1|0)=(0|1|0)=0$ and $(1|2)(2|1)$ has just been computed.
3. **Vertex projectives.** The left modules $P_j=A_2e_j$ are free $\mathbb Z$-modules
   on the paths ending at $j$:
   $$P_0=\mathbb Z(0)\oplus\mathbb Z(1|0),\qquad P_1=\mathbb Z(1)\oplus\mathbb Z(0|1)\oplus\mathbb Z(2|1)\oplus\mathbb Z(1|0|1),\qquad P_2=\mathbb Z(2)\oplus\mathbb Z(1|2)\oplus\mathbb Z(2|1|2),$$
   of ranks $2,4,3$ and with graded ranks $P_0=(1,1)$, $P_1=(2,2)$, $P_2=(2,1)$
   in internal degrees $d=0,1$. Ignoring all arrows gives
   $A_2/(\text{arrows})=\mathbb Z^{3}$ spanned by the three vertex idempotents.
4. **Right projectives.** Symmetrically ${}_jP=e_jA_2$ is free on the paths
   beginning at $j$, so ${}_0P=\mathbb Z(0)\oplus\mathbb Z(0|1)$,
   ${}_1P=\mathbb Z(1)\oplus\mathbb Z(1|0)\oplus\mathbb Z(1|2)\oplus\mathbb Z(1|0|1)$
   and ${}_2P=\mathbb Z(2)\oplus\mathbb Z(2|1)\oplus\mathbb Z(2|1|2)$, again of
   ranks $2,4,3$.

Fix $m\ge1$ and let $A_m$ be the Khovanov–Seidel type A algebra of
[[def-khovanov-seidel-type-a-quiver-algebra]], graded by internal degree, with
the vertex idempotents $e_i:=(i)$ and the generators $u_i:=(i|i+1)$,
$d_i:=(i+1|i)$.

**The finite module category.** $A_m\text{-mod}$ is the category whose objects
are the **finitely generated graded left $A_m$-modules** and whose morphisms are
the **degree-zero $A_m$-linear maps** $f:M\to N$, that is
$f(M_d)\subseteq N_d$ for every $d$, with composition of maps. Throughout this
page every left module, right module and bimodule over $A_m$ is graded and every
homomorphism is degree-zero unless stated otherwise. Finite generation is in the
sense of [[def-finitely-generated-graded-projective-module]], and graded
modules, degree-zero maps and internal shifts are those of
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]].

**Internal shift.** For $r\in\mathbb Z$ and a graded left $A_m$-module $M$ the
**internal shift** $M\{r\}$ is the graded module with
$$(M\{r\})_d=M_{d-r}\qquad(d\in\mathbb Z),$$
carrying the same left $A_m$-action as $M$. The shift $\{1\}$ moves the grading
upwards by one: an element of $M_d$ is an element of $(M\{1\})_{d+1}$.

**Vertex projectives.** Put
$$P_i:=A_me_i,\qquad {}_iP:=e_iA_m\qquad(0\le i\le m),$$
equipped with the grading in which a homogeneous element of $A_m$ of degree $d$
lies in degree $d$. Because paths are written left to right and the product is
concatenation, $P_i$ consists of the classes of the paths **ending** at $i$ and
${}_iP$ of the classes of the paths **beginning** at $i$. The algebra splits as
$$A_m=\bigoplus_{i=0}^mP_i=\bigoplus_{i=0}^m{}_iP$$
as a left, respectively right, module over itself; the decomposition into vertex
projectives is displayed as proved below.

**Claims proved below.** $A_m\text{-mod}$ is an abelian category; the internal
shift $\{r\}$ is an automorphism of $A_m\text{-mod}$; each $P_i$ is a finite
graded projective left $A_m$-module and each ${}_iP$ a finite graded projective
right $A_m$-module, generated by $e_i$.

**Notation.** The source writes $P_i=A_m(i)$ for the summand $A_me_i$, and
$\{r\}$ for the internal shift; the parentheses in $A_m(i)$ are part of that
summand notation and never denote a shift. On this page only the braces $\{r\}$
denote the internal shift, and only the brackets $[r]$ of
[[def-bounded-projective-homotopy-category-for-a-m]] denote the homological
shift, which is not defined yet.

derivations.claim: *The map $P_0\to P_1$.* By [L4] right multiplication by $(0|1)$ is the degree-zero $A_2$-linear map $P_0\to P_1$ with $(0)\mapsto(0)(0|1)=(0|1)$ and $(1|0)\mapsto(1|0)(0|1)=(1|0|1)$ by [L1]; both images are basis elements of $P_1$ by [L1], the degrees are preserved because $(0)$ and $(0|1)$ have degree $0$ and $(1|0)$ and $(1|0|1)$ have degree $1$, and the map is injective because it carries a basis to a linearly independent set.

*The map $P_1\to P_2$.* Right multiplication by $(1|2)$ is the degree-zero $A_2$-linear map $P_1\to P_2$ with $(1)\mapsto(1|2)$, $(2|1)\mapsto(2|1)(1|2)=(2|1|2)$, $(0|1)\mapsto(0|1)(1|2)=(0|1|2)=0$ and $(1|0|1)\mapsto(1|0|1)(1|2)=(1|0|1|2)=0$, the last two being respectively a monotone length-two path and a length-three path; again $(1)$ and $(1|2)$ have degree $0$ while $(2|1)$ and $(2|1|2)$ have degree $1$.

*The map $P_2\to S_2$.* Define $\varepsilon$ to be the $A_2$-linear map with $\varepsilon(e_2)=1$ and $\varepsilon((1|2))=\varepsilon((2|1|2))=0$, which is well defined by the formula $\varepsilon(ae_2)=a\cdot1$: if $ae_2=0$, then $a\cdot1=(ae_2)\cdot1=0$ since $e_2\cdot1=1$. This formula is $A_2$-linear by the module action in [F2]; it is surjective because $S_2=\mathbb Z\cdot1$ and it is degree zero because $e_2$ has degree $0$.

*Every composite in the sequence is zero.* The composite $P_0\to P_1\to P_2$ is right multiplication by $(0|1)(1|2)=(0|1|2)=0$ by step 1.1, step 1.2 and [L1]; the composite $P_1\to P_2\to S_2$ kills the image of the second map, namely the basis elements $(1|2)$ and $(2|1|2)$, which are sent to $0$ by step 1.3.

*Exactness at $P_1$.* By step 1.2 the kernel of right multiplication by $(1|2)$ is the span of the two basis elements that are killed, $(0|1)$ and $(1|0|1)$, and by step 1.1 the image of right multiplication by $(0|1)$ is exactly the span of $(0|1)$ and $(1|0|1)$; the two submodules of $P_1$ are therefore equal, so $\ker(P_1\to P_2)=\mathrm{im}(P_0\to P_1)$.

*Exactness at $P_2$.* A basis element of $P_2$ is in the kernel of $\varepsilon$ exactly when it is not $(2)$, since $\varepsilon((2))=1$, so $\ker\varepsilon=\mathbb Z(1|2)\oplus\mathbb Z(2|1|2)$ by step 1.3; by step 1.2 that span is exactly the image of right multiplication by $(1|2)$, so $\ker\varepsilon=\mathrm{im}(P_1\to P_2)$.

*Conclusion.* The displayed sequence $0\to P_0\to P_1\to P_2\to S_2\to0$ has finitely generated graded projective resolution terms $P_0,P_1,P_2$, all maps are degree-zero $A_2$-linear maps by steps 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3, the first map is injective by step 1.1, the last is surjective by step 1.3, every composite is zero by step 2.1 and the sequence is exact at $P_1$ and at $P_2$ by steps 2.2 and 2.3; hence it is a finite graded projective resolution of the vertex module $S_2$, of length $2$, as in [L3]. The two inner differentials are right multiplications by the degree-zero arrows $(0|1)$ and $(1|2)$, exactly the arrows ascending toward the vertex $2$; the module $S_2$ is a rank-one $\mathbb Z$-module and is therefore not a simple module over $A_2$ in the ungraded sense, the word "simple" belonging to the inherited identifier only.

boundaries.evidence: The resolution terms P_0,P_1,P_2 and target S_2 are nonzero. The zero modules at the two displayed ends carry zero maps; the three maps between nonzero modules have the nonzero basis images computed in steps 1.1-1.3.

The endpoint vertex $0$ is the source of the resolution: $P_0$ is free on $(0),(1|0)$ by [L1], and step 2.2 computes the image of right multiplication by $(0|1)$ as exactly the kernel of right multiplication by $(1|2)$, spanned by $(0|1)$ and $(1|0|1)$.

Each map is specified on one displayed basis: step 1.1 on the two basis elements of $P_0$, step 1.2 on the four of $P_1$, and step 1.3 defines $\varepsilon$ by $\varepsilon(e_2)=1$ and $\varepsilon((1|2))=\varepsilon((2|1|2))=0$.

The degenerate product $(0|1|2)=0$ is exactly what makes the composite $P_0\to P_1\to P_2$ vanish in step 2.1, and $\ker\varepsilon$ is spanned in step 2.3 by the two non-endpoint basis elements $(1|2),(2|1|2)$ of $P_2$.

The right end of the sequence: step 1.3 defines $\varepsilon$ at the vertex $2$ by $\varepsilon(e_2)=1$, and step 2.3 computes its kernel; the left end is the injective first map of step 2.2, whose image is the kernel there.

The maps are defined by explicit right multiplication and by specifying values on displayed bases, and exactness is checked by the basis computations of steps 2.1 to 2.3; no element is selected from a nonempty family and no choice principle is used.

boundaries.reason: No biconditional is asserted. The augmentation is the well-defined A_2-linear map ae_2 to a.1 because e_2 acts as identity on S_2; arbitrary values on an abelian basis would not alone imply module linearity.
No converse is claimed: exactness at each spot is checked separately in steps 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3, and the Example does not assert that this is the only resolution of $S_2$ with these terms.

**The total differential.** On the summand $R^p\otimes_{A_m}X^q$ put
$$d^{n}\bigl(r\otimes x\bigr):=d_R^p(r)\otimes x+(-1)^p\,r\otimes d_X^q(x),\qquad r\otimes x\in R^p\otimes_{A_m}X^q,\ p+q=n .$$
The sign $(-1)^p$ uses the **homological** degree $p$ of the first factor only;
the internal degrees of the two factors are never used, and no internal sign
occurs anywhere in the construction. The differential is written additively over
the direct sum, so $d^n$ maps each summand into
$\bigl(R^\bullet\otimes_{A_m}X^\bullet\bigr)^{n+1}$, since $d_R^p$ raises the
homological degree by one and $d_X^q$ raises the second index by one.

**The positive twist.** Let
$$R_i:=\bigl[\,U_i\xrightarrow{\ \beta_i\ }A_m\,\bigr]$$
be the two-term cochain complex of graded $(A_m,A_m)$-bimodules with
$R_i^{-1}=U_i$, $R_i^{0}=A_m$ and zero in all other homological degrees, so that
$A_m$ sits in homological degree $0$ and the differential is $\beta_i$. That is,
$R_i$ is the mapping cone $\operatorname{Cone}(\beta_i)$ of
[[def-mapping-cone-of-a-chain-map]] of the map $\beta_i$ between complexes
concentrated in degree $0$, as verified below.

Fix $m\ge1$, let $A_m$ be the Khovanov–Seidel type A algebra with its internal
grading and its left-to-right path multiplication of
[[def-khovanov-seidel-type-a-quiver-algebra]] and
[[def-path-ring-of-a-finite-quiver-over-the-integers]], and for $1\le i\le m$
let
$$P_i=A_me_i\quad(\text{paths ending at }i),\qquad {}_iP=e_iA_m\quad(\text{paths beginning at }i),\qquad U_i=P_i\otimes_{\mathbb Z}{}_iP$$
be the graded $(A_m,A_m)$-bimodule of
[[def-two-sided-projective-khovanov-seidel-bimodule-functors]], with left action
$a\cdot(x\otimes y)=(ax)\otimes y$ and right action $(x\otimes y)\cdot a=x\otimes(ya)$.

**The total object.** For each $n\in\mathbb Z$ put
$$\bigl(R^\bullet\otimes_{A_m}X^\bullet\bigr)^n:=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}R^p\otimes_{A_m}X^q,$$
the direct sum over the $n$-th diagonal of balanced tensor products of
[[def-graded-balanced-tensor-product-and-homogeneous-hom]], each carrying its
total internal grading, in which the elementary tensor of homogeneous elements of
degrees $i$ and $j$ has degree $i+j$. This is the cohomological rewriting of the
familiar direct-sum totalization of the tensor product of a right and a left
complex of [[def-tensor-product-total-complex-of-chain-complexes]].

2. For every graded left $R$-module $N$ and graded right $R$-module $M$ the
tensor-unit maps $\lambda_N:R\otimes_RN\to N$, $r\otimes n\mapsto rn$, and
$\rho_M:M\otimes_RR\to M$, $m\otimes r\mapsto mr$, are degree-zero isomorphisms,
compatible with outer actions.

**Internal shift.** For $r\in\mathbb Z$ and a graded left $A_m$-module $M$ the
**internal shift** $M\{r\}$ is the graded module with
$$(M\{r\})_d=M_{d-r}\qquad(d\in\mathbb Z),$$
carrying the same left $A_m$-action as $M$. The shift $\{1\}$ moves the grading

$$P_i:=A_me_i,\qquad {}_iP:=e_iA_m\qquad(0\le i\le m),$$
equipped with the grading in which a homogeneous element of $A_m$ of degree $d$
lies in degree $d$. Because paths are written left to right and the product is
concatenation, $P_i$ consists of the classes of the paths **ending** at $i$ and
${}_iP$ of the classes of the paths **beginning** at $i$. The algebra splits as
$$A_m=\bigoplus_{i=0}^mP_i=\bigoplus_{i=0}^m{}_iP$$

projectives is displayed as proved below.

shift $\{r\}$ is an automorphism of $A_m\text{-mod}$; each $P_i$ is a finite
graded projective left $A_m$-module and each ${}_iP$ a finite graded projective
right $A_m$-module, generated by $e_i$.

Fix $m\ge1$, let $C_m=K^b(\operatorname{proj}^{gr}A_m)$ be the bounded homotopy
category of finite graded projective left $A_m$-modules of
[[def-bounded-projective-homotopy-category-for-a-m]], with its homological shift
$[1]$ and its distinguished triangles. To provide a literal set of indices,
form the presentation-code category $\mathcal M_m^{\mathrm{code}}$: its objects
are pairs $(\mathbf r,N)$ where $\mathbf r=(r_1,\dots,r_s)$ is a finite list of
integers, $F_{\mathbf r}:=\bigoplus_{j=1}^s A_m\{r_j\}$, and $N$ is a graded
submodule of $F_{\mathbf r}$; the pair represents $F_{\mathbf r}/N$. Its
morphisms are all degree-zero $A_m$-module maps between the represented
quotients. The proof shows that this is a small category and every object of
$A_m\text{-mod}$ is isomorphic to a represented quotient. Let
$\mathcal C_m^{\mathrm{code}}$ be the small homotopy category of bounded
complexes of these codes whose represented terms are finite graded projective,
with finite direct sums encoded by concatenating presentations, and with
distinguished triangles given by cone triangles and their isomorphic images.
Every object of $C_m$ and every distinguished triangle in $C_m$ is represented up to
isomorphism in $\mathcal C_m^{\mathrm{code}}$. Write
$\operatorname{Iso}_{\mathrm{code}}(C_m)$ for the set of isomorphism types in
this coded category, and for $X\in C_m$ let $\tau(X)$ be its unique represented
type.

**The group.** Let
$$F:=\mathbb Z^{(\operatorname{Iso}_{\mathrm{code}}(C_m))}$$
be the free abelian group on the set $\operatorname{Iso}_{\mathrm{code}}(C_m)$ of
[[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]], with standard basis element
$e_{\tau(X)}$ attached to the represented type of $X$, and let $R\le F$ be the subgroup
generated by all elements
$$e_{\tau(Y)}-e_{\tau(X)}-e_{\tau(Z)}$$
attached to the distinguished triangles $X\to Y\to Z\to X[1]$ in
$\mathcal C_m^{\mathrm{code}}$. The
**zeroth $K$-group** of $C_m$ is
$$K_0(C_m):=F/R,$$
and the class of an object $X\in C_m$ is written $[X]:=e_{\tau(X)}+R$. This is the
usual isomorphism-type presentation of the zeroth $K$-group defined in Stacks
Project, Definition 13.28.1: its triangle relations identify isomorphic
objects, as verified for $C_m$ in step 4.1.

**Why the notation denotes.** Every claim needed to make the display meaningful
is proved below: the coded category is small and represents all objects and
triangle types of $C_m$, so the free abelian group on its isomorphism types
exists and $R$ is generated by a set; moreover $C_m$ is triangulated, so that
"distinguished triangle" refers to an actual triangulated structure. No
skeleton or global choice of representatives is needed: the generators are
isomorphism types in the explicit set of finite presentation codes, and any two
codes for the same object determine the same type.

**Elementary consequences.** For isomorphic objects $X\cong Y$ one has
$[X]=[Y]$ in $K_0(C_m)$, and for the zero object $[0]=0$; moreover
$[X\oplus Y]=[X]+[Y]$, so the group operation is compatible with finite direct
sums in the expected way.

**Scope.** This is the $K_0$ used on this page for the shift comparison: it is
formed from the distinguished triangles of $C_m$ only, and it imports no
graded Cartan pairing, no generic perfect-complex machinery and no ungraded
$K_0$-of-an-abelian-category theorem beyond the definition.

3.1 **Reduction of every presentation word.** We prove by induction on $k$
that every word of $k$ letters $t_i$ in $C_n$ equals a reduced $t$-word for
its image under $\Phi$. Every group word can first be put in this form:
$t_i^{-1}=t_i$ by the involution relator, so replace each inverse letter.
For $k=0$ the empty word is reduced for the identity. For the induction step
write the word as $u t_i$ with $u$ of length $k-1$, and let
$\tau=\Phi(u)$ and $\sigma=\tau s_i$. By induction $u$ equals a reduced
$t$-word $q$ for $\tau$. By [F1], either
$\operatorname{inv}(\sigma)=\operatorname{inv}(\tau)+1$ or it is
$\operatorname{inv}(\tau)-1$.

If the inversion number increases, $q t_i$ is reduced for $\sigma$ by
[F1], so it is the required representative. If it decreases, choose a
reduced $s$-word $r$ for $\sigma$; one exists because the $s_i$ generate
$S_n$ and minimal finite word length exists. Since
$\sigma s_i=\tau$ and
$\operatorname{inv}(\tau)=\operatorname{inv}(\sigma)+1$, the word $r s_i$
is reduced for $\tau$ by [F1]. Thus the two reduced words $q$ and $r s_i$
for $\tau$ are braid-connected by step 2.1; replacing $s$ by $t$ gives
$q=r t_i$ in $C_n$. Consequently
$u t_i=q t_i=r t_i^2=r$ in $C_n$, and $r$ is reduced for $\sigma$.
This completes the induction.

4.1 **Injectivity and the presentation (b).** If $g\in\ker\Phi$, represent
$g$ by a finite word and use step 3.1 to replace it in $C_n$ by a reduced
word for the identity of $S_n$. By [F1] the identity has inversion number
zero, so its only reduced word is empty; hence $g=1$. Thus $\Phi$ is
injective, and with step 1.1 it is an isomorphism.

$S_n$ is trivial, so the empty presentation is trivial as well. Every
argument above uses only finite words and induction on their lengths. ∎

**The bimodule.** Keep the ring $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ with $\deg x_i=2$,
the simple reflections $s_i$ and the invariants $R^{s_i}$ of
[[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]], and recall that $R$ is
a graded $(R,R)$-bimodule and that shifts are defined as in
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]]. For $1\le i\le n-1$ put
$$B_i:=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1),$$
the balanced tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]])
of the $(R,R^{s_i})$-bimodule $R$ with the $(R^{s_i},R)$-bimodule $R$, equipped
with the total internal grading of the tensor product and then shifted so that
$$(B_i)_d=\bigl(R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R\bigr)_{d+1}\qquad(d\in\mathbb Z).$$
In the notation of Elias–Williamson the shift $(r)$ has $M(r)_d=M_{d+r}$, so
$M(1)_d=M_{d+1}$; in the library convention $M\{r\}_d=M_{d-r}$ this is
$M(1)=M\{-1\}$, i.e. $M(r)=M\{-r\}$ for every integer $r$. Both conventions
appear on this page, and every shifted formula is read through this dictionary;
when no ambiguity is possible we write $M(r)$.

derivations.claim: The decomposition $R=R^{s_i}\oplus\alpha_iR^{s_i}$ is a direct sum of graded $(R^{s_i},R^{s_i})$-submodules, because the averaging idempotent $e=\tfrac12(1+s_i)$ satisfies $e^2=e$, $s_ie=es_i=e$ and $\ker e=(1-e)R=R(1-e)$ with $1-e=\tfrac12(1-s_i)$; applied to any $f$ this gives $f=e(f)+(1-e)(f)$ with $e(f)\in R^{s_i}$ and $(1-e)(f)=\tfrac12(f-s_i(f))=\tfrac12\alpha_i\partial_i(f)=\delta_i\partial_i(f)\in\alpha_iR^{s_i}$, by the formula $\partial_i(f)=\alpha_i^{-1}(f-s_i(f))$ and $\delta_i=\alpha_i/2$.

Left side: tensoring the decomposition of step 1.1 over $R^{s_i}$ in the *right* tensor slot gives the decomposition $R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R=(R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R^{s_i})\oplus(R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}\alpha_iR^{s_i})$ of graded left $R$-modules (the left action multiplies the first slot), with summands $\{r\otimes1:r\in R\}$ and $\{r\otimes\alpha_ir':r,r'\in R\}$: the first is isomorphic to $R$ as a graded left $R$-module through $r\otimes1\mapsto r$ with inverse $r\mapsto r\otimes1$, and the second is free of rank one as a left $R$-module with generator $1\otimes\alpha_i$, hence isomorphic to $R$ through $r\otimes\alpha_ir'\mapsto rr'$ (well defined by the balanced relation $r\otimes\alpha_ir'=(rr')\otimes\alpha_i$, and left $R$-linear because $r''(r\otimes\alpha_ir')=r''r\otimes\alpha_ir'$), with inverse $t\mapsto t\otimes\alpha_i$. Hence the elements $1\otimes1$ and $1\otimes\alpha_i$ form a graded left $R$-basis, of degrees $0$ and $2$ before the shift.

Right side: since $\alpha_iR^{s_i}\subseteq R$ is also an $(R^{s_i},R^{s_i})$-sub-bimodule, tensoring the decomposition of step 1.1 in the *left* tensor slot gives the decomposition $R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R=(R^{s_i}\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R)\oplus(\alpha_iR^{s_i}\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R)$ of graded right $R$-modules (the right action multiplies the second slot); the first summand is the set of elements $r'\otimes r$ and is isomorphic to $R$ through $1\otimes r\mapsto r$ with inverse $r\mapsto1\otimes r$, and the second summand is the set of elements $\alpha_ir'\otimes r=\alpha_i\otimes r'r$, free of rank one as a right $R$-module with generator $\alpha_i\otimes1$ and isomorphic to $R$ through $\alpha_i\otimes r\mapsto r$. Hence $1\otimes1$ and $\alpha_i\otimes1$ form a graded right $R$-basis, again of degrees $0$ and $2$; note that $1\otimes\alpha_i=(1\otimes1)\cdot\alpha_i$ is $\alpha_i$ times the first basis element and is not a right-basis element.

Applying the external shift $(1)$, which lowers degrees by one and preserves freeness with the same ranks, gives $B_i\cong R(-1)\oplus R(1)$ as a graded left $R$-module and as a graded right $R$-module, with left basis $1\otimes1$ of degree $-1$ and $1\otimes\alpha_i$ of degree $1$ and right basis $1\otimes1$ of degree $-1$ and $\alpha_i\otimes1$ of degree $1$; in particular $B_i$ is finite free of rank two on each side.

Tensor products: if $M$ is finite free as a left $R$-module with basis $m_1,\ldots,m_a$ and $N$ is finite free as a left $R$-module with basis $n_1,\ldots,n_b$, then $M\otimes_RN$ has the left $R$-basis $m_p\otimes n_q$: the map $R^a\otimes_RR^b\to R^{ab}$, $(r_p)\otimes(s_q)\mapsto(r_ps_q)$, is an isomorphism of left $R$-modules with inverse sending the standard basis vector to $m_p\otimes n_q$. The same computation with right modules and with homogeneous bases keeps track of gradings, so an iterated tensor product of the $B_i$ is finite free of rank $2^r$ on each side.

Therefore $B_i$ is free of rank two on both sides and every Bott–Samelson product $B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$ is finite free on both sides, with left and right bases obtained by tensoring the two-element bases of the factors and with degrees the sums of the factor degrees.

**Standard bimodules.** For $w\in S_n$ let $R_w$ be the graded $(R,R)$-bimodule
which equals $R$ as a graded $k$-vector space and has
$$f\cdot x=fx,\qquad x\cdot g=w(g)\,x\qquad(f,g,x\in R),$$
where $w(g)(\lambda):=g(w^{-1}\lambda)$; $R_w$ is generated by the element $1$ of
degree $0$. Write $(k)$ for the *external* shift $M(k):=M\{-k\}$ of
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]], so that
$M(k)_d=M_{d+k}$; this is the shift convention of the type-A sources, and it is
the one in which $B_i=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1)$ of
[[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]] has $1\otimes1$ of
degree $-1$. Put
$$\Delta_w(d):=R_w(d-\ell(w)),\qquad \nabla_w(d):=R_w(d+\ell(w))\qquad(d\in\mathbb Z),$$
so that $\Delta_w(d)$ is the standard bimodule $R_w$ with its generator in
degree $\ell(w)-d$, and $\nabla_w(d)$ is $R_w$ with its generator in degree
$-\ell(w)-d$. Thus $\Delta_w(0)=R_w\{\ell(w)\}$,
$\nabla_w(0)=R_w\{-\ell(w)\}$ and $\Delta_e(d)=\nabla_e(d)=R(d)$ is generated
in degree $-d$; in particular $\Delta_e(0)=\nabla_e(0)=R_e=R$.

derivations.claim: Set $I:=I(Gr(x))=\operatorname{Ann}(R_x)$, generated by $\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_n$, and fix a homogeneous lift $e\in E$ of the generator $1_{R_x(a)}$, so that the sub identifies with $R_y(b)$ through a chosen generator $\iota$ of degree $-b$. Since every $h\in I$ kills the image of $e$ in $R_x(a)$, one has $h\cdot e\in R_y(b)$, so $h\cdot e=c(h)\iota$ for a unique homogeneous element $c(h)\in R$, and $E$ is generated over $R$ by $e$ and $\iota$ with the single family of relations $h\cdot e=c(h)\iota$.

The assignment $h\mapsto c(h)$ is additive and satisfies $c(hh')=(\text{action of }h\text{ on }R_y)\cdot c(h')$ because $(hh')\cdot e=h\cdot(c(h')\iota)=h\cdot(c(h')\iota)$ in the sub-bimodule $R_y(b)$; writing $u_i$ for the image of $\ell_i$ under $R\otimes R\to R_y$, $h\mapsto h\cdot1_{R_y}$, one has $u_i\,c(\ell_j)=u_j\,c(\ell_i)$ for all $i,j$, since $\ell_i\ell_j=\ell_j\ell_i$ and $c(\ell_i\ell_j)=u_i\,c(\ell_j)$. Writing $m_i:=c(\ell_i)$, the extension is thus encoded by elements $m_1,\ldots,m_n\in R$ with $u_im_j=u_jm_i$ for all $i,j$, and nothing else.

The forms $\ell_i$ lie in the linear span of the variables of $R\otimes R$, and their images are $u_i=x_i-x_{yx^{-1}i}$: acting on $1_{R_y}$ one has $x_i\cdot1=x_i$ and $(1\otimes x_{x^{-1}i})\cdot1=x_{yx^{-1}i}$. Hence the ideal generated by the $u_i$ is the ideal of the subspace $V^{yx^{-1}}$ of $V$, the rank of the family $(u_i)$ is $r=n-\dim V^{yx^{-1}}=n-\dim V^{x^{-1}y}$, and $Gr(x)\cap Gr(y)=\{(x\lambda,\lambda):x^{-1}y\lambda=\lambda\}$, of dimension $\dim V^{x^{-1}y}$ in either graph.

Splitting: the extension splits iff there is $m\in R$ with $m_i=u_im$ for all $i$. Indeed a splitting of the sequence is exactly a homogeneous $R$-bimodule section of $E\to R_x(a)$, which has the form $1_{R_x(a)}\mapsto e'$ with $e'\in E$ lifting the generator; writing $e'=e-m\iota$ for some $m\in R$, the section is well defined iff $I\cdot e'=0$, i.e. iff $\ell_i\cdot(e-m\iota)=0$ for all $i$, that is $m_i=u_im$ for all $i$. Conversely such an $m$ makes $h\mapsto h\cdot e'$ a well-defined splitting.

Reduction of the $r\ge2$ case to two coprime forms: view $\sigma:=yx^{-1}$ as a permutation of the coordinate set, so $u_i=x_i-x_{\sigma i}$. If some cycle of $\sigma$ has length $\ge3$, two consecutive forms of that cycle, $x_i-x_{\sigma i}$ and $x_{\sigma i}-x_{\sigma^2i}$, are distinct irreducible elements of the polynomial ring and hence coprime in the UFD $R$; if all cycles have length $\le2$ and $r\ge2$, there are at least two transposition cycles and one form from each is a pair with disjoint supports, again coprime. In both cases pick such indices $p,q$.

Conclusion in the case $r\ge2$: from $u_pm_q=u_qm_p$ and $\gcd(u_p,u_q)=1$ in the UFD $R$ we get $u_p\mid m_p$ and $u_q\mid m_q$; write $m_p=u_pm$ and $m_q=u_qm'$; substituting gives $u_pu_qm'=u_qu_pm$, hence $m'=m$ as $R$ is a domain. For every index $i$, $u_pm_i=u_im_p=u_iu_pm$ forces $m_i=u_im$, since $u_p\ne0$ and $R$ is a domain. By step 3.1 the extension splits.

The case $r=1$: then $\sigma=yx^{-1}$ is a reflection, so it exchanges two coordinates $p\ne q$ and fixes the rest; hence $u_p=x_p-x_q$, $u_q=-u_p$ and $u_i=0$ for all other $i$. The relations $u_im_j=u_jm_i$ give $m_i=0$ for $i\notin\{p,q\}$ and $m_q=-m_p$, and by step 3.1 the extension splits iff $u_p\mid m_p$. In the localization at $u_p$ the obstruction dies because $u_p$ becomes a unit; moreover $u_p$ is a unit multiple of $\alpha_\sigma$, the equation of the hyperplane of fixed points of $\sigma=yx^{-1}$, and for $y=xt$ that reflection is $xtx^{-1}$ with equation $x(\alpha_t)$.

Both assertions follow: for $r\ge2$ every extension splits by step 4.1, and for $r=1$ with $y=xt$ every extension splits in the stated localization by step 4.2. All constructions were made on homogeneous lifts, so the argument applies degree by degree in the graded category.

**(c) The rank-one calculus.** Let $s=s_i$, $R^s=R^{s_i}$, $\alpha=\alpha_i$,
$\delta:=\alpha/2$, and $B_s=R\otimes_{R^s}R(1)$ with the images
$u:=1\otimes1$ of degree $-1$ and $w_0:=1\otimes\delta$ of degree $1$
([[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]]); these two elements
form a graded left $R$-basis of $B_s$, and every $g\in R$ has a unique
decomposition $g=g^++\delta g^-$ with $g^\pm\in R^s$, given by
$g^+=\tfrac12(g+s(g))$. The right action on the basis is
$$u\cdot g=g^+u+g^-w_0,\qquad w_0\cdot g=\delta^2g^-u+g^+w_0,$$
as follows from $1\otimes g=1\otimes(g^++\delta g^-)=g^+u+g^-w_0$ and
$\delta g=\delta g^++\delta^2g^-$ with $\delta^2=\alpha^2/4\in R^s$. Hence
$$(\delta u+w_0)\cdot g=g\,(\delta u+w_0),\qquad (\delta u-w_0)\cdot g=s(g)(\delta u-w_0),$$
so $R(\delta u+w_0)\cong R(-1)$ and $R(\delta u-w_0)\cong R_s(-1)$ are
sub-bimodules of $B_s$, generated in degree $1$. Moreover for
$f,h\in R$ one has $(fu+hw_0)\mapsto f+h\delta$ under $f\otimes g\mapsto fg$
and $(fu+hw_0)\mapsto f-h\delta$ under $f\otimes g\mapsto f s(g)$, because
$1\otimes g=g^+u+g^-w_0$ and $s(g)=g^+-\delta g^-$; both maps are surjective,
their kernels are the two displayed sub-bimodules, and all four maps of
$$0\to R(-1)\xrightarrow{\;1\mapsto\delta u+w_0\;}B_s \xrightarrow{\;f\otimes g\mapsto f s(g)\;}R_s(1)\to0,$$
$$0\to R_s(-1)\xrightarrow{\;1\mapsto\delta u-w_0\;}B_s \xrightarrow{\;f\otimes g\mapsto fg\;}R(1)\to0$$
are degree zero: sources and targets are generated in degree whose shifts match
the degree-$1$ elements $\delta u\pm w_0\in B_s$. Finally the two quotients are
the image of $u$, a free rank-one $R$-module with right action
$u\cdot g\equiv gu$ modulo $\delta u-w_0$ and $u\cdot g\equiv s(g)u$ modulo
$\delta u+w_0$ respectively, that is $R(1)$ and $R_s(1)$.

For each simple reflection $s_i$ the graded $(R,R)$-bimodule $B_i$ is free of
rank two as a left $R$-module and free of rank two as a right $R$-module, with
left basis $\{1\otimes1,\,1\otimes\alpha_i\}$ and right basis
$\{1\otimes1,\,\alpha_i\otimes1\}$, both of degrees $-1$ and $1$; and every
Bott–Samelson tensor product $B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$ is finite
free as a left $R$-module and finite free as a right $R$-module.

**(a) Maps between standard bimodules.** For $v,w\in S_n$ and $a,b\in\mathbb Z$,
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}\bigl(R_v(a),R_w(b)\bigr)\cong \begin{cases}R(b-a),&v=w,\\ 0,&v\ne w,\end{cases}$$
where $R(c)$ denotes the free graded $R$-module on one generator of degree $-c$.
Indeed a bimodule map is determined by $\varphi(1)=h\in R$, and $f\cdot1\cdot g\mapsto
f\,h\,w(g)$ must equal $v(g)\,f\,h$; since $R$ is a domain this forces
$v(g)h=w(g)h$ for all $g$, hence $h=0$ or $v=w$. The generator $1$ of $R_v(a)$
has degree $-a$ and maps to $h$, which has degree $\deg h-b$ as an element of
$R_w(b)$, so the homogeneous map $\varphi_h$ has degree $\deg h+a-b$ and
$\operatorname{Hom}(R_v(a),R_w(b))\cong R(b-a)$ in the case $v=w$.

**(b) Composition.** The $R$-balanced assignment
$$R_w\otimes_RR_v\longrightarrow R_{wv},\qquad a\otimes b\longmapsto a\,w(b),$$
where $w(b)(\lambda)=b(w^{-1}\lambda)$ and the product is taken in $R$, is a
well-defined degree-zero isomorphism of graded $(R,R)$-bimodules. It is well
defined because for $f\in R$ the relation $(a\cdot f)\otimes b=a\otimes(fb)$
reads $w(f)a\otimes b=a\otimes fb$ and maps to $w(f)\,a\,w(b)=a\,w(f)w(b)$ on
both sides; it is left $R$-linear, and it respects the right actions because
$w(bh)=w(b)w(h)$ for $h\in R$. It sends the $1$-tensor $1\otimes1$ of degree $0$
to $1$ and is therefore surjective, and both sides are free of rank one as left
$R$-modules, so it is an isomorphism. In particular
$R_w\otimes_RR_v\cong R_{wv}$ (and $R_w\otimes_RR_v\cong R_w$ only when $v=e$),
while tensoring with $w=e$ shows that the assignment is compatible with the
unit. The single assignment $1\otimes1\mapsto1$ does extend uniquely to a bimodule
map, and the map it extends to is exactly the twisted one above; what fails is
the untwisted formula $a\otimes b\mapsto ab$, which is not balanced when $w\ne e$: the equality $(1\cdot f)\otimes1=1\otimes f$ in $R_w\otimes_RR_v$ would map to $w(f)$ on the left and $f$ on the right, and these differ for a polynomial moved by $w$.

1. *Closure under tensoring with a generator.* (Proposition 5.7(1) and
   Proposition 5.9(1).) If $M\in F_\Delta$ then $R\otimes_{R^s}M\in F_\Delta$,
   and if $M\in F_\nabla$ then $R\otimes_{R^s}M\in F_\nabla$; in both cases the
   quotients of the resulting flag are again standard bimodules, indexed by the
   quotients of the flag of $M$. Moreover (the proofs of the same two
   propositions) the multiplicities of the new flag are given, for
   $\ell(x)>\ell(sx)$, by the recursions
   $$(B_s\otimes_RM:\Delta_x(d))=(M:\Delta_x(d+1))+(M:\Delta_{sx}(d)),\qquad (B_s\otimes_RM:\Delta_{sx}(d))=(M:\Delta_x(d))+(M:\Delta_{sx}(d-1)),$$
   and dually
   $$(B_s\otimes_RM:\nabla_x(d))=(M:\nabla_x(d-1))+(M:\nabla_{sx}(d)),\qquad (B_s\otimes_RM:\nabla_{sx}(d))=(M:\nabla_x(d))+(M:\nabla_{sx}(d+1)).$$
   In Notation 5.6 the source uses the shifted reflection functor
   $\theta_s=R[1]\otimes_{R^s}(-)=B_s\otimes_R-$, with $[1]=(1)=\{-1\}$.
   Read in the other direction, the two
   recursions say that a flag quotient of $M$ with graph $y$ and index $e$
   produces the two quotients with graphs $sy$ and $y$ of $B_s\otimes_RM$: the
   quotient with graph $sy$ carries the same index $e$, while the index of the
   quotient with graph $y$ changes by $-1$ in the $\Delta$-chart when
   $\ell(y)>\ell(sy)$ and by $+1$ when $\ell(sy)>\ell(y)$, the two signs being
   exchanged in the $\nabla$-chart. The two pairs match the two Hecke expansions
   of $(\widetilde T_s+v)h_\Delta(M)$ and $(\widetilde T_s+v)h_\nabla(M)$ in
   the basis $\{\widetilde T_x\}$, which is the source's own interpretation of
   the recursions.

**(e) Opposite bimodules.** For a graded $(R,R)$-bimodule $M$ let
$M^{\mathrm{op}}$ be the graded $(R,R)$-bimodule with the same underlying
graded $k$-module and operations $r\cdot^{\mathrm{op}}m\cdot^{\mathrm{op}}s=s\,m\,r$;
since $R$ is commutative this is again a graded $(R,R)$-bimodule, and the
following four remarks are used by the later support-filtration items.

1. The flip $m\otimes n\mapsto n\otimes m$ is a well-defined degree-zero
   bijection $(M\otimes_RN)^{\mathrm{op}}\to N^{\mathrm{op}}\otimes_RM^{\mathrm{op}}$,
   because $mr\otimes n=m\otimes rn$ maps to
   $n\otimes mr=(n\cdot^{\mathrm{op}}r)\otimes m=rn\otimes m$ in
   $N^{\mathrm{op}}\otimes_RM^{\mathrm{op}}$.
2. $R_x^{\mathrm{op}}\cong R_{x^{-1}}$ through $m\mapsto x^{-1}(m)$, and
   $B_s^{\mathrm{op}}\cong B_s$ through the flip $f\otimes g\mapsto g\otimes f$;
   both are degree-zero isomorphisms of graded $(R,R)$-bimodules.
3. Write $\tau$ for the flip of the two factors of $V\times V$. A nonzero
   element $m$ of a standard bimodule has support exactly the single graph of
   its standard, since the annihilator of the generator of $R_w$ is the prime
   ideal $I(Gr(w))$; for the same reason
   $\operatorname{Ann}_{M^{\mathrm{op}}}(m)=\sigma(\operatorname{Ann}_M(m))$ under
   the flip $\sigma(f\otimes g)=g\otimes f$, so
   $\operatorname{supp}_{M^{\mathrm{op}}}(m)=\tau(\operatorname{supp}_M(m))$.
   Since $\tau(Gr(x))=Gr(x^{-1})$ and $\ell(x^{-1})=\ell(x)$, the length
   filtrations satisfy $\Gamma_{\ge i}(M^{\mathrm{op}})=\Gamma_{\ge i}M$ and
   $\Gamma_{\le i}(M^{\mathrm{op}})=\Gamma_{\le i}M$ as $k$-submodules.
4. Consequently a $\Delta$-flag of $M$ with quotients $R_{x_j}\{a_j\}$ is a
   $\Delta$-flag of $M^{\mathrm{op}}$ with quotients $R_{x_j^{-1}}\{a_j\}$ in
   the same order, and a $\nabla$-flag of $M$ is a $\nabla$-flag of
   $M^{\mathrm{op}}$ in the same order: the graph index inverts, the length is
   unchanged by item 3, and the refined length filtration is preserved by the
   opposite functor, so this functor preserves *each* of the two flag
   categories, $M\in F_\Delta\iff M^{\mathrm{op}}\in F_\Delta$ and
   $M\in F_\nabla\iff M^{\mathrm{op}}\in F_\nabla$.

**Support filtrations.** A $\Delta$-flag of a graded $R$-bimodule $M$ is a
finite chain $0=M_0\subseteq M_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq M_k=M$ of graded
sub-bimodules which refines the length filtration
$$M=\Gamma_{\ge0}M\supseteq\Gamma_{\ge1}M\supseteq\cdots\supseteq\Gamma_{\ge\ell(w_0)+1}M=0$$
of $M$ (here $\Gamma_{\ge0}M=M$ for every bimodule supported on
$Gr(S_n)=\bigcup_{w}Gr(w)$, which all bimodules of this page are, and
$\Gamma_{\ge i}M=0$ for $i>\ell(w_0)$ because no graph $Gr(x)$ with
$\ell(x)>i$ remains) and whose successive quotients are
standard bimodules $M_j/M_{j-1}\cong R_{x_j}\{a_j\}$. We require each
length layer to be a finite direct sum of shifted graph bimodules of that
length, as in Soergel's Definition 5.4. Thus the
quotients carry a numbering with $\ell(x_1)\ge\cdots\ge\ell(x_k)$ and each
$R_{x_j}\{a_j\}$ is one graph, so that $M$ has a "support flag" in the sense of
Soergel's $F_\Delta$. A $\nabla$-flag has the same direct-sum condition on its length layers, with the reverse length
filtration $\Gamma_{\le i}M$ and $\ell(x_1)\le\cdots\le\ell(x_k)$. The
refinement condition is a condition on supports, not an ordering of incomparable
quotients of equal length; only the lengths are ordered. For $i=\ell(x)$ the
graded multiplicity is
$$(M:\Delta_x(d)):=\text{multiplicity of }\Delta_x(d)\text{ in } \Gamma_{\ge i}M/\Gamma_{\ge i+1}M,$$
and, for a $\nabla$-flag, $(M:\nabla_x(d))$ is the multiplicity of
$\nabla_x(d)$ in $\Gamma_{\le i}M/\Gamma_{\le i-1}M$; a priori both symbols
refer to a chosen compatible enumeration (the next items on this page prove that
they do not depend on it). With $T_x$ the Hecke basis of
[[lem-type-a-hecke-standard-basis-for-soergel-comparison]] and
$\widetilde T_x:=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$, the character sums attached to a flag are

2. *Stability of the flag categories.* (Bemerkung 5.5.) The layers

   under direct summands as well; the same holds for $F_\nabla$ with the

7. *Bruhat-refining enumerations.* (Lemma 6.3 and its proof.) Let $B\in F_\nabla$
   and let $y_0,y_1,\ldots$ be an enumeration of $S_n$ in which Bruhat-larger

   the evident map $\Gamma_{\le y}B/\Gamma_{<y}B\to\Gamma_{C(k)}B/\Gamma_{C(k-1)}B$
   is an isomorphism, both sides are finite direct sums of objects of the form
   $\nabla_y(\mu)$, and $\nabla_y(\mu)$ occurs in this quotient exactly

derivations.claim: Intrinsicness: choose a Bruhat-compatible enumeration $y_0,y_1,\ldots$ of $S_n$, listing larger elements later, and group the flag quotients by their graph index. For each $y$, [F3] identifies the quotient at that position with the canonical Bruhat layer $\Gamma_{\le y}M/\Gamma_{<y}M$ and says it is a direct sum of $\nabla_y(\mu)$ with multiplicities exactly $(M:\nabla_y(\mu))$. This canonical layer depends only on $M$, so the multiplicities are independent of the compatible enumeration; the analogous assertion for $\Delta$ follows from the $F_\Delta$ clause of [F3] and its canonical upper Bruhat layer. For a fixed graph, the multiplicities of its shifts are determined by the graded dimension after quotienting its free graph module by $R_+$; thus they are intrinsic even among repeated copies of that graph. The comparison in [F3] swaps distinct incomparable graph indices, with the extension-vanishing argument already included there; grouping by graph index means no swap of repeated copies of one standard is needed. Hence both character sums depend only on $M$.

Additivity: for every support set $A$ one has $\Gamma_A(M'\oplus M'')=\Gamma_AM'\oplus\Gamma_AM''$. Indeed the support of $(m',m'')$ is the union of the two component supports, so it lies in $Gr(A)$ exactly when each component does. Taking consecutive length cutoffs therefore identifies every length layer of $M$ with the direct sum of the corresponding layers of $M'$ and $M''$. Decomposing these layers into shifted graph modules adds their multiplicities. Equivalently one interleaves the two flags in length order, preserving the order within each flag. This proves additivity for both charts.

Direct summands: if $N$ is a direct summand of $M$ and $N\in F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$, write $M=N\oplus N'$. By [F2], the complement $N'$ is also in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$. Additivity from step 2.1 shows that each multiplicity in $M$ is the sum of the corresponding multiplicities in $N$ and $N'$, and therefore the intrinsic formulas also apply to the summands. The flags are finite by the definition of these classes.

**Invariants and the Demazure operator.** Let $R^{s_i}$ denote the subring of
$s_i$-invariants and, in the balanced normalization, define
$$\partial_i(f):=\frac{f-s_i(f)}{\alpha_i}\qquad(f\in R),$$
so that $\partial_i=\varepsilon_i\partial_i^\beta$ with
$\partial_i^\beta(f)=(f-s_i(f))/\beta_i$; the kernel and the surjectivity below
are the same for both operators, and the algebraic items of this page may use
either.
This is well defined and lands in $R^{s_i}$: $R$ is free over $R^{s_i}$ with
basis $\{1,\alpha_i\}$, because $2$ is invertible in $\mathbb Q$ and every
polynomial can be written uniquely as $f=g+\alpha_i h$ with
$g=\tfrac12(f+s_i(f))$ and $h=\tfrac12\partial_i(f)$; the two summands are
independent over $R^{s_i}$ since $\alpha_i$ is not a zero divisor. Hence
$s_i(\alpha_i h)=-\alpha_i s_i(h)$ forces the $\alpha_i$-part of $f-s_i(f)$ to be
$2\alpha_i h$, so $\partial_i(g)=0$ for $g\in R^{s_i}$ and
$$\partial_i(\alpha_ih)=2h\qquad(h\in R^{s_i}).$$
The factor $2$ is the one displayed: applying $\partial_i$ to
$\delta_i h$ with $\delta_i:=\alpha_i/2$ returns $h$, so $\partial_i$ is
$R^{s_i}$-linear and surjective onto $R^{s_i}$ (and the same operator annihilates
$R^{s_i}$, so its kernel is exactly $R^{s_i}$).

**The bimodule.** Keep the ring $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ with $\deg x_i=2$,
the simple reflections $s_i$ and the invariants $R^{s_i}$ of
[[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]], and recall that $R$ is
a graded $(R,R)$-bimodule and that shifts are defined as in
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]]. For $1\le i\le n-1$ put
$$B_i:=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1),$$
the balanced tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]])
of the $(R,R^{s_i})$-bimodule $R$ with the $(R^{s_i},R)$-bimodule $R$, equipped
with the total internal grading of the tensor product and then shifted so that
$$(B_i)_d=\bigl(R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R\bigr)_{d+1}\qquad(d\in\mathbb Z).$$
In the notation of Elias–Williamson the shift $(r)$ has $M(r)_d=M_{d+r}$, so
$M(1)_d=M_{d+1}$; in the library convention $M\{r\}_d=M_{d-r}$ this is
$M(1)=M\{-1\}$, i.e. $M(r)=M\{-r\}$ for every integer $r$. Both conventions
appear on this page, and every shifted formula is read through this dictionary;
when no ambiguity is possible we write $M(r)$.

For each simple reflection $s_i$ the graded $(R,R)$-bimodule $B_i$ is free of
rank two as a left $R$-module and free of rank two as a right $R$-module, with
left basis $\{1\otimes1,\,1\otimes\alpha_i\}$ and right basis
$\{1\otimes1,\,\alpha_i\otimes1\}$, both of degrees $-1$ and $1$; and every
Bott–Samelson tensor product $B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$ is finite
free as a left $R$-module and finite free as a right $R$-module.
$$B_{\underline i}:=B_{i_1}\otimes_RB_{i_2}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r},$$

derivations.claim: Since $\alpha$ is $s$-anti-invariant, $\partial_s$ is $R^s$-linear and $\partial_s(h)=0$ for $h\in R^s$, while $\partial_s(\delta)=\tfrac12\partial_s(\alpha)=1$ by [F1]; and $\delta^2=\alpha^2/4\in R^s$ lies in the kernel, so in the basis $(1,\delta)$ the form $\langle f,g\rangle_s=\partial_s(fg)$ has $\langle1,1\rangle_s=0$, $\langle1,\delta\rangle_s=1$, $\langle\delta,\delta\rangle_s=0$, that is Gram matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, whence $(1,\delta)$ and $(\delta,1)$ are mutually dual bases.

The assignment $\Phi_M(f\otimes m)(g):=\partial_s(fg)m$ is well defined on the balanced tensor product, since $\partial_s(hfg)m=\partial_s(fg)\,hm$ for $h\in R^s$, and its values are $R^s$-linear in $g$. For the left $R$-action $(r\cdot\psi)(g)=\psi(rg)$ on $\operatorname{Hom}_{R^s}(R,M)$, one has $\Phi_M(rf\otimes m)(g)=\Phi_M(f\otimes m)(rg)$, so $\Phi_M$ is $R$-linear. On the unshifted tensor product its formula lowers degree by two because $\partial_s$ has degree $-2$; hence the domain shift $R\{-2\}$ makes $\Phi_M$ homogeneous of degree zero.

Hom-tensor adjunction over $R^s$ as in [F3] turns $B_s\otimes_RM=R\otimes_{R^s}(R\{-1\}\otimes_RM)$ into the hom space $\operatorname{Hom}_{R^s\text{-}R}(R\{-1\}\otimes_RM,N)$, and a second adjunction identifies the latter with $\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,\operatorname{Hom}_{R^s}(R\{-1\},N))$.

Put $b_1=1$, $b_2=\delta$ and $b^1=\delta$, $b^2=1$. The Gram matrix of step 1.1 gives the two dual-basis identities $r=\sum_i b_i\partial_s(b^i r)=\sum_i\partial_s(r b_i)b^i$ for every $r\in R$. For any graded $R^s$-module $M$ define $\Psi_M(\psi):=1\otimes\psi(\delta)+\delta\otimes\psi(1)$ in $R\{-2\}\otimes_{R^s}M$ for $\psi\in\operatorname{Hom}_{R^s}(R,M)$. The first identity and $R^s$-linearity of $\psi$ give $\Phi_M\Psi_M(\psi)(r)=\psi(r)$. Conversely, writing $f=h_0+\delta h_1$ with $h_0,h_1\in R^s$, we have $\partial_s(f\delta)=h_0$ and $\partial_s(f)=h_1$, so $\Psi_M\Phi_M(f\otimes m)=1\otimes h_0m+\delta\otimes h_1m=f\otimes m$. If $\psi$ has degree $d$, then $1\otimes\psi(\delta)$ has degree $-2+(d+2)=d$ and $\delta\otimes\psi(1)$ has degree $0+d=d$; thus $\Psi_M$ is degree zero. Both formulas commute with every graded $R^s$-linear map $M\to M'$, so $\Phi_M$ is a natural degree-zero $R$-linear isomorphism for every graded $M$, without a freeness assumption.

Applying step 2.1 to the graded $R^s$-module $N\{1\}$ gives $\operatorname{Hom}_{R^s}(R\{-1\},N)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{R^s}(R,N\{1\})\cong R\{-2\}\otimes_{R^s}N\{1\}\cong R\{-1\}\otimes_{R^s}N$. The last object is $B_s\otimes_RN$: by the balanced tensor relation, $(R\otimes_{R^s}R\{-1\})\otimes_RN\cong R\otimes_{R^s}N\{-1\}\cong R\{-1\}\otimes_{R^s}N$, with no extra $R$ factor. These are degree-zero $(R,R)$-bimodule identifications by the shift convention; composing them with the two Hom-tensor adjunctions of step 1.3 gives the first displayed natural bijection.

The flip $f\otimes g\mapsto g\otimes f$ on $R\otimes_{R^s}R\{-1\}$ is well defined because $R$ is commutative and $R^s$ is central, is homogeneous because the factor degrees add, and is its own inverse. It intertwines the left and right $R$-actions, so it is a graded bimodule isomorphism $B_s\to B_s^{\mathrm{op}}$. In particular it fixes $u=1\otimes1$ and sends $w_0=1\otimes\delta$ to $\delta\otimes1$, both with their original degrees; it does not swap $u$ and $w_0$. Applying the first adjunction of step 3.1 to opposite bimodules yields the second displayed natural degree-zero bijection $\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M\otimes_RB_s,N)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,N\otimes_RB_s)$.

For completeness, the two triangle maps can be checked directly. Under $B_s\otimes_RB_s\cong R\otimes_{R^s}R\otimes_{R^s}R\{-2\}$, evaluation is the degree-zero bimodule map $\varepsilon((a\otimes b)\otimes(c\otimes d))=a\partial_s(bc)d$, and coevaluation is the degree-zero bimodule map sending $1\in R$ to $E:=\sum_i(b_i\otimes1)\otimes(1\otimes b^i)$, with the dual bases of step 2.1. The underlying degree of $E$ is two and the total shift is $-2$; $E$ is central for the outer $R$-actions, as is checked on the generators $R^s$ and $\delta$ using $\delta^2\in R^s$. For $z=a\otimes b\in B_s$, the composite $(\operatorname{id}_{B_s}\otimes\varepsilon)(E\otimes z)$ equals $\sum_i b_i\otimes\partial_s(b^i a)b=a\otimes b$, while $(\varepsilon\otimes\operatorname{id}_{B_s})(z\otimes E)$ equals $\sum_i a\partial_s(b b_i)\otimes b^i=a\otimes b$, by the two dual-basis identities of step 2.1. Tensoring these maps with any graded bimodule gives the unit and counit triangle identities for both adjunctions; all maps are natural and degree zero.

**Graphs and supports.** Keep $k=\mathbb Q$, $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ with
$\deg x_i=2$, and the affine scheme $V=\mathbb A^n_k=\operatorname{Spec}R$,
whose $k$-points are $V(k)=k^n$. Use the place-permuting action of $S_n$
from [[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]].
For $w\in S_n$ let
$$Gr(w):=\operatorname{Graph}(w:V\to V)\subseteq V\times_kV,\quad Gr(w)(k)=\{(w\lambda,\lambda):\lambda\in k^n\},\qquad Gr(A):=\bigcup_{w\in A}Gr(w)\ \ (A\subseteq S_n),$$
so that $V\times_kV=\operatorname{Spec}(R\otimes_kR)$ and $Gr(w)$ is the graph
of the map $\lambda\mapsto w\lambda$. A graded $(R,R)$-bimodule $M$ is the
same thing as a graded module over $R\otimes_kR$, and the support of $m\in M$ is
the zero set $\operatorname{supp}(m):=V(\operatorname{Ann}(m))\subseteq V\times V$
of its annihilator ideal in $R\otimes_kR$. For $A\subseteq S_n$ put
$$\Gamma_AM:=\{m\in M:\operatorname{supp}(m)\subseteq Gr(A)\},$$
a graded sub-bimodule of $M$. Since $Gr(A)$ is closed with radical ideal
$I(Gr(A))=\bigcap_{w\in A}I(Gr(w))$ (an intersection of prime ideals, since each
$Gr(w)$ is a linear subspace of $V\times V$ complementing the second factor), an
element $m$ lies in $\Gamma_AM$ exactly when $I(Gr(A))^N m=0$ for some $N\ge0$:
this is the Nullstellensatz together with the Noetherianity of
$R\otimes_kR$. The ideal itself need not annihilate such an element — in
$(R\otimes_kR)/I(Gr(e))^2$ the class of $1$ is supported on $Gr(e)$ but is not
killed by $I(Gr(e))$ — which is why the criterion is stated with a power of the
ideal. For $i\in\mathbb Z$ we write
$$\Gamma_{\ge i}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\ell(x)\ge i\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{\le i}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\ell(x)\le i\}}M,$$
using the length function of [[lem-type-a-reduced-words-are-connected-by-braid-moves]],
while for $y\in S_n$ the $y$-indexed symbols denote the *Bruhat
principal-set* cutoffs of Soergel's Notation 6.1,
$$\Gamma_{\le y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x\le y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{<y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x<y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{\ge y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x\ge y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{>y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x>y\}}M,$$
with $\Gamma_yM:=\Gamma_{\{y\}}M$ the elements concentrated on the single graph
$Gr(y)$ and $\Gamma_{\ne y}M:=\Gamma_{S_n\setminus\{y\}}M$ the elements
concentrated off $Gr(y)$. The integer-indexed symbols of the previous display are
the *length* cutoffs used to define the flags below, and they must not be
confused with the element-indexed Bruhat cutoffs: for $y=s_1$ in $S_4$ the
submodule $\Gamma_{\le1}M$ contains $Gr(s_3)$ while
$\Gamma_{\le y}M=\Gamma_{\{e,s_1\}}M$ does not, and the two cutoffs agree at
the extremes, $\Gamma_{\le w_0}=\Gamma_{\le\ell(w_0)}=M$ and
$\Gamma_{<e}=\Gamma_{\le-1}=0$. So
$\Gamma^yM:=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$ is Soergel's $y$-layer
*quotient*; following Soergel's
Notation 6.1 we write the two $y$-layer quotients with an underline,
$$\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M:=\Gamma_{\le y}M/\Gamma_{<y}M,\qquad \underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M:=\Gamma_{\ge y}M/\Gamma_{>y}M,$$
so that $\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$ is the quotient of the lower support
submodule by $\Gamma_{<y}M$ and $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M$ the quotient of
the upper support submodule by the part supported strictly above $Gr(y)$.

**Standard bimodules.** For $w\in S_n$ let $R_w$ be the graded $(R,R)$-bimodule
which equals $R$ as a graded $k$-vector space and has
$$f\cdot x=fx,\qquad x\cdot g=w(g)\,x\qquad(f,g,x\in R),$$
where $w(g)(\lambda):=g(w^{-1}\lambda)$; $R_w$ is generated by the element $1$ of
degree $0$. Write $(k)$ for the *external* shift $M(k):=M\{-k\}$ of
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]], so that
$M(k)_d=M_{d+k}$; this is the shift convention of the type-A sources, and it is
the one in which $B_i=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1)$ of
[[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]] has $1\otimes1$ of
degree $-1$. Put
$$\Delta_w(d):=R_w(d-\ell(w)),\qquad \nabla_w(d):=R_w(d+\ell(w))\qquad(d\in\mathbb Z),$$
so that $\Delta_w(d)$ is the standard bimodule $R_w$ with its generator in
degree $\ell(w)-d$, and $\nabla_w(d)$ is $R_w$ with its generator in degree
$-\ell(w)-d$. Thus $\Delta_w(0)=R_w\{\ell(w)\}$,
$\nabla_w(0)=R_w\{-\ell(w)\}$ and $\Delta_e(d)=\nabla_e(d)=R(d)$ is generated
in degree $-d$; in particular $\Delta_e(0)=\nabla_e(0)=R_e=R$.

For graded free $R$-modules in this type-A page, a homogeneous free generator of degree $a$ contributes $v^a$ to graded rank. This is the $v\mapsto v^{-1}$ transform of Soergel's rank convention in his Notation 5.2; all rank formulas below use this convention.

**Support filtrations.** A $\Delta$-flag of a graded $R$-bimodule $M$ is a
finite chain $0=M_0\subseteq M_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq M_k=M$ of graded
sub-bimodules which refines the length filtration
$$M=\Gamma_{\ge0}M\supseteq\Gamma_{\ge1}M\supseteq\cdots\supseteq\Gamma_{\ge\ell(w_0)+1}M=0$$
of $M$ (here $\Gamma_{\ge0}M=M$ for every bimodule supported on
$Gr(S_n)=\bigcup_{w}Gr(w)$, which all bimodules of this page are, and
$\Gamma_{\ge i}M=0$ for $i>\ell(w_0)$ because no graph $Gr(x)$ with
$\ell(x)>i$ remains) and whose successive quotients are
standard bimodules $M_j/M_{j-1}\cong R_{x_j}\{a_j\}$. We require each
length layer to be a finite direct sum of shifted graph bimodules of that
length, as in Soergel's Definition 5.4. Thus the
quotients carry a numbering with $\ell(x_1)\ge\cdots\ge\ell(x_k)$ and each
$R_{x_j}\{a_j\}$ is one graph, so that $M$ has a "support flag" in the sense of
Soergel's $F_\Delta$. A $\nabla$-flag has the same direct-sum condition on its length layers, with the reverse length
filtration $\Gamma_{\le i}M$ and $\ell(x_1)\le\cdots\le\ell(x_k)$. The
refinement condition is a condition on supports, not an ordering of incomparable
quotients of equal length; only the lengths are ordered. For $i=\ell(x)$ the
graded multiplicity is
$$(M:\Delta_x(d)):=\text{multiplicity of }\Delta_x(d)\text{ in } \Gamma_{\ge i}M/\Gamma_{\ge i+1}M,$$
and, for a $\nabla$-flag, $(M:\nabla_x(d))$ is the multiplicity of
$\nabla_x(d)$ in $\Gamma_{\le i}M/\Gamma_{\le i-1}M$; a priori both symbols
refer to a chosen compatible enumeration (the next items on this page prove that
they do not depend on it). With $T_x$ the Hecke basis of
[[lem-type-a-hecke-standard-basis-for-soergel-comparison]] and
$\widetilde T_x:=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$, the character sums attached to a flag are
$$h_\Delta(M):=\sum_{x,d}(M:\Delta_x(d))\,v^d\,\widetilde T_x,\qquad h_\nabla(M):=\sum_{x,d}(M:\nabla_x(d))\,v^{-d}\,\widetilde T_x,$$
and they are used only through the items that prove these sums intrinsic.

**Small $n$.** For $n\le1$ there is a single element $e$ and every object is a finite direct sum of shifts $\bigoplus_j R(d_j)$. Its one-graph flags have these summands as quotients, so $h_\Delta=\sum_jv^{d_j}\widetilde T_e$ and $h_\nabla=\sum_jv^{-d_j}\widetilde T_e$; in particular both characters send the unit $R$ to $1$.

**Standard bimodules.** For $w\in S_n$ let $R_w$ be the graded $(R,R)$-bimodule
which equals $R$ as a graded $k$-vector space and has
$$f\cdot x=fx,\qquad x\cdot g=w(g)\,x\qquad(f,g,x\in R),$$
where $w(g)(\lambda):=g(w^{-1}\lambda)$; $R_w$ is generated by the element $1$ of
degree $0$. Write $(k)$ for the *external* shift $M(k):=M\{-k\}$ of
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]], so that
$M(k)_d=M_{d+k}$; this is the shift convention of the type-A sources, and it is
the one in which $B_i=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1)$ of
[[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]] has $1\otimes1$ of
degree $-1$. Put
$$\Delta_w(d):=R_w(d-\ell(w)),\qquad \nabla_w(d):=R_w(d+\ell(w))\qquad(d\in\mathbb Z),$$
so that $\Delta_w(d)$ is the standard bimodule $R_w$ with its generator in
degree $\ell(w)-d$, and $\nabla_w(d)$ is $R_w$ with its generator in degree
$-\ell(w)-d$. Thus $\Delta_w(0)=R_w\{\ell(w)\}$,
$\nabla_w(0)=R_w\{-\ell(w)\}$ and $\Delta_e(d)=\nabla_e(d)=R(d)$ is generated

**Graphs and supports.** Keep $k=\mathbb Q$, $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ with
$\deg x_i=2$, and the affine scheme $V=\mathbb A^n_k=\operatorname{Spec}R$,
whose $k$-points are $V(k)=k^n$. Use the place-permuting action of $S_n$
from [[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]].
For $w\in S_n$ let
$$Gr(w):=\operatorname{Graph}(w:V\to V)\subseteq V\times_kV,\quad Gr(w)(k)=\{(w\lambda,\lambda):\lambda\in k^n\},\qquad Gr(A):=\bigcup_{w\in A}Gr(w)\ \ (A\subseteq S_n),$$
so that $V\times_kV=\operatorname{Spec}(R\otimes_kR)$ and $Gr(w)$ is the graph
of the map $\lambda\mapsto w\lambda$. A graded $(R,R)$-bimodule $M$ is the
same thing as a graded module over $R\otimes_kR$, and the support of $m\in M$ is
the zero set $\operatorname{supp}(m):=V(\operatorname{Ann}(m))\subseteq V\times V$
of its annihilator ideal in $R\otimes_kR$. For $A\subseteq S_n$ put
$$\Gamma_AM:=\{m\in M:\operatorname{supp}(m)\subseteq Gr(A)\},$$
a graded sub-bimodule of $M$. Since $Gr(A)$ is closed with radical ideal
$I(Gr(A))=\bigcap_{w\in A}I(Gr(w))$ (an intersection of prime ideals, since each
$Gr(w)$ is a linear subspace of $V\times V$ complementing the second factor), an
element $m$ lies in $\Gamma_AM$ exactly when $I(Gr(A))^N m=0$ for some $N\ge0$:
this is the Nullstellensatz together with the Noetherianity of
$R\otimes_kR$. The ideal itself need not annihilate such an element — in
$(R\otimes_kR)/I(Gr(e))^2$ the class of $1$ is supported on $Gr(e)$ but is not
killed by $I(Gr(e))$ — which is why the criterion is stated with a power of the
ideal. For $i\in\mathbb Z$ we write
$$\Gamma_{\ge i}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\ell(x)\ge i\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{\le i}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\ell(x)\le i\}}M,$$
using the length function of [[lem-type-a-reduced-words-are-connected-by-braid-moves]],
while for $y\in S_n$ the $y$-indexed symbols denote the *Bruhat
principal-set* cutoffs of Soergel's Notation 6.1,
$$\Gamma_{\le y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x\le y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{<y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x<y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{\ge y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x\ge y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{>y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x>y\}}M,$$
with $\Gamma_yM:=\Gamma_{\{y\}}M$ the elements concentrated on the single graph
$Gr(y)$ and $\Gamma_{\ne y}M:=\Gamma_{S_n\setminus\{y\}}M$ the elements
concentrated off $Gr(y)$. The integer-indexed symbols of the previous display are
the *length* cutoffs used to define the flags below, and they must not be
confused with the element-indexed Bruhat cutoffs: for $y=s_1$ in $S_4$ the
submodule $\Gamma_{\le1}M$ contains $Gr(s_3)$ while
$\Gamma_{\le y}M=\Gamma_{\{e,s_1\}}M$ does not, and the two cutoffs agree at
the extremes, $\Gamma_{\le w_0}=\Gamma_{\le\ell(w_0)}=M$ and
$\Gamma_{<e}=\Gamma_{\le-1}=0$. So
$\Gamma^yM:=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$ is Soergel's $y$-layer
*quotient*; following Soergel's
Notation 6.1 we write the two $y$-layer quotients with an underline,
$$\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M:=\Gamma_{\le y}M/\Gamma_{<y}M,\qquad \underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M:=\Gamma_{\ge y}M/\Gamma_{>y}M,$$
so that $\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$ is the quotient of the lower support
submodule by $\Gamma_{<y}M$ and $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M$ the quotient of

**Standard bimodules.** For $w\in S_n$ let $R_w$ be the graded $(R,R)$-bimodule
which equals $R$ as a graded $k$-vector space and has
$$f\cdot x=fx,\qquad x\cdot g=w(g)\,x\qquad(f,g,x\in R),$$
where $w(g)(\lambda):=g(w^{-1}\lambda)$; $R_w$ is generated by the element $1$ of
degree $0$. Write $(k)$ for the *external* shift $M(k):=M\{-k\}$ of
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]], so that
$M(k)_d=M_{d+k}$; this is the shift convention of the type-A sources, and it is
the one in which $B_i=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1)$ of
[[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]] has $1\otimes1$ of
degree $-1$. Put
$$\Delta_w(d):=R_w(d-\ell(w)),\qquad \nabla_w(d):=R_w(d+\ell(w))\qquad(d\in\mathbb Z),$$
so that $\Delta_w(d)$ is the standard bimodule $R_w$ with its generator in
degree $\ell(w)-d$, and $\nabla_w(d)$ is $R_w$ with its generator in degree
$-\ell(w)-d$. Thus $\Delta_w(0)=R_w\{\ell(w)\}$,
$\nabla_w(0)=R_w\{-\ell(w)\}$ and $\Delta_e(d)=\nabla_e(d)=R(d)$ is generated
in degree $-d$; in particular $\Delta_e(0)=\nabla_e(0)=R_e=R$.

For graded free $R$-modules in this type-A page, a homogeneous free generator of degree $a$ contributes $v^a$ to graded rank. This is the $v\mapsto v^{-1}$ transform of Soergel's rank convention in his Notation 5.2; all rank formulas below use this convention.

**Support filtrations.** A $\Delta$-flag of a graded $R$-bimodule $M$ is a
finite chain $0=M_0\subseteq M_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq M_k=M$ of graded
sub-bimodules which refines the length filtration
$$M=\Gamma_{\ge0}M\supseteq\Gamma_{\ge1}M\supseteq\cdots\supseteq\Gamma_{\ge\ell(w_0)+1}M=0$$
of $M$ (here $\Gamma_{\ge0}M=M$ for every bimodule supported on
$Gr(S_n)=\bigcup_{w}Gr(w)$, which all bimodules of this page are, and
$\Gamma_{\ge i}M=0$ for $i>\ell(w_0)$ because no graph $Gr(x)$ with
$\ell(x)>i$ remains) and whose successive quotients are
standard bimodules $M_j/M_{j-1}\cong R_{x_j}\{a_j\}$. We require each
length layer to be a finite direct sum of shifted graph bimodules of that
length, as in Soergel's Definition 5.4. Thus the
quotients carry a numbering with $\ell(x_1)\ge\cdots\ge\ell(x_k)$ and each
$R_{x_j}\{a_j\}$ is one graph, so that $M$ has a "support flag" in the sense of
Soergel's $F_\Delta$. A $\nabla$-flag has the same direct-sum condition on its length layers, with the reverse length
filtration $\Gamma_{\le i}M$ and $\ell(x_1)\le\cdots\le\ell(x_k)$. The
refinement condition is a condition on supports, not an ordering of incomparable
quotients of equal length; only the lengths are ordered. For $i=\ell(x)$ the
graded multiplicity is
$$(M:\Delta_x(d)):=\text{multiplicity of }\Delta_x(d)\text{ in } \Gamma_{\ge i}M/\Gamma_{\ge i+1}M,$$
and, for a $\nabla$-flag, $(M:\nabla_x(d))$ is the multiplicity of
$\nabla_x(d)$ in $\Gamma_{\le i}M/\Gamma_{\le i-1}M$; a priori both symbols
refer to a chosen compatible enumeration (the next items on this page prove that
they do not depend on it). With $T_x$ the Hecke basis of
[[lem-type-a-hecke-standard-basis-for-soergel-comparison]] and
$\widetilde T_x:=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$, the character sums attached to a flag are
$$h_\Delta(M):=\sum_{x,d}(M:\Delta_x(d))\,v^d\,\widetilde T_x,\qquad h_\nabla(M):=\sum_{x,d}(M:\nabla_x(d))\,v^{-d}\,\widetilde T_x,$$
and they are used only through the items that prove these sums intrinsic.

**Small $n$.** For $n\le1$ there is a single element $e$ and every object is a finite direct sum of shifts $\bigoplus_j R(d_j)$. Its one-graph flags have these summands as quotients, so $h_\Delta=\sum_jv^{d_j}\widetilde T_e$ and $h_\nabla=\sum_jv^{-d_j}\widetilde T_e$; in particular both characters send the unit $R$ to $1$.

For each simple reflection $s_i$ the graded $(R,R)$-bimodule $B_i$ is free of
rank two as a left $R$-module and free of rank two as a right $R$-module, with
left basis $\{1\otimes1,\,1\otimes\alpha_i\}$ and right basis

**The bimodule.** Keep the ring $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ with $\deg x_i=2$,

with the total internal grading of the tensor product and then shifted so that
$$(B_i)_d=\bigl(R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R\bigr)_{d+1}\qquad(d\in\mathbb Z).$$
In the notation of Elias–Williamson the shift $(r)$ has $M(r)_d=M_{d+r}$, so
$M(1)_d=M_{d+1}$; in the library convention $M\{r\}_d=M_{d-r}$ this is
$M(1)=M\{-1\}$, i.e. $M(r)=M\{-r\}$ for every integer $r$. Both conventions
appear on this page, and every shifted formula is read through this dictionary;
when no ambiguity is possible we write $M(r)$.
