citations.quote: An integral domain $R$ is a **unique factorisation domain** (UFD) when every nonzero nonunit is a finite product of irreducible elements, and whenever $$a=p_1\cdots p_m=q_1\cdots q_n$$ are products of irreducibles, then $m=n$ and, after a permutation, each $p_i$ is associate to the corresponding $q_i$.

Let $R$ be an integral domain and let $p\in R$ be nonzero and not a unit. The element $p$ is **irreducible** if every factorisation $p=ab$ has $a$ or $b$ a unit. It is **prime** if $$p\mid ab\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p\mid a\text{ or }p\mid b$$ for all $a,b\in R$.

Let $R$ be a unique factorisation domain and let $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$. 1. If $f,g\in R[x]$ are primitive, then $fg$ is primitive. 2. If $p\in R[x]$ is primitive and has positive degree, then $p$ is irreducible in $R[x]$ if and only if it is irreducible in $K[x]$.

If $D$ is an integral domain, then $D\setminus\{0\}$ is multiplicative. Its localisation $$ \operatorname{Frac}(D)=(D\setminus\{0\})^{-1}D $$ is the **field of fractions** of $D$. Thus its elements are fractions $a/b$ with $a,b\in D$ and $b\ne0$, modulo the localisation equivalence relation.

For every integral domain $D$, the localisation $\operatorname{Frac}(D)$ is a field. Its canonical map $$ D\longrightarrow\operatorname{Frac}(D),\qquad d\longmapsto d/1, $$ is an injective unital ring homomorphism.
For every field $F$, the polynomial ring $F[x]$ is a unique factorisation domain.
Let $R$ be a commutative ring. Define polynomial rings in finitely many commuting indeterminates recursively by $$ R[x_1,\ldots,x_0]:=R,\qquad R[x_1,\ldots,x_{n+1}]:=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n][x_{n+1}].
If $R$ is an integral domain, then $R[x]$ is an integral domain.
If $R$ is an integral domain and $f,g\in R[x]$ are nonzero, then $fg\ne0$ and $$ \deg(fg)=\deg f+\deg g,\qquad \operatorname{lc}(fg)=\operatorname{lc}(f)\operatorname{lc}(g). $$
$R/P$ is an integral domain if and only if $P$ is a prime ideal. Here $R$ is commutative and $P\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}R$ is an ideal.

Let $R,S$ be commutative rings, let $\varphi\colon R\to S$ be a unital ring homomorphism, and let $s\in S$. There is a unique unital ring homomorphism $$ \operatorname{ev}_{\varphi,s}\colon R[x]\to S $$ that extends $\varphi$ on constant polynomials and sends $x$ to $s$.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]), with addition $+$, multiplication $\cdot$, and distinguished elements $0 \ne 1$. Then 1. $(F, +, \cdot, 0, 1)$ is a ring ([[def-ring]]), and it is commutative ([[def-commutative-ring]]), with $1 \ne 0$; 2. $F$ is an integral domain ([[def-zero-divisor-and-integral-domain]]); 3.

Let $R$ be a nonzero commutative ring. A **strict chain of prime ideals of length $n$** is a sequence $$ \mathfrak p_0\subsetneq\mathfrak p_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\mathfrak p_n $$ of prime ideals of $R$. The **Krull dimension** of $R$ is the supremum of all integers $n\ge 0$ for which such a chain exists.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}(R)$. The **height** of $\mathfrak p$ is the Krull dimension of the local ring $R_{\mathfrak p}$: $$ \operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)=\dim(R_{\mathfrak p}). $$

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $S\subseteq R$ be a multiplicative subset, and let $\lambda:R\to S^{-1}R$ be the localization map. Then contraction along $\lambda$ induces an inclusion-preserving bijection $\operatorname{Spec}(S^{-1}R)\to\{\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}(R):\mathfrak p\cap S=\varnothing\}$.

derivations.claim: For $r=0$ the ring is the field $k$ by [L6]. Every nonzero element of a field is a unit by [L7], so there are no nonzero nonunits at all; the existence and uniqueness clauses of [L1] hold vacuously, and by [L2] there is no irreducible element, so the statement about irreducibles is vacuous too. This is the base case of the induction on $r$.

Let $R$ be any UFD and $p\in R$ irreducible. Then $p$ is prime: if $p\mid ab$ with $a,b\ne0$, factor $a=\prod_ia_i$, $b=\prod_jb_j$ and write $ab=pc$ with $c\ne0$ factored as $\prod_kc_k$, as [L1] allows whenever the element in question is a nonzero nonunit, the unit cases being immediate from $p\mid ab$; comparing the two products of irreducibles for $ab$ and $pc$ by the uniqueness clause of [L1] shows that $p$ is associate to one of the $a_i$ or one of the $b_j$, hence divides $a$ or $b$.

Now let $R$ be a UFD, $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ by [L4], and $0\ne f\in R[x]$. For each associate class $C$ of irreducibles in $R$, let $v_C(a)$ be the exponent of that class in the factorization of a nonzero $a\in R$; it is well-defined by the uniqueness clause of [L1]. Let $\mathcal C(f)$ be the finite set of such classes appearing in the factorizations of the nonzero coefficients of $f$, and for each $C\in\mathcal C(f)$ choose one representative $p_C$. Set $e_C=\min\{v_C(a):a\ne0\text{ is a coefficient of }f\}$ and $c(f)=\prod_{C\in\mathcal C(f)}p_C^{e_C}$. This finite product is a common divisor of the coefficients, every common divisor divides it up to associates, and $f^\ast:=f/c(f)$ is primitive in the sense of [L3]; thus $f=c(f)f^\ast$. For $\lambda\in K^\times$, define $v_C(\lambda)=v_C(a)-v_C(b)$ when $\lambda=a/b$ with nonzero $a,b\in R$; this is well-defined, and $v_C(\lambda)=0$ for every associate class exactly when $\lambda$ is a unit of $R$. Note also that an irreducible $f$ of positive degree is primitive: a nonunit constant $r\in R$ dividing all coefficients would write $f=r\cdot(f/r)$ with both factors nonunits, since $f/r$ has positive degree by [L7]. The content $c(f)$ factors into irreducibles of $R$ by [L1], and each such constant is irreducible in $R[x]$, because a factorization of a constant in $R[x]$ has both factors constant by [L7] and so is a factorization in $R$. For the primitive part, [L5] gives a factorization $f^\ast=u g_1\cdots g_n$ in $K[x]$, with $u\in K^\times$ and each $g_j$ irreducible in $K[x]$; if $n=0$, then $f^\ast$ is a nonzero constant in $R$ and, being primitive, is a unit of $R$. For each $j$ choose $a_j\in R\setminus\{0\}$ with $a_jg_j\in R[x]$ and write $a_jg_j=d_jh_j$, where $d_j\in R$ is a content and $h_j\in R[x]$ is primitive; then $g_j=(d_j/a_j)h_j$, so $h_j$ is a nonzero scalar multiple of $g_j$ in $K[x]$, hence irreducible in $K[x]$ and in $R[x]$ by [L3]. By [L3] the product $h_1\cdots h_n$ is primitive, and $f^\ast=\lambda\,h_1\cdots h_n$ with $\lambda=u\prod_j(d_j/a_j)\in K^\times$. Since both $f^\ast$ and $h_1\cdots h_n$ are primitive, comparison of the least exponents in each associate class gives $v_C(\lambda)=0$ for every $C$, so $\lambda$ is a unit of $R$. Thus $f$ is a product of irreducibles of $R[x]$.
Assume now that $r\ge1$ and that $k[x_1,\ldots,x_{r-1}]$ is a UFD in which every irreducible element is prime; this is the induction hypothesis.

For uniqueness, let $p_1\cdots p_m=q_1\cdots q_n$ be two factorizations of the same element $f\ne0$ of $R[x]$ into irreducibles. Multiply the positive-degree factors of each side together, using the primitivity noted in 1.3; the result is primitive by [L3] on each side, so comparing contents as in 1.3 shows that the two sides' constant factors are associates and that the products of positive-degree factors are associates of one another. Each positive-degree factor is irreducible in $K[x]$ by [L3], and $K[x]$ is a UFD by [L5], so the two products of positive-degree factors agree up to order, associates in $K[x]$, and a unit scalar; that scalar is a unit of $R$ by the exponent comparison of 1.3, so they agree up to order and associates in $R[x]$. The constant factors are products of irreducibles of $R$ and agree up to order and associates by the uniqueness clause of [L1]. Hence $R[x]$ satisfies the uniqueness clause of [L1], and with 1.3 it is a UFD.

Every irreducible element of $R[x]$ is prime. Let $p\in R[x]$ be irreducible. If $\deg p=0$ then $p\in R$ is irreducible in $R$, hence prime in $R$ by 1.2; if $p\mid ab$ in $R[x]$, then the induced map $R[x]\to(R/(p))[x]$ of [L7] kills $ab$, and $(R/(p))[x]$ is a domain by [L7] because $R/(p)$ is a domain for the prime element $p$; so all coefficients of $a$ or all coefficients of $b$ lie in $(p)$, that is, $p\mid a$ or $p\mid b$. If $\deg p\ge1$, then $p$ is primitive by 1.3, hence irreducible in $K[x]$ by [L3], hence prime in the UFD $K[x]$ by 1.2; if $p\mid ab$ in $R[x]$, then $p\mid ab$ in $K[x]$, so after possibly swapping $a,b$ we have $a=pq$ for some $q\in K[x]$. Write $q=\lambda q^\ast$ with $\lambda\in K^\times$ and $q^\ast\in R[x]$ primitive, by the content construction of 1.3 applied to a polynomial clearing the denominators of $q$; then $a=\lambda\,(pq^\ast)$, and the product $pq^\ast$ is primitive by [L3]. Comparing contents in the equality $a=\lambda\,(pq^\ast)$ shows that $\lambda$ is associate to the content $c(a)\in R$ of step 1.3: clearing the denominators of $\lambda$ by some $u\ne0$ gives $ua=(\lambda u)(pq^\ast)$, whose left side has content $u\,c(a)$ and whose right side has content $\lambda u$ up to units because $pq^\ast$ is primitive, the exponents $v_p$ of step 1.3 being additive in a constant factor. Hence $\lambda\in R$ and $q=\lambda q^\ast\in R[x]$, so $a=pq$ with $q\in R[x]$ and $p\mid a$ in $R[x]$.

In any UFD $A$, every prime ideal of height one is generated by an irreducible element. By [L8], $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)=1=\dim A_{\mathfrak p}$ means that inside $\mathfrak p$ there is a strict chain of primes of length one and none of length two; in particular $\mathfrak p$ contains a nonzero element, so choose $0\ne f\in\mathfrak p$. Factoring $f$ into irreducibles and using that $\mathfrak p$ is prime, some irreducible factor $p$ lies in $\mathfrak p$ by [L1] and [L2]; then $p$ is prime by 1.2, so $(p)$ is a nonzero prime ideal contained in $\mathfrak p$. Were $(p)\subsetneq\mathfrak p$, the strict chain $0\subsetneq(p)\subsetneq\mathfrak p$ of primes of $A$ would, by the inclusion-preserving bijection of [L8], give a chain of length two in $\operatorname{Spec}A_{\mathfrak p}$, contradicting $\dim A_{\mathfrak p}=1$. Hence $\mathfrak p=(p)$.

By [L6] the ring $k[x_1,\ldots,x_r]$ is the polynomial ring $A[x_r]$ over $A=k[x_1,\ldots,x_{r-1}]$, which is a UFD by step 1.4. Steps 1.3 and 2.1 therefore make $k[x_1,\ldots,x_r]$ a UFD, and step 2.2 shows that every irreducible element of it is prime, using the primitivity results quoted in those steps. So the UFD clause and the irreducible-is-prime clause hold for this $r\ge1$ whenever they hold for $r-1$.

The base case 1.1 and the induction step 3.1 prove the UFD clause and the irreducible-is-prime clause for every $r\ge0$. Finally, if $\mathfrak p\subseteq k[x_1,\ldots,x_r]$ is a prime ideal of height one, then $k[x_1,\ldots,x_r]$ is a UFD by 3.1, so 2.3 exhibits an irreducible element generating $\mathfrak p$; for $r=0$ the case is vacuous, a field having no nonzero prime ideal. This proves all three clauses of the statement.

Let $R$ be a commutative unital ring, let $M$ be an $R$-module, and let $\mathbf x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ be a finite ordered sequence in $R$. The sequence is $M$-regular when $M/(x_1,\ldots,x_{i-1})M\ne0$ and multiplication by $x_i$ is injective on it for every $i$, and $M/(\mathbf x)M\ne0$.
If $R$ is an integral domain, then $R[x]$ is an integral domain.

Put $S=k[x_0,\ldots,x_n]$ with total-degree grading. A polynomial is homogeneous of degree $d$ if each occurring monomial has total degree $d$; $0$ is homogeneous in every degree. An ideal $J\subseteq S$ is homogeneous if $F=\sum_dF_d\in J$ implies $F_d\in J$ for every $d$.

Let $R$ be an integral domain and let $p\in R$ be nonzero and not a unit. The element $p$ is **irreducible** if every factorisation $p=ab$ has $a$ or $b$ a unit. It is **prime** if $$p\mid ab\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p\mid a\text{ or }p\mid b$$ for all $a,b\in R$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}(R)$. The **height** of $\mathfrak p$ is the Krull dimension of the local ring $R_{\mathfrak p}$: $$ \operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)=\dim(R_{\mathfrak p}). $$

Let $R$ be a nonzero commutative ring. A **strict chain of prime ideals of length $n$** is a sequence $$ \mathfrak p_0\subsetneq\mathfrak p_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\mathfrak p_n $$ of prime ideals of $R$. The **Krull dimension** of $R$ is the supremum of all integers $n\ge 0$ for which such a chain exists.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $S\subseteq R$ be a multiplicative subset, and let $\lambda:R\to S^{-1}R$ be the localization map. Then contraction along $\lambda$ induces an inclusion-preserving bijection $\operatorname{Spec}(S^{-1}R)\to\{\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}(R):\mathfrak p\cap S=\varnothing\}$.

derivations.claim: Since $S$ is an integral domain by [L3] and $F\ne0$, multiplication by $F$ is injective on $S=S/(0)S$, and $S\ne0$.

A nonconstant element $h\in S$ divides both $F$ and $G$ if and only if some irreducible element $p\in S$ divides both: given such $h$, factor $h$ into irreducibles using [L1]; every irreducible factor is a nonzero nonunit, hence nonconstant, since the constants of $S$ are $0$ and the units of $k$; conversely an irreducible common divisor is a common nonconstant factor by [L5].

Suppose no irreducible element divides both $F$ and $G$, and let $G,H\in S$ with $GH\in(F)$, that is, $F\mid GH$. Write $F=u\,p_1^{a_1}\cdots p_r^{a_r}$ with $u$ a unit and the $p_i$ irreducible, using [L1] and $F\ne0$; no $p_i$ divides $G$, and $p_i\mid GH$, so $p_i\mid H$ for every $i$ because $p_i$ is prime by [L1]; hence $F\mid H$ and $H\in(F)$. Therefore multiplication by $G$ is injective on $S/(F)$.

Both $F$ and $G$ are nonzero homogeneous of positive degree, so by [L4] every monomial of $F$ and of $G$ lies in $\mathfrak m=(x_0,x_1,x_2)$; hence $(F,G)\subseteq\mathfrak m$, which is a proper ideal, and $S/(F,G)\ne0$.

If $p\in S$ is irreducible, then $(p)$ has height one. By [L1] the element $p$ is prime, so $(p)$ is a prime ideal, nonzero and proper; and the only prime ideals of $S$ contained in $(p)$ are $0$ and $(p)$: indeed if $0\ne\mathfrak q\subseteq(p)$ is prime, factor a nonzero element $q\in\mathfrak q$ into irreducibles by [L1], so that some irreducible $r$ divides $q$ and lies in $\mathfrak q\subseteq(p)$, which forces $p\mid r$ and hence $r$ associate to $p$, so $p\in\mathfrak q$ and $(p)\subseteq\mathfrak q$. Hence $\operatorname{Spec}S_{(p)}$ consists of the two primes corresponding to $0$ and $(p)$, a chain of length one, so $\dim S_{(p)}=1$ and $\operatorname{ht}(p)=1$ by [L6].

By 1.3, multiplication by $G$ is injective on the module $S/(F)=(S/(F))S$. Moreover $S/(F)\ne0$: otherwise $1\in(F)$, so $F$ would be a unit of the domain $S$ by [L3], contradicting that $F$ is a nonzero nonunit, being homogeneous of positive degree.

The regular condition is equivalent to the height-one condition. If a height-one prime $\mathfrak p$ contains both $F$ and $G$, then $\mathfrak p=(p)$ with $p$ irreducible by [L1], so $p$ divides both and by 1.2 the forms have a common nonconstant factor. Conversely, if a nonconstant $h$ divides both, then by 1.2 an irreducible $p$ divides both; by 1.5 the principal prime $(p)$ has height one, and it contains both $F$ and $G$. Hence no common nonconstant factor is equivalent to: no height-one prime of $S$ contains both forms.

The sequence $(F,G)$ is $S$-regular: $S\ne0$ and multiplication by $F$ is injective on $S$ by 1.1; multiplication by $G$ is injective on $S/(F)$, which is nonzero, by 2.1; and $S/(F,G)\ne0$ by 1.4. This meets the definition [L2] in both slots.

Steps 3.1 and 2.2 prove the two equivalent formulations of the statement: the pair $(F,G)$ is an $S$-regular sequence, and no prime ideal of height one contains both $F$ and $G$. No hypothesis beyond the stated ones was used, and the arguments are valid over an arbitrary field $k$.

Let $R$ be a commutative unital ring, let $M$ be an $R$-module, and let $\mathbf x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ be a finite ordered sequence in $R$. The sequence is $M$-regular when $M/(x_1,\ldots,x_{i-1})M\ne0$ and multiplication by $x_i$ is injective on it for every $i$, and $M/(\mathbf x)M\ne0$.

A **nonnegatively graded ring** is a commutative ring $$ S=\bigoplus_{n\ge 0} S_n $$ such that $S_nS_m\subseteq S_{n+m}$ for all $m,n\ge 0$. An element of $S_n$ is called **homogeneous of degree $n$**.

Let $F$ be a field. Every polynomial in the iterated ring $F[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ has a unique finite expansion $$f=\sum_{\mathbf{t}}c_{\mathbf{t}}x^{\mathbf{t}},\qquad x^{\mathbf{t}}:=x_1^{t_1}\cdots x_n^{t_n},$$ over finitely many multi-indices $\mathbf{t}=(t_1,\dots,t_n)\in\mathbb{N}^n$.

Let $S=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}S_n$ be a graded ring and $M=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb Z}M_n$ a graded $S$-module. Assume each homogeneous piece $M_n$ has finite length as an $S_0$-module and that $M_n=0$ for all sufficiently negative $n$. The **Hilbert function** of $M$ is $$ H_M(n):=\ell_{S_0}(M_n)\qquad (n\in\mathbb Z).

For a short exact sequence $0\to N\to M\to Q\to0$, the module $M$ has finite length if and only if $N$ and $Q$ do, and then $$\ell_R(M)=\ell_R(N)+\ell_R(Q).$$ See [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]].
A left $R$-module $M$ is **simple** if $M\ne0$ and its only submodules are $0$ and $M$. Equivalently, $M$ has no proper nonzero submodule.

A **composition series** of a left $R$-module $M$ is a finite chain $$0=M_0<M_1<\cdots<M_n=M$$ whose factors $M_i/M_{i-1}$ are simple. If such a series exists, the **length** $\ell_R(M)$ is its number $n$ of factors; [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]] proves independence of the chosen series.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. A **formal power series over $R$** is a coefficient function $a:\mathbb N\to R$, written $$f=\sum_{n\ge 0}a_nx^n,$$ and $R\llbracket x\rrbracket$ is the set of all such functions. The symbol $x$ is an indeterminate. The notation asserts no analytic convergence and no value of $x$ is being chosen.

derivations.claim: Fix $n$. Because $F$ is a nonzerodivisor on $S$ of degree $d$ by [L2], multiplication by $F$ maps $S_{n-d}$ isomorphically onto $F\cdot S_{n-d}=(F)_n$, so there is an exact sequence of $k$-vector spaces $$0\to S_{n-d}\xrightarrow{\cdot F}S_n\to(S/(F))_n\to0.$$ Here $S_{n-d}:=0$ when $n<d$. Likewise $G$ is a nonzerodivisor on $S/(F)$ and has degree $e$, so $$0\to(S/(F))_{n-e}\xrightarrow{\cdot G}(S/(F))_n\to(S/(F,G))_n\to0$$ is exact, with $(S/(F))_{n-e}:=0$ when $n<e$. All terms are finite-dimensional over $k=S_0$, and $\ell_k(V)=\dim_kV$ for a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space, since a basis $v_1,\ldots,v_m$ gives the composition series $0\subsetneq\langle v_1\rangle\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq V$ with one-dimensional, hence simple, factors by [L6].

Taking dimensions over $k$ in the two exact sequences of 1.1 and using $\ell_k=\dim_k$ by [L4] on each piece, we get for every $n$ $$\dim_k(S/(F,G))_n=\dim_kS_n-\dim_kS_{n-d}-\dim_kS_{n-e}+\dim_kS_{n-d-e},$$ with $\dim_kS_m:=0$ for $m<0$. Moreover $\dim_kS_m$ is the number of triples $(a,b,c)\in\mathbb N^3$ with $a+b+c=m$, since those triples index the monomial basis of $S_m$ by [L3].

Work in $\mathbb Z\llbracket t\rrbracket$, so the coefficients retain the integer dimensions even when $k$ has positive characteristic. Write $G(t):=\sum_{n\ge0}\dim_kS_nt^n$ for the Hilbert series of $S$. By the Cauchy product rule of [L7], the cube of $\sum_{n\ge0}t^n$ is $\sum_nt^n$ convolved three times, whose coefficient at $t^n$ is exactly the number of triples $(a,b,c)\in\mathbb N^3$ with $a+b+c=n$, that is, $\dim_kS_n$ by 2.1. Hence $G(t)=\bigl(\sum_{n\ge0}t^n\bigr)^3$; and since $1-t$ times $\sum_{n\ge0}t^n$ has constant coefficient one and all other coefficients zero, $\sum_{n\ge0}t^n$ is the inverse of $1-t$ in $\mathbb Z\llbracket t\rrbracket$ and $G(t)=(1-t)^{-3}$. Multiplying the dimension identity of 2.1 by $t^n$ and summing over $n\ge0$, the shifts by $d$ and $e$ contribute $t^d$ and $t^e$ by the twist rule of [L4], so $$\operatorname{HS}_{S/(F,G)}(t)=(1-t^d)(1-t^e)G(t)=\frac{(1-t^d)(1-t^e)}{(1-t)^3}.$$

Since $(1-t^d)=(1-t)(1+t+\cdots+t^{d-1})$ and likewise for $e$, the series of 3.1 equals $P(t)/(1-t)$ where $P(t)$ is the polynomial $(1+t+\cdots+t^{d-1})(1+t+\cdots+t^{e-1})=\sum_{m=0}^{d+e-2}p_mt^m$ with $p_m\ge0$; here $p_m$ counts the pairs $(i,j)$ with $i\le d-1$, $j\le e-1$ and $i+j=m$, so $\sum_mp_m=de$. By the Cauchy product rule of [L7] and the inverse $\sum_nt^n=(1-t)^{-1}$ from 3.1, the coefficient of $t^n$ in $P(t)/(1-t)$ is $\sum_{m\le n}p_m$, which equals $\sum_{m}p_m=de$ for every $n\ge d+e-2$. Hence $H_{S/(F,G)}(n)=de$ in all those degrees.

By [L1], the hypothesis of the statement holds in particular for every pair of nonzero homogeneous plane forms of positive degrees $d,e$ with no common nonconstant factor, so the computed series and the eventual value $de$ apply to those pairs. Steps 3.1 and 4.1 prove both displayed identities and the eventual constancy; no Artinianity or finite dimensionality of $S/(F,G)$ was used anywhere.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited here from
the affine structure-sheaf construction
([[thm-structure-sheaf-affine-scheme]]): its localization data form a sheaf
on distinguished opens using the prime-existence and finite-subcover results.
The finite chart gluing makes no additional choice.

Let $k$ be a field, let $R=k[x_0,\ldots,x_n]$ carry the standard grading in
which every $x_i$ has degree one
([[def-graded-ring-and-graded-module]],
[[def-homogeneous-polynomial-and-homogeneous-ideal]]), let $I\subseteq R$ be a
homogeneous ideal, and put $S=R/I$ with the induced grading. Write

$$S_+=(x_0,\ldots,x_n)S=\bigoplus_{m\ge1}S_m$$

for the **irrelevant ideal** of $S$, generated by the images of the variables.

1. **Underlying set.** The **projective spectrum** $\operatorname{Proj}S$ has as
   its points the homogeneous prime ideals $\mathfrak p\subseteq S$ with
   $S_+\nsubseteq\mathfrak p$; equivalently $x_i\notin\mathfrak p$ for at least
   one $i$.
2. **Standard charts.** For each $i$ let $S_{x_i}$ be the localization of $S$ in
   which the powers of $x_i$ are inverted; it is a graded ring and its
   degree-zero part $(S_{x_i})_0$ is a $k$-algebra. The **standard chart**
   $D_+(x_i)$ is the affine scheme $\operatorname{Spec}\bigl((S_{x_i})_0\bigr)$
   with its structure sheaf ([[def-affine-scheme]]), whose sections on a
   distinguished open $D(a)$ are $((S_{x_i})_0)_a$.
   Concretely, $(S_{x_i})_0$ is the image of
   the subring of fractions of $S$ of total degree zero with denominator a power
   of $x_i$; in the polynomial case with $I=0$ it is the polynomial ring in the
   ratios $x_j/x_i$ for $j\ne i$.
3. **Overlaps and gluing.** For all $i,j$ the localizations $(S_{x_i})_0$ and
   $(S_{x_j})_0$ have the common localization $(S_{x_ix_j})_0$, obtained from
   either one by inverting the degree-zero ratio $x_j/x_i$ respectively
   $x_i/x_j$; these identifications of
   $\operatorname{Spec}\bigl((S_{x_ix_j})_0\bigr)$ with distinguished open
   subschemes of the two charts are isomorphisms of locally ringed spaces
   ([[lem-spectrum-localization-open-immersion]]). They are the transition
   isomorphisms, and they
   satisfy the identity and cocycle conditions because both composites are the
   canonical identification inside the double localization $S_{x_ix_jx_k}$. The
   affine schemes $D_+(x_i)$ therefore glue to a scheme
   $\operatorname{Proj}S$ ([[thm-gluing-affine-schemes]], [[def-scheme]]), the
   standard charts forming an open affine cover, with the points of part 1 as its
   underlying set and the subset $D_+(x_ix_j)\subseteq D_+(x_i)$ as the locus
   where $x_j/x_i$ is invertible.
4. **Conventions.** The construction is available over an arbitrary field $k$
   and for an arbitrary homogeneous ideal $I$, including a nonradical one; it
   makes $\operatorname{Proj}S$ a $k$-scheme locally of finite type, with
   residue fields $\kappa(\mathfrak p)=S_{(\mathfrak p)}/\mathfrak m_{(\mathfrak p)}$
   that need not equal $k$. Here $T$ is the multiplicative set of homogeneous
   elements of $S$ outside $\mathfrak p$, $S_{(\mathfrak p)}=(T^{-1}S)_0$,
   and $\mathfrak m_{(\mathfrak p)}=(T^{-1}\mathfrak p)_0$ is its maximal
   ideal: a degree-zero fraction with numerator outside $\mathfrak p$ has its
   inverse by interchanging numerator and denominator. It is not the same object as the classical
   projective algebraic set of [[def-projective-space-points]], which is defined
   over an algebraically closed field and is reduced: the classical set records
   only the $\bar k$-points of the reduced subscheme, while
   $\operatorname{Proj}S$ retains the scheme structure on its charts, including any
   nilpotents that survive localization. When $k$ is algebraically closed and $I$ is radical, the closed
   points of $\operatorname{Proj}S$ correspond to the points of $V_+(I)$ in the
   classical sense; that dictionary is not asserted here.

For the empty case: if $S_+=0$, that is, if the images of all $x_i$ vanish in
$S$, then $S$ has no homogeneous prime avoiding $S_+$ and
$\operatorname{Proj}S=\varnothing$; every $D_+(x_i)=\operatorname{Spec}0$ is
empty, consistently with the gluing. In particular
$\operatorname{Proj}\bigl(k[x_0,\ldots,x_n]/(x_0,\ldots,x_n)\bigr)=\varnothing$.

A **nonnegatively graded ring** is a commutative ring $$ S=\bigoplus_{n\ge 0} S_n $$ such that $S_nS_m\subseteq S_{n+m}$ for all $m,n\ge 0$. An element of $S_n$ is called **homogeneous of degree $n$**.

Put $S=k[x_0,\ldots,x_n]$ with total-degree grading. A polynomial is homogeneous of degree $d$ if each occurring monomial has total degree $d$; $0$ is homogeneous in every degree. An ideal $J\subseteq S$ is homogeneous if $F=\sum_dF_d\in J$ implies $F_d\in J$ for every $d$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $S\subseteq R$ be a multiplicative subset, and let $\lambda:R\to S^{-1}R$ be the localization map. Then contraction along $\lambda$ induces an inclusion-preserving bijection $\operatorname{Spec}(S^{-1}R)\to\{\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}(R):\mathfrak p\cap S=\varnothing\}$.
For $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}A$, there is a canonical isomorphism $\mathcal O_{\operatorname{Spec}A,\mathfrak p}\cong A_{\mathfrak p}$.

Let $\mathcal F$ be a presheaf on a topological space $X$, and let $x\in X$. The **neighbourhood category of $x$** is the full subcategory $$\mathcal N_x\subseteq \operatorname{Open}(X)$$ whose objects are the open neighbourhoods of $x$.

Let $S,T\subseteq R$ be multiplicative, let $\overline T$ be the image of $T$ in $S^{-1}R$, and let $U\subseteq R$ be the multiplicative subset generated by $S\cup T$. Then there is a unique $R$-algebra isomorphism $$ \overline T^{-1}(S^{-1}R)\cong U^{-1}R.
$R/P$ is an integral domain if and only if $P$ is a prime ideal. Here $R$ is commutative and $P\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}R$ is an ideal.
If $R$ is an integral domain, then $R[x]$ is an integral domain.

Let $f:R\to A$ be a unital homomorphism of commutative rings such that $f(s)$ is a unit for every $s\in S$. There is a unique unital ring homomorphism $\widetilde f:S^{-1}R\to A$ satisfying $\widetilde f\circ\lambda_S=f$, namely $$ \widetilde f(r/s)=f(r)f(s)^{-1}. $$

Let $\lambda:R\to L$ and $\lambda':R\to L'$ be unital homomorphisms of commutative rings. Suppose each map sends every $s\in S$ to a unit and has the localisation universal property: every homomorphism from $R$ that inverts $S$ factors uniquely through it.

Let $A,B,C$ be commutative $R$-algebras. For every pair of $R$-algebra homomorphisms $f:A\to C$ and $g:B\to C$, there is a unique $R$-algebra homomorphism $$h:A\otimes_RB\longrightarrow C$$ such that $h(a\otimes1)=f(a)$ and $h(1\otimes b)=g(b)$.

Let $\varphi:R\to A$ be a ring homomorphism of commutative rings. Then contraction along $\varphi$ defines a map $$ \operatorname{Spec}(\varphi):\operatorname{Spec}(A)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Spec}(R),\qquad \mathfrak q\longmapsto\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak q).

derivations.claim: Let $z\in S_{x_i}$ be homogeneous of degree $m$ and write $z=s/x_i^e$ with $s\in S$ and $e\ge0$; writing $s=\sum_ds_d$ for the homogeneous components of $s$, the elements $s_d/x_i^e$ are homogeneous of degree $d-e$ in $S_{x_i}$ and sum to $z$. Since $z$ is homogeneous of degree $m$, only the summand with $d-e=m$ can be nonzero, so $z=s_{m+e}/x_i^e=(s_{m+e}/x_i^{m+e})x_i^m$ with $a:=s_{m+e}/x_i^{m+e}\in(S_{x_i})_0=A_i$. Because the direct-sum expression in a graded ring is unique [L2], it follows that $S_{x_i}=\bigoplus_{m\in\mathbb Z}A_ix_i^m$, that $a_mx_i^m$ is the degree-$m$ component of $\sum_ma_mx_i^m$, and that $x_i$ is a unit; in particular the degree-$m$ part of $S_{x_i}$ is exactly $A_ix_i^m$.

Let $k\subseteq K$ be a field extension and $S_K=S\otimes_kK$, graded by $\deg(s\otimes\mu)=\deg s$. The $k$-algebra maps $S_{x_i}\to(S_K)_{x_i}$, $s/x_i^e\mapsto(s\otimes1)(x_i\otimes1)^{-e}$, and $K\to(S_K)_{x_i}$, $\mu\mapsto1\otimes\mu$, induce by the coproduct property [L8] a $k$-algebra map $S_{x_i}\otimes_kK\to(S_K)_{x_i}$; conversely the map $S_K\to S_{x_i}\otimes_kK$ built from $S\to S_{x_i}\otimes_kK$ and $K\to S_{x_i}\otimes_kK$ inverts $x_i\otimes1$, whose inverse is $x_i^{-1}\otimes1$, so by [L7] it induces $(S_K)_{x_i}\to S_{x_i}\otimes_kK$. Each composite is a map fixing the base ring and the inverted element, hence is the identity by the uniqueness in [L7] and [L8]; thus $(S_K)_{x_i}\cong S_{x_i}\otimes_kK$, compatibly with the gradings, since the maps send homogeneous elements to homogeneous elements of the same degree. As $K$ lies in degree zero, the degree-$m$ part of $S_{x_i}\otimes_kK$ is $(S_{x_i})_m\otimes_kK=A_ix_i^m\otimes_kK$ by 1.1, so $((S_K)_{x_i})_0=A_i\otimes_kK$ and $S_K$ is standard graded over $K$ with the images of the $x_i$ as degree-one generators.

If $\mathfrak a\subseteq S$ is homogeneous, then $\mathfrak aS_{x_i}$ is a homogeneous ideal of $S_{x_i}$: writing an element as a finite sum $\sum_\ell a^{(\ell)}/x_i^{e_\ell}$ with $a^{(\ell)}\in\mathfrak a$ and decomposing each $a^{(\ell)}=\sum_da^{(\ell)}_d$ into components, which lie in $\mathfrak a$ by [L2], exhibits the element as a sum of homogeneous elements of $S_{x_i}$, so each of its homogeneous components lies in $\mathfrak aS_{x_i}$. If $\mathfrak b\subseteq S_{x_i}$ is a homogeneous ideal and $s=\sum_ds_d\in\lambda_i^{-1}(\mathfrak b)$, then $\lambda_i(s)=\sum_d\lambda_i(s_d)$ with $\lambda_i(s_d)$ homogeneous of degree $d$ by [L1], so each $\lambda_i(s_d)\in\mathfrak b$ and hence each $s_d\in\lambda_i^{-1}(\mathfrak b)$. Thus extension and contraction along $\lambda_i$ preserve homogeneity of ideals.

Let $\mathfrak p_0\subseteq A_i$ be a prime. By 1.1 the ideal it generates in $S_{x_i}$ is $\mathfrak p_0S_{x_i}=\bigoplus_{m\in\mathbb Z}\mathfrak p_0x_i^m$, which is homogeneous and satisfies $\mathfrak p_0S_{x_i}\cap A_i=\mathfrak p_0$; its quotient is $\bigoplus_m(A_i/\mathfrak p_0)x_i^m$, a ring in which $x_i$ is a unit, and a product of two nonzero elements there has nonzero coefficient at the lowest occurring power of $x_i$ because $A_i/\mathfrak p_0$ is a domain by [L6]. Hence $\mathfrak p_0S_{x_i}$ is a homogeneous prime. Conversely, if $\mathfrak q\subseteq S_{x_i}$ is a homogeneous prime with $\mathfrak q_0:=\mathfrak q\cap A_i$, then every homogeneous $z\in\mathfrak q$ of degree $m$ equals $ax_i^m$ with $a\in A_i$ by 1.1, and $a=x_i^{-m}z\in\mathfrak q$ because $x_i$ is a unit, so $z\in\mathfrak q_0S_{x_i}$; since homogeneous ideals are generated by their homogeneous elements [L2] we get $\mathfrak q=\mathfrak q_0S_{x_i}$. Therefore $\mathfrak p_0\mapsto\mathfrak p_0S_{x_i}$ and $\mathfrak q\mapsto\mathfrak q\cap A_i$ are inverse bijections between $\operatorname{Spec}(A_i)$ and the homogeneous primes of $S_{x_i}$, both given by extension respectively contraction of ideals and therefore inclusion-preserving.

Applying [L3] to $S$ and the multiplicative set of powers of $x_i$: contraction along $\lambda_i$ is an inclusion-preserving bijection from $\operatorname{Spec}(S_{x_i})$ onto the primes of $S$ avoiding $x_i$, with inverse $\mathfrak p\mapsto\mathfrak pS_{x_i}$. By 2.2 this bijection and its inverse carry homogeneous primes to homogeneous primes, and since the two maps are given by contraction and extension of ideals, they restrict to inverse inclusion-preserving bijections between the homogeneous primes of $S$ avoiding $x_i$ and the homogeneous primes of $S_{x_i}$.

Composing the bijections of 3.1 and 2.3 gives inverse bijections between the homogeneous primes $\mathfrak p$ of $S$ with $x_i
otin\mathfrak p$ and the points $\mathfrak p_0$ of $\operatorname{Spec}(A_i)$: the composite sends $\mathfrak p$ to $\mathfrak pS_{x_i}\cap A_i$ and $\mathfrak p_0$ to $\lambda_i^{-1}(\mathfrak p_0S_{x_i})$, both maps are inclusion-preserving, and each composite is the identity because $\mathfrak p_0S_{x_i}\cap A_i=\mathfrak p_0$ by 2.3 and because for a homogeneous prime $\mathfrak p$ of $S$ avoiding $x_i$, the ideal $\mathfrak pS_{x_i}$ is a homogeneous prime of $S_{x_i}$ by 3.1 to which $\mathfrak q=(\mathfrak q\cap A_i)S_{x_i}$ applies, while its contraction to $S$ is $\mathfrak p$ by the inverse property in [L3]. A homogeneous prime with $x_i
otin\mathfrak p$ satisfies $S_+
subseteq\mathfrak p$ since $x_i\in S_+$, and it lies in $D_+(x_i)$ by [L1]; these are exactly the points of the chart. This is claim 1.

By [L1] the chart $D_+(x_i)$ is the affine scheme $\operatorname{Spec}(A_i)$ and, by 4.1, the point of $D_+(x_i)$ corresponding to $\mathfrak p$ is the prime $\mathfrak p_0=\mathfrak pS_{x_i}\cap A_i$ of $A_i$. Since the stalk of a scheme at a point may be computed in any open chart containing it and the stalk of an affine scheme at a prime is the localization at that prime [L4], we get $\mathcal O_{X,\mathfrak p}\cong(A_i)_{\mathfrak p_0}$. This is claim 2.

Assume now $x_i,x_j\notin\mathfrak p$ and set $\mathfrak p_{0,i}=\mathfrak pS_{x_i}\cap A_i$, $\mathfrak p_{0,j}=\mathfrak pS_{x_j}\cap A_j$. By [L3] applied to $S$ and the multiplicative set generated by $x_i$ and $x_j$, which $\mathfrak p$ avoids, the ideal $\mathfrak pS_{x_ix_j}$ is a prime of $S_{x_ix_j}$, so $\mathfrak p_{0,ij}:=\mathfrak pS_{x_ix_j}\cap A_{ij}$ is a prime of $A_{ij}$ by [L8]. Its contraction $Q:=\mathfrak pS_{x_ix_j}\cap S_{x_i}$ is a prime of $S_{x_i}$ containing $\mathfrak pS_{x_i}$, and $Q\cap S=\mathfrak p$: an element $z\in Q$ satisfies $x_j^Nz\in\mathfrak pS_{x_i}$ for some $N\ge0$, because $\mathfrak pS_{x_ix_j}$ is the localization of $\mathfrak pS_{x_i}$ at $x_j$ and $\frac z1$ is a fraction with numerator in $\mathfrak pS_{x_i}$; so for $s\in S\cap Q$ we get $x_j^Ns\in\mathfrak pS_{x_i}\cap S=\mathfrak p$ by the inverse property in [L3], whence $s\in\mathfrak p$ as $x_j\notin\mathfrak p$ and $\mathfrak p$ is prime. Contraction is injective on primes of $S_{x_i}$ by [L3], so $Q=\mathfrak pS_{x_i}$, and intersecting with $A_i\subseteq S_{x_i}$ gives $\mathfrak p_{0,ij}\cap A_i=\mathfrak p_{0,i}$. By [L1] the ring $A_{ij}$ is the localization of $A_i$ at the element $x_j/x_i$, which does not lie in $\mathfrak p_{0,i}$: otherwise $x_j=x_i\cdot(x_j/x_i)\in\mathfrak pS_{x_i}\cap S=\mathfrak p$, since the contraction of $\mathfrak pS_{x_i}$ to $S$ is $\mathfrak p$. So [L3] applied to $A_i$ and the powers of $x_j/x_i$ shows that $\mathfrak p_{0,i}A_{ij}$ is the unique prime of $A_{ij}$ contracting to $\mathfrak p_{0,i}$; since $\mathfrak p_{0,ij}$ is such a prime, $\mathfrak p_{0,ij}=\mathfrak p_{0,i}A_{ij}$, and by the same argument with $i,j$ exchanged, $\mathfrak p_{0,ij}=\mathfrak p_{0,j}A_{ij}$. Hence $\mathfrak p_{0,i}A_{ij}=\mathfrak p_{0,j}A_{ij}$.

Let $\mathfrak q$ be a homogeneous prime of $S_K$ with $x_i\notin\mathfrak q$ and $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\cap S$. Since $S\to S_K$, $s\mapsto s\otimes1$, is degree-preserving, the degree-$d$ component of $\mathfrak p$ is the contraction of the degree-$d$ component of $\mathfrak q$; hence $\mathfrak p$ is homogeneous [L2], and $x_i\notin\mathfrak p$ is clear. Let $\mathfrak q_0=\mathfrak q(S_K)_{x_i}\cap(A_i\otimes_kK)$ and $\mathfrak p_0=\mathfrak pS_{x_i}\cap A_i$ be the chart primes of $\mathfrak q$ for $X_K=\operatorname{Proj}S_K$ and of $\mathfrak p$, both given by claim 1 (4.1) applied to the standard graded $K$-algebra $S_K$ of 2.1 and to $S$. Under the identifications of 2.1 we have $A_i\subseteq A_i\otimes_kK\subseteq(S_K)_{x_i}$ and $S_{x_i}\subseteq(S_K)_{x_i}$. The contraction $Q:=\mathfrak q(S_K)_{x_i}\cap S_{x_i}$ is a prime of $S_{x_i}$ containing $\mathfrak pS_{x_i}$ whose contraction to $S$ is $\mathfrak p$: if $s\in S\cap Q$ then $x_i^Ns\in\mathfrak q$ for some $N\ge0$, so $x_i^Ns\in\mathfrak q\cap S=\mathfrak p$ and hence $s\in\mathfrak p$. Contraction is injective on primes of $S_{x_i}$ by [L3], so $Q=\mathfrak pS_{x_i}$ and therefore $\mathfrak q_0\cap A_i=Q\cap A_i=\mathfrak pS_{x_i}\cap A_i=\mathfrak p_0$.

With the notation of 5.2, the point $\mathfrak p$ lies in both charts, so by 5.1 its stalk is $(A_i)_{\mathfrak p_{0,i}}$ when computed in chart $i$ and $(A_j)_{\mathfrak p_{0,j}}$ when computed in chart $j$. Since $A_{ij}$ is the localization of $A_i$ at $x_j/x_i$, the general form of [L5] applied to the multiplicative set $A_i\setminus\mathfrak p_{0,i}$ gives $(A_i)_{\mathfrak p_{0,i}}\cong(A_{ij})_{\mathfrak p_{0,i}A_{ij}}$; indeed, put $f=x_j/x_i\notin\mathfrak p_{0,i}$. Every element outside $\mathfrak p_{0,i}A_{ij}$ is a fraction $a/f^n$ with $a\notin\mathfrak p_{0,i}$. After inverting the images of $A_i\setminus\mathfrak p_{0,i}$, such a fraction is a unit, with inverse $f^n/a$. Conversely every image of an element of $A_i\setminus\mathfrak p_{0,i}$ is outside the extended prime. Thus inverting these images and inverting the entire prime complement have the same universal property [L7]. By 5.2, $\mathfrak p_{0,i}A_{ij}=\mathfrak p_{0,ij}=\mathfrak p_{0,j}A_{ij}$, so both charts give the localization of $A_{ij}$ at $\mathfrak p_{0,ij}$; in particular $(A_i)_{\mathfrak p_{0,i}}\cong(A_j)_{\mathfrak p_{0,j}}$, which completes claim 3.

With the notation of 5.3 and 2.1, 5.1 applied to the chart $(A_i\otimes_kK)_{\mathfrak q_0}$ of $X_K$ gives $\mathcal O_{X_K,\mathfrak q}\cong(A_i\otimes_kK)_{\mathfrak q_0}$, while $\mathcal O_{X,\mathfrak p}\otimes_kK\cong(A_i)_{\mathfrak p_0}\otimes_kK$. Put $B=A_i\otimes_kK$ and $S_0=A_i\setminus\mathfrak p_0\subseteq B$. The $k$-algebras $S_0^{-1}B$ and $(A_i)_{\mathfrak p_0}\otimes_kK$ are canonically isomorphic: by [L7] and [L8], homomorphisms from either of them into a commutative $k$-algebra $C$ correspond naturally to a pair consisting of a $k$-algebra map $A_i\to C$ inverting $S_0$ and a $k$-algebra map $K\to C$, so both are localizations of $B$ at $S_0$ and [L7] identifies them. By 5.3 we have $\mathfrak q_0\cap A_i=\mathfrak p_0$, so $S_0\subseteq B\setminus\mathfrak q_0$; the general form of [L5] applied to the multiplicative sets $S_0$ and $B\setminus\mathfrak q_0$ in $B$ therefore gives $$\mathcal O_{X_K,\mathfrak q}\cong B_{\mathfrak q_0}\cong\overline{(B\setminus\mathfrak q_0)}^{-1}\bigl(S_0^{-1}B\bigr),$$ the localization of $\mathcal O_{X,\mathfrak p}\otimes_kK\cong S_0^{-1}B$ at the multiplicative set generated by the image of $B\setminus\mathfrak q_0$. Every element outside the prime $\mathfrak q_0S_0^{-1}B$ is a fraction $b/s$ with $b\notin\mathfrak q_0$ and $s\in S_0$. Inverting the image of $B\setminus\mathfrak q_0$ makes $b/s$ a unit, with inverse $s/b$. Conversely those images lie outside the extended prime, so the two localizations have the same universal property [L7]. Hence $\mathcal O_{X_K,\mathfrak q}$ is the localization of $\mathcal O_{X,\mathfrak p}\otimes_kK$ at the prime induced by $\mathfrak q_0$, which completes claim 4.

Claim 1 is 4.1 and claim 2 is 5.1; claim 3 is 5.2 together with 6.1; claim 4 is 2.1, 5.3 and 6.2. The degenerate case is covered: if $x_i$ is nilpotent in $S$, then $1=0$ in $A_i$, so $\operatorname{Spec}(A_i)$ is empty, and no prime of $S$ avoids $x_i$, so both sides of the bijection in claim 1 are empty, consistently with $D_+(x_i)=\operatorname{Spec}0$. No choice principle was used and no hypothesis on the homogeneous ideal $I$ beyond homogeneity was needed; the arguments are valid over an arbitrary field $k$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited here from
the affine structure-sheaf construction
([[thm-structure-sheaf-affine-scheme]]): its localization data form a sheaf
on distinguished opens using the prime-existence and finite-subcover results.
The finite chart gluing makes no additional choice.

Let $k$ be a field, let $R=k[x_0,\ldots,x_n]$ carry the standard grading in
which every $x_i$ has degree one
([[def-graded-ring-and-graded-module]],
[[def-homogeneous-polynomial-and-homogeneous-ideal]]), let $I\subseteq R$ be a
homogeneous ideal, and put $S=R/I$ with the induced grading. Write

$$S_+=(x_0,\ldots,x_n)S=\bigoplus_{m\ge1}S_m$$

for the **irrelevant ideal** of $S$, generated by the images of the variables.

1. **Underlying set.** The **projective spectrum** $\operatorname{Proj}S$ has as
   its points the homogeneous prime ideals $\mathfrak p\subseteq S$ with
   $S_+\nsubseteq\mathfrak p$; equivalently $x_i\notin\mathfrak p$ for at least
   one $i$.
2. **Standard charts.** For each $i$ let $S_{x_i}$ be the localization of $S$ in
   which the powers of $x_i$ are inverted; it is a graded ring and its
   degree-zero part $(S_{x_i})_0$ is a $k$-algebra. The **standard chart**
   $D_+(x_i)$ is the affine scheme $\operatorname{Spec}\bigl((S_{x_i})_0\bigr)$
   with its structure sheaf ([[def-affine-scheme]]), whose sections on a
   distinguished open $D(a)$ are $((S_{x_i})_0)_a$.
   Concretely, $(S_{x_i})_0$ is the image of
   the subring of fractions of $S$ of total degree zero with denominator a power
   of $x_i$; in the polynomial case with $I=0$ it is the polynomial ring in the
   ratios $x_j/x_i$ for $j\ne i$.
3. **Overlaps and gluing.** For all $i,j$ the localizations $(S_{x_i})_0$ and
   $(S_{x_j})_0$ have the common localization $(S_{x_ix_j})_0$, obtained from
   either one by inverting the degree-zero ratio $x_j/x_i$ respectively
   $x_i/x_j$; these identifications of
   $\operatorname{Spec}\bigl((S_{x_ix_j})_0\bigr)$ with distinguished open
   subschemes of the two charts are isomorphisms of locally ringed spaces
   ([[lem-spectrum-localization-open-immersion]]). They are the transition
   isomorphisms, and they
   satisfy the identity and cocycle conditions because both composites are the
   canonical identification inside the double localization $S_{x_ix_jx_k}$. The
   affine schemes $D_+(x_i)$ therefore glue to a scheme
   $\operatorname{Proj}S$ ([[thm-gluing-affine-schemes]], [[def-scheme]]), the
   standard charts forming an open affine cover, with the points of part 1 as its
   underlying set and the subset $D_+(x_ix_j)\subseteq D_+(x_i)$ as the locus
   where $x_j/x_i$ is invertible.
4. **Conventions.** The construction is available over an arbitrary field $k$
   and for an arbitrary homogeneous ideal $I$, including a nonradical one; it
   makes $\operatorname{Proj}S$ a $k$-scheme locally of finite type, with
   residue fields $\kappa(\mathfrak p)=S_{(\mathfrak p)}/\mathfrak m_{(\mathfrak p)}$
   that need not equal $k$. Here $T$ is the multiplicative set of homogeneous
   elements of $S$ outside $\mathfrak p$, $S_{(\mathfrak p)}=(T^{-1}S)_0$,
   and $\mathfrak m_{(\mathfrak p)}=(T^{-1}\mathfrak p)_0$ is its maximal
   ideal: a degree-zero fraction with numerator outside $\mathfrak p$ has its
   inverse by interchanging numerator and denominator. It is not the same object as the classical
   projective algebraic set of [[def-projective-space-points]], which is defined
   over an algebraically closed field and is reduced: the classical set records
   only the $\bar k$-points of the reduced subscheme, while
   $\operatorname{Proj}S$ retains the scheme structure on its charts, including any
   nilpotents that survive localization. When $k$ is algebraically closed and $I$ is radical, the closed
   points of $\operatorname{Proj}S$ correspond to the points of $V_+(I)$ in the
   classical sense; that dictionary is not asserted here.

For the empty case: if $S_+=0$, that is, if the images of all $x_i$ vanish in
$S$, then $S$ has no homogeneous prime avoiding $S_+$ and
$\operatorname{Proj}S=\varnothing$; every $D_+(x_i)=\operatorname{Spec}0$ is
empty, consistently with the gluing. In particular
$\operatorname{Proj}\bigl(k[x_0,\ldots,x_n]/(x_0,\ldots,x_n)\bigr)=\varnothing$.

affine structure sheaves in [[def-projective-scheme-from-a-homogeneous-quotient]].
Let $k$ be a field, let $S=k[x_0,\ldots,x_n]/I$ be a standard graded quotient in
which the images of the variables have degree one, and let $X=\operatorname{Proj}S$
have standard charts $D_+(x_i)=\operatorname{Spec}(A_i)$ with
$A_i=(S_{x_i})_0$, as in
[[def-projective-scheme-from-a-homogeneous-quotient]].
Prime ideals and maximal ideals in a commutative ring. Let $R$ be a commutative ring. A proper ideal $P\subsetneq R$ is **prime** when $ab\in P$ implies $a\in P$ or $b\in P$.

Put $S=k[x_0,\ldots,x_n]$ with total-degree grading. A polynomial is homogeneous of degree $d$ if each occurring monomial has total degree $d$; $0$ is homogeneous in every degree. An ideal $J\subseteq S$ is homogeneous if $F=\sum_dF_d\in J$ implies $F_d\in J$ for every $d$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), as required by the
affine structure sheaves in [[def-projective-scheme-from-a-homogeneous-quotient]].
Let $k$ be a field, let $S=k[x_0,\ldots,x_n]/I$ be a standard graded quotient in
which the images of the variables have degree one, and let $X=\operatorname{Proj}S$
have standard charts $D_+(x_i)=\operatorname{Spec}(A_i)$ with
$A_i=(S_{x_i})_0$, as in
[[def-projective-scheme-from-a-homogeneous-quotient]].

Let $S,T\subseteq R$ be multiplicative, let $\overline T$ be the image of $T$ in $S^{-1}R$, and let $U\subseteq R$ be the multiplicative subset generated by $S\cup T$. Then there is a unique $R$-algebra isomorphism $$ \overline T^{-1}(S^{-1}R)\cong U^{-1}R.

Let $\lambda:R\to L$ and $\lambda':R\to L'$ be unital homomorphisms of commutative rings. Suppose each map sends every $s\in S$ to a unit and has the localisation universal property: every homomorphism from $R$ that inverts $S$ factors uniquely through it.

Let $f:R\to A$ be a unital homomorphism of commutative rings such that $f(s)$ is a unit for every $s\in S$. There is a unique unital ring homomorphism $\widetilde f:S^{-1}R\to A$ satisfying $\widetilde f\circ\lambda_S=f$, namely $$ \widetilde f(r/s)=f(r)f(s)^{-1}. $$
Let $R=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}R_n$ be a nonnegatively graded ring ([[def-graded-ring-and-graded-module]]) and let $t\in R_\delta$ be a homogeneous element of degree $\delta\ge1$.

Affine schemes equipped with open subschemes and isomorphisms on overlaps satisfying the identity and cocycle conditions glue to a scheme, uniquely up to unique isomorphism; the given affine schemes become an open affine cover.

All rings below are commutative with $1$. For a ring $A$, the **underlying topological spectrum** is the Zariski space whose points are the prime ideals of $A$; its basic opens are $D(f)=\{\mathfrak p:f\notin\mathfrak p\}$. This notation is deliberately topological until the structure sheaf is constructed.

A **scheme** is a locally ringed space $(X,\mathcal O_X)$ such that every point has an open neighbourhood which, with the restricted structure sheaf, is an affine scheme. The empty locally ringed space is consequently a scheme.

derivations.claim: On each standard chart D_+(x_i), the intersection with D_+(f) is D_+(fx_i), corresponding by the homogeneous-prime/chart dictionary to the distinguished open D(f/x_i^d) in Spec(A_i). Since the charts cover X, D_+(f) is open.

Inside the chart $D_+(x_i)=\operatorname{Spec}(A_i)$ the element $f$ has degree-zero dehomogenization $f/x_i^d\in A_i$, and a prime $\mathfrak q\subseteq A_i$ corresponds to a point of $D_+(fx_i)$ exactly when $f/x_i^d\notin\mathfrak q$ by [L2], so $D_+(fx_i)=\operatorname{Spec}\bigl((A_i)_{f/x_i^d}\bigr)$ is the distinguished open subscheme of $\operatorname{Spec}(A_i)$ determined by $f/x_i^d$.

Put B=(S_f)_0 and u_i=x_i^d/f. Every degree-zero fraction s/(f^a x_i^b) in (S_{fx_i})_0, with deg s=ad+b, equals (s x_i^{dc-b}/f^{a+c})u_i^{-c} when dc>=b, and also equals (s/x_i^{ad+b})(f/x_i^d)^{-a}. The parenthesized terms have degree zero in B and A_i respectively, so B_{u_i}=(S_{fx_i})_0=(A_i)_{f/x_i^d} as subrings of S_{fx_i}; reverse inclusions preserve degree, including in the zero-ring case.

The elements u_i=x_i^d/f generate the unit ideal of B=(S_f)_0: put N=n+1; every monomial of degree Nd has some x_i exponent at least d, so a polynomial representative of f^N equals sum_i x_i^d g_i with deg g_i=(N-1)d. Dividing by f^N yields 1=sum_i u_i(g_i/f^{N-1}) in B. Hence the distinguished opens D_B(u_i) cover Spec B, including the zero-ring case.

The ring maps $A_i\to(S_{fx_i})_0=((S_f)_0)_{x_i^d/f}$ are localizations of $A_i$ and are compatible on the overlaps $D_+(x_ix_j)$: in the double localization $S_{fx_ix_j}$ all comparisons become the identity of the canonical localization of $(S_f)_0$, so the cocycle condition holds.

By 1.4 the opens D_B(u_i)=Spec(B_{u_i}) cover Spec B. The maps of these pieces into the standard charts agree on overlaps by 2.1 and glue to Spec B -> X by [L4]. By 1.2 and 1.3, each piece is isomorphic onto D_+(fx_i)=D_+(f) intersect D_+(x_i); these target opens cover D_+(f) by [L1]. The local inverses agree on overlaps, so the glued morphism is an isomorphism Spec B -> D_+(f).

The isomorphism of 3.1 identifies global sections on D_+(f) with (S_f)_0 and restricts to the canonical localizations of 2.1 on D_+(fx_i). For f=x_i one has d=1 and (S_{x_i})_0=A_i, recovering the standard chart.

citations.quote: Let $k$ be a field and let $n\ge0$. Then $$ \dim k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]=n. $$

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}(R)$. The **height** of $\mathfrak p$ is the Krull dimension of the local ring $R_{\mathfrak p}$: $$ \operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)=\dim(R_{\mathfrak p}). $$

Let $R$ be a nonzero commutative ring. A **strict chain of prime ideals of length $n$** is a sequence $$ \mathfrak p_0\subsetneq\mathfrak p_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\mathfrak p_n $$ of prime ideals of $R$. The **Krull dimension** of $R$ is the supremum of all integers $n\ge 0$ for which such a chain exists.
If $R$ is an integral domain, then $R[x]$ is an integral domain.
$R/P$ is an integral domain if and only if $P$ is a prime ideal. Here $R$ is commutative and $P\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}R$ is an ideal.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $I\trianglelefteq R$ be an ideal, and let $\pi:R\to R/I$ be the quotient map. Then contraction along $\pi$ induces an inclusion-preserving bijection $\operatorname{Spec}(R/I)\to V(I)$, sending $\mathfrak q$ to $\pi^{-1}(\mathfrak q)$.

Put $S=k[x_0,\ldots,x_n]$ with total-degree grading. A polynomial is homogeneous of degree $d$ if each occurring monomial has total degree $d$; $0$ is homogeneous in every degree. An ideal $J\subseteq S$ is homogeneous if $F=\sum_dF_d\in J$ implies $F_d\in J$ for every $d$.

Let $k$ be a field and $S=k[x_0,x_1,x_2]$. Let $F,G\in S$ be nonzero homogeneous forms of positive degrees and suppose that $F$ and $G$ have no common nonconstant factor in $S$. Then $(F,G)$ is an $S$-regular sequence in that order ([[def-regular-sequence-on-a-module]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring, let $$ I=(x_1,\ldots,x_n) $$ be an ideal generated by $n\ge1$ elements, and let $\mathfrak p$ be a prime ideal minimal over $I$. Then $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)\le n$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $I\trianglelefteq R$ be a proper ideal. Then there exists a prime ideal $\mathfrak p$ of $R$ containing $I$ that is minimal with respect to inclusion among the prime ideals containing $I$.

Let $k$ be a field, let $R=k[x_0,\ldots,x_n]$ carry the standard grading in which every $x_i$ has degree one ([[def-graded-ring-and-graded-module]], [[def-homogeneous-polynomial-and-homogeneous-ideal]]), let $I\subseteq R$ be a homogeneous ideal, and put $S=R/I$ with the induced grading.

Let $k$ be a field, let $S=k[x_0,\ldots,x_n]/I$ be a standard graded quotient in which the images of the variables have degree one, and let $X=\operatorname{Proj}S$ have standard charts $D_+(x_i)=\operatorname{Spec}(A_i)$ with $A_i=(S_{x_i})_0$, as in [[def-projective-scheme-from-a-homogeneous-quotient]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $Z\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}(R)$ be a nonempty Zariski-closed subset. Write $\mathfrak a=I(Z)$ for its unique radical defining ideal. Then the following are equivalent: 1. $Z$ is irreducible. 2. $\mathfrak a$ is a prime ideal.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The space $X$ is **irreducible** when $X\neq\varnothing$ and whenever $$ X=F_1\cup F_2 $$ with $F_1,F_2\subseteq X$ closed, one has $X=F_1$ or $X=F_2$.

For a Noetherian topological space $T$, define $\dim T$ as the supremum of the lengths $s$ of strict chains $Z_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq Z_s$ of nonempty irreducible closed subsets of $T$. Thus a one-member chain has length zero. Set $\dim\varnothing=-\infty$, and allow $\dim T=+\infty$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement. > Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function > ([[def-choice-function]]). Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty, there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring. Then the iterated polynomial ring
$R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ of [[def-multivariate-polynomial-ring-by-iteration]] is
Noetherian for every $n\in\mathbb N$.
Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring and let $A$ be a commutative $R$-algebra of finite type ([[def-finite-type-and-module-finite-algebras]]). Then $A$ is a Noetherian ring.
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring. Then $\operatorname{Spec}(R)$ is a Noetherian topological space.

derivations.claim: The ring $R$ has dimension $3$ by [L1], and $0\subsetneq(x_0)\subsetneq(x_0,x_1)\subsetneq\mathfrak m$ is a strict chain of primes of $R$: each displayed ideal is prime, since the successive quotients are $k[x_1,x_2]$, $k[x_1]$, $k$ and polynomial rings over a domain are domains by [L2]. Hence $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak m)\ge3$, while $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak m)\le\dim R=3$ because chains of primes below $\mathfrak m$ are chains of primes of $R$; so $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak m)=3$, and every prime $P\subsetneq\mathfrak m$ satisfies $\operatorname{ht}(P)+1\le\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak m)$, that is, $\operatorname{ht}(P)\le2$. Finally, every proper homogeneous prime $P$ of $R$ lies in $\mathfrak m$ by [L3].

Let $\mathfrak q\subseteq R$ be a prime with $(F,G)\subseteq\mathfrak q$. Then $\mathfrak q\ne0$ because $F\in\mathfrak q$ and $F\ne0$, so $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak q)\ge1$ by the chain $0\subsetneq\mathfrak q$ of primes of the domain $R$; if $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak q)=1$, then $\mathfrak q$ is a height-one prime containing both $F$ and $G$, contradicting [L4]. Hence every prime of $R$ containing $(F,G)$ has height at least two.

By [L3] the primes of $S=R/(F,G)$ correspond inclusion-preservingly to the primes of $R$ containing $(F,G)$, and homogeneous primes to homogeneous primes; moreover the irrelevant ideal is $S_+=\mathfrak m/(F,G)$. Hence for a prime $\mathfrak q\subseteq S$ with preimage $Q\subseteq R$ one has $S_+\nsubseteq\mathfrak q$ if and only if $\mathfrak m\nsubseteq Q$; since a proper homogeneous prime $Q$ of $R$ satisfies $Q\subseteq\mathfrak m$ by 1.1, this is equivalent to $Q\subsetneq\mathfrak m$.

By [L9], $R$ is Noetherian. The ideal $(F,G)$ is proper because positive-degree homogeneous forms lie in $\mathfrak m=(x_0,x_1,x_2)\ne R$. Let $\mathfrak P$ be a prime minimal over $(F,G)$, which exists by [L5]. Then $\mathfrak P$ is homogeneous. Indeed, let $\mathfrak P'$ be the ideal generated by all homogeneous elements of $\mathfrak P$; it is a homogeneous ideal with $(F,G)\subseteq\mathfrak P'\subseteq\mathfrak P$, since $F,G$ are homogeneous elements of $\mathfrak P$. It is prime: for homogeneous $a,b$ with $ab\in\mathfrak P'$ we have $ab\in\mathfrak P$, so $a\in\mathfrak P$ or $b\in\mathfrak P$, hence $a\in\mathfrak P'$ or $b\in\mathfrak P'$; an ideal generated by homogeneous elements with this property is prime, because for arbitrary $x,y$ with $xy\in\mathfrak P'$ one inducts on $\deg_{\max}(x)+\deg_{\max}(y)$, where $\deg_{\max}$ is the largest degree of a homogeneous component: the components of top degree $d$ of $x$ and $e$ of $y$ multiply to the top-degree component $x_dy_e\in\mathfrak P'$, so $x_d\in\mathfrak P'$ or $y_e\in\mathfrak P'$, and in the first case $(x-x_d)y\in\mathfrak P'$ with $\deg_{\max}(x-x_d)<d$ gives $x-x_d\in\mathfrak P'$ or $y\in\mathfrak P'$ by induction, whence $x\in\mathfrak P'$ or $y\in\mathfrak P'$, the other case being symmetric. Thus $\mathfrak P'$ is a prime containing $(F,G)$ and contained in $\mathfrak P$, so minimality forces $\mathfrak P'=\mathfrak P$ and $\mathfrak P$ is homogeneous. By 1.2, $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak P)\ge2$, and by the Noetherian Krull height theorem in [L5] applied to the two generators $F,G$ we have $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak P)\le2$, so $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak P)=2$; since $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak m)=3$ by 1.1, the inclusion $\mathfrak P\subseteq\mathfrak m$ of 1.1 is strict: $\mathfrak P\subsetneq\mathfrak m$.

Every standard chart ring $A_i$ is either zero or of Krull dimension $0$. By [L6] the primes of $A_i$ correspond inclusion-preservingly to the homogeneous primes of $S$ avoiding $x_i$, so it suffices to rule out a strict chain $\mathfrak p_0\subsetneq\mathfrak p_1$ of homogeneous primes of $S$ with $x_i
otin\mathfrak p_1$. By 2.1 such a chain lifts to homogeneous primes $P_0\subsetneq P_1$ of $R$ containing $(F,G)$ and, since $x_i$ lies in neither $\mathfrak p_j$, with $x_i
otin P_1$. Then $\operatorname{ht}(P_0)\ge2$ by 1.2; on the other hand $P_1$ is a proper homogeneous prime with $P_1
e\mathfrak m$, so $P_1\subsetneq\mathfrak m$ by 1.1 and $\operatorname{ht}(P_1)\le2$; and $\operatorname{ht}(P_0)+1\le\operatorname{ht}(P_1)$ by [L1]. Hence $2\le\operatorname{ht}(P_0)<\operatorname{ht}(P_1)\le2$, a contradiction. Therefore $A_i$ admits no strict chain of two primes.

By 2.2 the prime $\mathfrak P$ is homogeneous with $\mathfrak P\subsetneq\mathfrak m$ and $(F,G)\subseteq\mathfrak P$, so by 2.1 its image $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak P/(F,G)$ is a homogeneous prime of $S$ with $S_+\nsubseteq\mathfrak p$; hence $\mathfrak p$ is a point of $X$ by [L6] and $X\ne\varnothing$.

$\dim S=1$. For the lower bound, $\mathfrak P\subsetneq\mathfrak m$ from 2.2 gives via 2.1 a strict chain of primes of $S$, so $\dim S\ge1$ and $S\ne0$. For the upper bound, suppose $\mathfrak q_0\subsetneq\mathfrak q_1\subsetneq\mathfrak q_2$ is a strict chain of primes of $S$; by 2.1 it lifts to primes $Q_0\subsetneq Q_1\subsetneq Q_2$ of $R$ all containing $(F,G)$. By 2.2 we have $\operatorname{ht}(Q_0)\ge2$, so there is a strict chain of length two of primes below $Q_0$; adjoining $Q_0\subsetneq Q_1\subsetneq Q_2$ gives a strict chain of length $4$ in $R$, contradicting $\dim R=3$ from 1.1. Hence $\dim S=1$, and in particular $S$ is not zero-dimensional: it is also not Artinian, because in an Artinian ring every prime is maximal ([[thm-artinian-ring-primes-are-maximal]]), which would force $\dim S=0$.

By [L10], $X$ is Noetherian, so its chain dimension in [L7] is defined. $X$ has no strict chain $Z_0\subsetneq Z_1$ of nonempty irreducible closed subsets. Suppose such a chain is given. Some standard chart $D=D_+(x_i)$ meets $Z_0$, since the charts cover $X$ by [L6]; then the subsets $W_j=Z_j\cap D$ of the affine chart $D=\operatorname{Spec}(A_i)$ are nonempty, closed in $D$, and satisfy $W_0\subseteq W_1$. A nonempty open subset $U$ of an irreducible space $Z$ is irreducible and dense: if $U=F_1\cup F_2$ with $F_1,F_2$ closed in $U$, then $Z=\overline{F_1}\cup\overline{F_2}\cup(Z\setminus U)$ is a union of closed subsets, so irreducibility of $Z$ forces one of the three to equal $Z$, and since $Z\setminus U\ne Z$ while $\overline{F_k}\cap U=F_k$, this gives $F_1=U$ or $F_2=U$; and if the closure of $U$ in $Z$ were a proper closed subset, then $Z=\overline U\cup(Z\setminus U)$ would be a union of two proper closed subsets. Applying this to the open subset $W_j$ of the irreducible space $Z_j$ shows that $W_j$ is irreducible and dense in $Z_j$, hence that its closure in $X$ is $Z_j$; thus $W_0\ne W_1$, since $W_0=W_1$ would give $Z_0=Z_1$. The $W_j$ are nonempty irreducible closed subsets of $\operatorname{Spec}(A_i)$, so by [L7] their radical defining ideals are distinct primes and form a strict chain of two primes of $A_i$, contradicting 3.1. Hence no such chain $Z_0\subsetneq Z_1$ exists, and the chain dimension of $X$ is $0$.

Claim 1 is 3.2, claim 2 is 3.1 together with 4.1, and claim 3 is 3.3. The hypotheses actually used are: $F,G$ nonzero homogeneous of positive degrees with no common nonconstant factor, over an arbitrary field $k$; the Axiom of Choice enters only through the minimal-prime and height-theorem suppliers of [L5] the irreducible-closed-subset characterisation of [L7], and the Noetherian-spectrum supplier of [L10], and it is the standing assumption [L8]. Noetherianity of the chart rings is used in [L10] to justify the topological dimension convention in 4.1. Finiteness of $X$ is not assumed, and the minimal prime chosen in 2.2 is proved homogeneous rather than chosen inside the homogeneous locus.

citations.quote:
Let $k$ be a field, let $R=k[x_0,\ldots,x_n]$ carry the standard grading in
which every $x_i$ has degree one
([[def-graded-ring-and-graded-module]],
[[def-homogeneous-polynomial-and-homogeneous-ideal]]), let $I\subseteq R$ be a
homogeneous ideal, and put $S=R/I$ with the induced grading. Write

$$S_+=(x_0,\ldots,x_n)S=\bigoplus_{m\ge1}S_m$$

for the **irrelevant ideal** of $S$, generated by the images of the variables.

1. **Underlying set.** The **projective spectrum** $\operatorname{Proj}S$ has as
   its points the homogeneous prime ideals $\mathfrak p\subseteq S$ with
   $S_+\nsubseteq\mathfrak p$; equivalently $x_i\notin\mathfrak p$ for at least
   one $i$.
2. **Standard charts.** For each $i$ let $S_{x_i}$ be the localization of $S$ in
   which the powers of $x_i$ are inverted; it is a graded ring and its
   degree-zero part $(S_{x_i})_0$ is a $k$-algebra. The **standard chart**
   $D_+(x_i)$ is the affine scheme $\operatorname{Spec}\bigl((S_{x_i})_0\bigr)$
   with its structure sheaf ([[def-affine-scheme]]), whose sections on a
   distinguished open $D(a)$ are $((S_{x_i})_0)_a$.
   Concretely, $(S_{x_i})_0$ is the image of
   the subring of fractions of $S$ of total degree zero with denominator a power
   of $x_i$; in the polynomial case with $I=0$ it is the polynomial ring in the
   ratios $x_j/x_i$ for $j\ne i$.
3. **Overlaps and gluing.** For all $i,j$ the localizations $(S_{x_i})_0$ and
   $(S_{x_j})_0$ have the common localization $(S_{x_ix_j})_0$, obtained from
   either one by inverting the degree-zero ratio $x_j/x_i$ respectively
   $x_i/x_j$; these identifications of
   $\operatorname{Spec}\bigl((S_{x_ix_j})_0\bigr)$ with distinguished open
   subschemes of the two charts are isomorphisms of locally ringed spaces
   ([[lem-spectrum-localization-open-immersion]]). They are the transition
   isomorphisms, and they
   satisfy the identity and cocycle conditions because both composites are the
   canonical identification inside the double localization $S_{x_ix_jx_k}$. The
   affine schemes $D_+(x_i)$ therefore glue to a scheme
   $\operatorname{Proj}S$ ([[thm-gluing-affine-schemes]], [[def-scheme]]), the
   standard charts forming an open affine cover, with the points of part 1 as its
   underlying set and the subset $D_+(x_ix_j)\subseteq D_+(x_i)$ as the locus
   where $x_j/x_i$ is invertible.
4. **Conventions.** The construction is available over an arbitrary field $k$
   and for an arbitrary homogeneous ideal $I$, including a nonradical one; it
   makes $\operatorname{Proj}S$ a $k$-scheme locally of finite type, with
   residue fields $\kappa(\mathfrak p)=S_{(\mathfrak p)}/\mathfrak m_{(\mathfrak p)}$
   that need not equal $k$. Here $T$ is the multiplicative set of homogeneous
   elements of $S$ outside $\mathfrak p$, $S_{(\mathfrak p)}=(T^{-1}S)_0$,
   and $\mathfrak m_{(\mathfrak p)}=(T^{-1}\mathfrak p)_0$ is its maximal
   ideal: a degree-zero fraction with numerator outside $\mathfrak p$ has its
   inverse by interchanging numerator and denominator. It is not the same object as the classical
   projective algebraic set of [[def-projective-space-points]], which is defined
   over an algebraically closed field and is reduced: the classical set records
   only the $\bar k$-points of the reduced subscheme, while
   $\operatorname{Proj}S$ retains the scheme structure on its charts, including any
   nilpotents that survive localization. When $k$ is algebraically closed and $I$ is radical, the closed
   points of $\operatorname{Proj}S$ correspond to the points of $V_+(I)$ in the
   classical sense; that dictionary is not asserted here.

For the empty case: if $S_+=0$, that is, if the images of all $x_i$ vanish in
$S$, then $S$ has no homogeneous prime avoiding $S_+$ and
$\operatorname{Proj}S=\varnothing$; every $D_+(x_i)=\operatorname{Spec}0$ is
empty, consistently with the gluing. In particular
$\operatorname{Proj}\bigl(k[x_0,\ldots,x_n]/(x_0,\ldots,x_n)\bigr)=\varnothing$.

Let $k$ be a field, let $S=k[x_0,\ldots,x_n]/I$ be a standard graded quotient in which the images of the variables have degree one, and let $X=\operatorname{Proj}S$ have standard charts $D_+(x_i)=\operatorname{Spec}(A_i)$ with $A_i=(S_{x_i})_0$, as in [[def-projective-scheme-from-a-homogeneous-quotient]].

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $A$ be a commutative $R$-algebra with structure map $\eta_A\colon R\to A$ ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). **The subalgebra generated by finitely many elements.** Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in A$.

A **composition series** of a left $R$-module $M$ is a finite chain $$0=M_0<M_1<\cdots<M_n=M$$ whose factors $M_i/M_{i-1}$ are simple. If such a series exists, the **length** $\ell_R(M)$ is its number $n$ of factors; [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]] proves independence of the chosen series.
A left $R$-module $M$ is **simple** if $M\ne0$ and its only submodules are $0$ and $M$. Equivalently, $M$ has no proper nonzero submodule.

Let $k$ be a field and let $A$ be a nonzero finite-type $k$-algebra. Then there exist algebraically independent elements $z_1,\ldots,z_d\in A$ such that $A$ is a module-finite algebra over the polynomial ring $k[z_1,\ldots,z_d]$.

Let $A\subseteq B$ be commutative rings with $A\ne0$, and let $b\in B$. The following are equivalent: $b$ is integral over $A$; $A[b]$ is finitely generated as an $A$-module; and there exists a faithful $A[b]$-module that is finitely generated over $A$, where faithful means that $rM=0$ implies $r=0$ for $r\in A[b]$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f:A\to B$ be an integral ring map, and let $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}(A)$ with $\ker f\subseteq\mathfrak p$. Then there exists a prime ideal $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}(B)$ such that $f^{-1}(\mathfrak q)=\mathfrak p$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f:A\to B$ be an integral ring map, let $$ \mathfrak p_0\subseteq\mathfrak p_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\mathfrak p_n $$ be a finite chain of prime ideals in $A$, and let $\mathfrak q_0$ be a prime ideal of $B$ with $f^{-1}(\mathfrak q_0)=\mathfrak p_0$.
If $R$ is an integral domain, then $R[x]$ is an integral domain.
$R/P$ is an integral domain if and only if $P$ is a prime ideal. Here $R$ is commutative and $P\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}R$ is an ideal.
A unital ring $R$ is **left Artinian** when ${}_R R$ is Artinian, and **right Artinian** when $R_R$ is Artinian. Unqualified “Artinian ring” means left Artinian here.
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). In a nonzero commutative ring, every proper ideal is contained in a maximal ideal.
Let $R$ be a commutative Artinian ring. Then $R$ has only finitely many maximal ideals. This theorem uses dependent choice only through the minimum condition for Artinian modules.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a commutative Artinian ring. If $R=0$, then it has no maximal ideals. Otherwise let $\mathfrak m_1,\ldots,\mathfrak m_r$ be its maximal ideals. Then the canonical localization map $$ R\longrightarrow \prod_{i=1}^r R_{\mathfrak m_i} $$ is an isomorphism.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement. > Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function > ([[def-choice-function]]). Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty, there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

derivations.claim: Each $A_i$ is generated as a $k$-algebra by the finitely many ratios $x_j/x_i$, $j\ne i$, computed in $S_{x_i}$: an element of $A_i$ has the form $s/x_i^e$ with $s\in S$ homogeneous of degree $e$, the degree-$e$ piece of $S$ is spanned by the images of the monomials $x_0^{a_0}\cdots x_n^{a_n}$ with $a_0+\cdots+a_n=e$, and such a monomial satisfies $x_0^{a_0}\cdots x_n^{a_n}/x_i^e=\prod_{j\ne i}(x_j/x_i)^{a_j}$. Hence each $A_i$ is a finitely generated $k$-algebra, and $A_i=0$ exactly when the chart $D_+(x_i)$ is empty; by [L1] the finitely many nonempty charts cover $X$.

If $C$ is a finite-dimensional $k$-algebra, every $C$-submodule of $C$ is a $k$-subspace, and a strict inclusion of $C$-submodules strictly raises $k$-dimension. Starting with $C_0=C$, if $C_j\ne0$, choose a proper $C$-submodule $C_{j+1}\subsetneq C_j$ of largest possible $k$-dimension; $0$ is one candidate, and the possible dimensions lie in the finite set $\{0,\ldots,\dim_k C_j-1\}$. No submodule lies strictly between $C_{j+1}$ and $C_j$, since it would have larger dimension, so $C_j/C_{j+1}$ is simple. The dimensions strictly decrease, hence the process reaches $0$ in at most $\dim_kC$ steps and gives a composition series of $C$-modules. Thus $\ell_C(C)\le\dim_kC$. A flag of arbitrary $k$-basis spans would not suffice, because those spans need not be $C$-submodules.

If $A_i\ne0$, then by [L4] there are algebraically independent $z_1,\ldots,z_d\in A_i$ such that $A_i$ is module-finite over $B=k[z_1,\ldots,z_d]$. The inclusion $B\subseteq A_i$ is then integral by [L5] and has zero kernel, so the kernel hypothesis of lying over is satisfied for $(0)$. If $d\ge1$, then $(0)\subsetneq(z_1)$ is a strict chain of primes of $B$ by [L7], lying over [L6] gives a prime $\mathfrak q_0$ of $A_i$ contracting to $(0)$, and the chain-lifting part of [L6] produces a prime $\mathfrak q_1\supseteq\mathfrak q_0$ contracting to $(z_1)$; since the two contractions differ, $\mathfrak q_0\ne\mathfrak q_1$, so $A_i$ contains a strict chain of two primes, contradicting $\dim A_i=0$. Hence $d=0$, so $B=k$ and $A_i$ is a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space. In particular $A_i$ is Artinian by [L8]: a strictly descending chain of ideals of $A_i$ is a strictly descending chain of $k$-subspaces, and every strict inclusion strictly lowers the $k$-dimension, so no infinite strictly descending chain exists.

Let $A_i\ne0$. By 2.1 it is Artinian, and its primes are maximal: a prime $\mathfrak p$ is contained in some maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ by [L8], and $\mathfrak p\subsetneq\mathfrak m$ would be a strict chain of two primes, contradicting $\dim A_i=0$. There are therefore only finitely many primes, they are the maximal ideals $\mathfrak m_{i,1},\ldots,\mathfrak m_{i,r_i}$ of $A_i$, and the structure theorem [L8] gives an isomorphism $A_i\cong\prod_j(A_i)_{\mathfrak m_{i,j}}$, under which the factor $(A_i)_{\mathfrak m_{i,j}}$ is a quotient of the finite-dimensional $k$-algebra $A_i$, hence finite-dimensional, local as a localization at a maximal ideal, and has nilpotent maximal ideal because $A_i\cong\prod_jA_i/\mathfrak m_{i,j}^{n_j}$. The points of the chart $\operatorname{Spec}(A_i)$ are exactly these maximal ideals by [L1].

$X$ has finitely many points, all closed, whence its underlying space is finite and discrete. The charts are finitely many and each chart has the finitely many points $\mathfrak m_{i,1},\ldots,\mathfrak m_{i,r_i}$ of 3.1, so $X$ is finite. A subset $Z\subseteq X$ is closed exactly when every trace $Z\cap D_+(x_i)$ is closed in $D_+(x_i)$, because the charts are an open cover; for a point $x\in X$ the trace is empty whenever $x\notin D_+(x_i)$, and otherwise it is the singleton $\{x\}\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}(A_i)$, which is closed because $x$ corresponds to a maximal ideal of $A_i$ by 3.1. Hence every point of $X$ is closed, and in a finite space with all points closed every subset is a finite union of closed points, so the space is discrete.

Let $x\in X$ and let $D_+(x_i)$ be any standard chart containing it. By 3.1 the point corresponds to a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ of the chart ring $A_i$, and by [L1] we have $\mathcal O_{X,x}\cong(A_i)_{\mathfrak m}$. By 3.1 this factor is a finite-dimensional local $k$-algebra with nilpotent maximal ideal and is a quotient of $A_i$; its residue field is $A_i/\mathfrak m$, a quotient of the finite-dimensional $k$-algebra $A_i$, hence finite-dimensional over $k$; and it has finite length as a module over itself by 1.2. The same description holds for every chart containing $x$, and different charts give isomorphic local rings by the overlap statement in [L1].

Let $A_i\ne0$. With the notation of step 3.1, write $A_i\cong\prod_jB_j$ where $B_j=(A_i)_{\mathfrak m_{i,j}}$. If $e_j$ is the coordinate idempotent of this product, a prime contains all but exactly one $e_j$: two omitted idempotents would have product zero, contrary to primality, and all cannot belong to a proper ideal because their sum is $1$. Thus every prime comes from one factor $B_j$. The maximal ideal of each local factor is nilpotent by step 3.1, so every prime contains it and must equal it; each factor has exactly one prime. Hence $\operatorname{Spec}(A_i)$ is the disjoint union of the spectra of the factors. By [L1] and step 3.1 each $B_j$ is the local ring $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ at the corresponding point $x$, so $\operatorname{Spec}(A_i)=\bigsqcup_{x\in D_+(x_i)}\operatorname{Spec}(\mathcal O_{X,x})$. For a point lying in two charts, [L1] identifies the point and the two local rings, so the decompositions agree on the overlap; since the standard charts cover $X$, this glues them into the finite disjoint union of the spectra of the local rings at all points of $X$.

Claim 1 is 1.1 and 3.1, claim 2 is 4.1, claim 3 is 4.2, and claim 4 is 4.3. The zero-dimensional hypothesis was used only through the chart rings $A_i$; the Axiom of Choice enters in the lying-over and chain-lifting suppliers of [L6], in the maximal-ideal and Artinian-structure suppliers of [L8], and it is the standing assumption [L9]. No finiteness of $X$ or Noetherianity was assumed in advance.
